News.title: North Korean ‘women slave labourers’ arrive in Russia as 50k of Kim Jong-Un’s cannon fodder fighters prepare to join war
News.content:
FEMALE “slaves” have arrived in Russia as Kim Jong-Un sends 50,000 fighters to boost Putin’s war machine.

Uniformed workers in crisp white shirts from North Korea have crossed into Russian territory to work on assembly lines, in kitchens, and on farms for pathetic wages.



The women are paid notionally around £4.36 an hour with some of their earnings reportedly siphoned off to the North Korean state.

This has led to allegations they are treated as “slaves”.



It comes amid reports Kim Jong-Un deployed troops, weapons and a missile unit to bolster Russia in the war.

Stringent rules for the new influx of North Koreans dictate that they must be employed in groups of 40.



The women are strictly segregated and remain under the strict control and supervision of male minders from Pyongyang.

Their documents are confiscated and they have no right to free movement inside Russia.



The arrival of the army of women to boost Russia’s wartime economy comes as Volodymyr Zelensky has warned Putin is recruiting up to 50,000 North Korean men to fight against Ukraine.

Footage shows these Kim troops “undergoing training in Russia for assaults on Ukraine”.

Far-right Russian propagandist Vladislav Pozdnyakov claimed – citing unspecified GRU-military intelligence linked propaganda outlets – that tens of thousands of North Korean troops were already in Russia awaiting fresh assault operations.



He said the “North Korean missiles” would soon be “launched on Kim’s orders.”

The reportedly sighting of the Pyongyang soldiers comes after Ukraine’s GUR military intelligence agency claimed a unit of 90 soldiers equipped with 120 ballistic missiles and six launchers has been deployed to Russia.

The unit is being formed in Russia’s Voronezh region, a major strategic military and logistics hub in the southwest of the state.



Ukraine has alleged that on July 30 a North Korean-made ballistic missile allegedly wiped out the family in Radushne, near Kryvyi Rih.

Nine members of the Voronov family, including seven children, were killed.

South Korean intelligence believes the North reaped almost £10 billion from the previous deployment.

Since the beginning of the war, Kim Jong-un and his cronies have sent tens of thousands of workers overseas to replace Russians killed or wounded in the invasion of Ukraine.

Between 2,000 and 3,000 North Koreans are believed to have been killed in the war, mainly in Kursk region where they fought off a Ukrainian invasion of Putin’s territory.



Referring to Kim’s fighters, Zelensky said: “A decision has been made for between 30,000 and 50,000 North Koreans to be on the territory of Russia.”

The war has seen Russia and North Korea forging closer ties, with fears Putin’s missile and nuclear knowhow is being transferred to Pyongyang.

In March, The Sun revealed the deplorable conditions North Korean men are forced to endure when they move to Russia for work.

Packed side by side, they sleep under constant watch before being awoken by a loudspeaker for their shift that could last up to 16 hours a day, seven days a week.

The men have no holiday and no day’s off and sleep on stiff plywood bunks in cockroach-infested huts.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

The forced labour system has been introduced as Russia becomes more and more desperate for manpower after Russian men are deployed en masse to die on the frontline.

Testimonies, shared in a report by Global Rights Compliance, say the labour system operates under a routine of “control, abuse and coercion.”

News.title: Is the A31 still closed? Latest on the New Forest fire after blaze near Ringwood closes road
News.content:
A LORRY fire broke out on Sunday evening and spread into the New Forest, causing significant disruption to a major road.

The blaze meant that the A31 near Ringwood had to be closed in both directions – here’s everything you need to know about the latest.



Is the A31 still closed?

The A31 remains closed in both directions on Monday morning, with drivers facing lengthy diversions and delays.

National Highways said: “The road is likely to be closed into the day, and at this stage there is no estimated time for re-opening.”



The westbound carriageway is closed between M27 junction 2 at Ower and the A338 at Ringwood.

Eastbound traffic can’t use the stretch between the A338 and M27 junction 1 at Cadnam.



National Highways contractors have found significant damage to the road surface and safety barrier, as well as an oil spill from the burnt-out vehicle.

National Highways has described the fire as a “major incident” after it moved beyond the vehicle and into surrounding land.

Its contractors remain at the scene alongside emergency services.

Drivers have been warned to avoid the area, follow the official diversion and allow extra time for their journeys.



What caused the New Forest fire near Ringwood?

Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Service received more than 160 emergency calls at around 5.24pm on Sunday, August 9, reporting a vehicle fire on the eastbound A31.

The flames spread to the central reservation before reaching nearby heathland.

Crews from across Hampshire were sent to the scene, supported by firefighters from Dorset and Wiltshire.

The response included 26 fire engines, four water carriers, six off-road vehicles and multiple command vehicles.

Firefighters continued tackling the blaze throughout the night and warned they would maintain a significant presence in the area for the “foreseeable future”.



The fire service said countryside fires can be particularly challenging, especially when crews need to secure sufficient water for the incident.

It plans to use a high-volume pump to draw water from Hightown Lake in Ringwood and carry it to the fire.

A long hose may have to run across or through some private properties, with affected residents due to be contacted directly.

No properties currently need to be evacuated, although the fire service said households would be contacted if that changed.

The fire service said: “Please follow diversion signs, allow extra time for your journey and avoid the area to allow emergency crews to work safely.”



A firefighter was also overheard telling a police officer: “We want all the cars and people off the carriageway. Unattended cars are basically bombs when they go off.”

What is the A31 diversion route?

Westbound motorists should leave the M27 at junction 2 (Ower Interchange) and use the A326 and A35 through Ashurst, Lyndhurst and Christchurch.

They should then take the A3060 and travel north on the A338 to rejoin the A31 at Ashley Heath.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Eastbound drivers should leave the A31 at the Ashley Heath roundabout onto the A338, then take the A3060 and A35 before joining the A326 north to M27 junction 2 (Ower Interchange).

With firefighting and road repairs both continuing, anyone travelling between Southampton, the New Forest, Ringwood and Bournemouth should prepare for disruption.

News.title: Swimmer, 24, dies after being pulled from sea at popular UK beach
News.content:
BEACH TRAGEDY Swimmer, 24, dies after being pulled from sea at popular UK beach

A 24-YEAR-OLD man has tragically died after being pulled from the water following a huge search operation at a UK beach.

Emergency services launched their frantic search at Camber Sands, East Sussex, following reports three people had gotten into difficulty in the water last night.

A Coastguard helicopter, rescue teams and lifeboat were deployed to the area alongside police and paramedics as crews worked to rescue the struggling swimmers.

Two people who entered the water, a 16-year-old boy and an 18-year-old man, safely made their way out of the water.





A 24-year-old man was later rescued at around 7pm and was tragically pronounced dead at the scene, despite the best efforts of paramedics.

His family have been informed of the tragedy as police conduct enquiries into the sad death.

A spokesman for Sussex Police said: “Just before 7pm on Sunday (August 9), emergency services were called to Camber Sands Beach in Rye, after it was reported that three people had got into difficulty after entering the water.

“A large search operation was conducted and two of the three, a 16-year-old boy and an 18-year-old man, safely exited the water.

“A third man, aged 24, was pulled from the water at around 7.30pm.

“Sadly, despite lifesaving attempts by paramedics at the scene, he was pronounced deceased a short while later.

“His next of kin have been informed, and our thoughts are with them.

“Enquiries in the area remain ongoing, and an increased emergency presence is visible at this time.”



A spokesman for the coastguard said: “At 6.37pm last night, HM Coastguard was called to an incident at Camber Sands, East Sussex.

“An HM Coastguard Search and Rescue Helicopter was sent, along with Pett Level lifeboat, Coastguard Rescue Teams from Rye Bay and Romney Marsh, Sussex Police and South East Coast Ambulance Service.”

News.title: Daniel Kinahan wakes up in max security Irish prison cell charged with directing crime organisation after life in Dubai
News.content:
A MAN accused of being an organised crime boss has woken up in an Irish jail after several years of living in Dubai.

Daniel Kinahan, 49, was flown to Ireland on an Irish Government jet on Sunday, and immediately taken by high-speed Garda escort to court in Dublin.



He was last night charged with directing the activities of a criminal organisation.

With no legal representation, the Dublin man was remanded into custody and transferred to the maximum-security Portlaoise Prison in the Irish midlands.



Kinahan was brought to Portlaoise by Gardai who drove in a convoy of BMWs and was admitted to the A-block.

Some of the most high-profile residents in the prison and others facing trial at the Special Criminal Court are housed in the wing.

Sources say that Gerard Cruise, serving a seven-year sentence for his logistical role in the run up and after the murder of Drogheda teenager Keane Mulready Woods in 2020, was moved out of a cell to make way for Kinahan in Unit 4 of Ireland’s most secure jail block.

The cell was “refreshed” according to sources, cleaned and given a fresh lick of paint.



Kinahan, alleged to be a leader of the Kinahan organised crime group, was arrested in the United Arab Emirates on April 15 on foot of an arrest warrant issued by the Irish courts.

This was carried out in accordance with a bilateral agreement on extradition between Ireland and the UAE.

After the plane left Dubai on Sunday, the justice ministers for Ireland and the UAE welcomed the extradition in a joint statement.

Jim O’Callaghan and Abdullah bin Sultan bin Awad Al Nuaimi said the Irish national being extradited was “regarded as one of the most high-profile individuals sought for prosecution in connection with transnational organised crime”.

They confirmed the extradition after a formal request submitted by Irish authorities, and the final decision was issued after a judgment by the Dubai Court of Cassation, in accordance with the extradition treaty between the two countries.



The two ministers added that the final extradition decision “reflects the steadfast commitment of both countries to the rule of law and reinforces international judicial co-operation”.

Crowds gathered outside both the Casement Aerodrome in Baldonnel on the outskirts of Dublin yesterday for the landing of the plane, and the Special Criminal Court, to try to get a glimpse of Mr Kinahan.

They watched two separate high speed convoys pass by, in an additional precaution, to transport the man believed to have been the target of a gun attack at a boxing weigh-in in Dublin in 2016.

Inside the court room, the dock was checked by gardai before Kinahan appeared, alongside several other gardai, for a hearing which lasted about 14 minutes.

At the judge-led hearing, Judge Fiona Lydon, Judge Patrick McGrath and Ms Justice Sarah Berkeley sat in the court which tries terrorism and organised crime cases.



Kinahan told the court he had been isolated from Friday afternoon, adding that he believed a family member would have contacted a legal representative on his behalf, and he was happy to proceed.

He did not react after being charged with directing the activities of a criminal organisation between October 18 2015 and April 6 2017.

Detective Sergeant Colin Davidson told the court that he had arrested Kinahan on foot of an arrest warrant issued by the Irish courts at Casement Aerodrome in Baldonnel at 6.49pm that day.

He said he ensured that the accused understood the charge.

Judge McGrath told Kinahan when the case would next be heard, and explained to him that because of the charge an application for bail would have to be made to the High Court.



Mr Kinahan said: “I understand. I think we know I won’t be getting bail, but thank you.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He will next appear in court on October 5, and was told that he has the option of either attending in person or appearing via video link.

He said he would decide later.

News.title: Months-old baby seen being hauled onto Channel migrant mega-dinghy to UK – as French police stand by and do nothing
News.content:
A MONTHS-old baby was seen being hauled aboard a packed mega-dinghy bound for UK shores as French cops stood by and did nothing.

Dozens of migrants, including several young children, crowded onto the inflatable boat as tourists and police watched on from a nearby beach.



Multiple young children, including a months-old baby, were seen being dragged onto the taxi boat at pit stops along the French coast.

Officers reportedly threatened to arrest a photographer who captured them standing by and doing nothing.



The small boat had been closely tracked by French authorities for nine-and-a-half hours as it picked up passengers along the coastline.

It appeared to have been launched near the Normandy fishing port of Dieppe – much further south than where the boats usually leave.



People-smuggling gangs are said to be using new launch sites to evade police detection.

The boat was followed up the shore by a French coastguard vessel, but only in case it sunk.



After 40 miles, the dinghy stopped at Berck beach, before travelling another 12 miles to Camiers beach.

There, photographer Ioannis Alexopoulos saw a group of migrants emerge from behind the dunes and make for the boat.

Alexopoulos captured shocking pictures of young children being taken on board, including a baby who was too small to wear a life jacket.



He said: “Three police turned up, gendarmes in military clothes – but all they did was film, and threaten to arrest me if I kept taking pictures.”

The migrants headed to the UK where they were picked up in the channel by a British Border Security Command vessel and taken to Dover.

They are just a small portion of more than 2,000 who have crossed the channel since Andy Burnham became Prime Minister three weeks ago.

It comes as the government admits criminal smuggling gangs could rapidly change tactics and wipe out progress on cutting small boat crossings.

Crossings are down 43 per cent year on year because of a crackdown on dinghies reaching beaches and increased enforcement on smugglers running the routes.



But the new Border Security Commander Duncan Capps, a former Army officer, has admitted in his first annual report that the progress is “not definitive”.

Despite the dip in crossings, the number of migrants in northern France ready and waiting for a chance to come to the UK has not changed.

Maj Gen Capps wrote: “Recent numbers are positive. But this could change rapidly.”

“Particularly given the likelihood that organised criminal gangs will adapt their tactics and seek to drive renewed flows.

“Especially over the summer months when conditions are more favourable.



“We have steadily forced organised crime groups into a less advantageous position.

“But we should be prepared for them to innovate to protect their profits.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

As of early August, 14,561 people have crossed the Channel in small boats this year.

A Home Office source insisted that new policies were “beginning to bear fruit” but “we are not complacent”.

News.title: Cops hunt man, 40, and blue van after dad, 56, attacked & ‘murdered’ in ‘violent’ street brawl – as 10 arrested
News.content:
FATAL BRAWL Cops hunt man, 40, and blue van after dad, 56, attacked & ‘murdered’ in ‘violent’ street brawl – as 10 arrested

A MAN and a blue van are wanted by police after a dad was allegedly murdered in a violent street brawl.

Anthony Paul Jones, 40, is wanted in connection with the chaos that took place in Pontnewynydd, Wales at around 7.15pm on August 6 which has led to the arrests of ten men.



Police rushed to the scene following reports of a violent brawl on Mill Street in Gwent.

Anthony “Tony” Jones, 56, from Brecon, was found badly injured before dying a few days later in hospital.



His family are being supported by specialist officers.

A further three men were also taken to hospital, with two said to be critically injured.

Jones’ death sparked a murder probe.

Cops have also launched a manhunt for Anthony Paul Jones, from Blaenavon, Torfaen, as they believe he can assist with the investigation.



Cops are also searching for a blue Ford Transit van, with the registration MA23 FLC, which was reportedly involved in the disorder.

Ten men, aged 31, 33, 34, 39, 40, 40, 45, 59, 61 and 73, have also been arrested in connection with the violence, and three men aged 39, 45 and 61 have since been released on bail.

Seven men remain in custody as police continue their enquiries.

Senior investigating officer, Detective Superintendent Laura Bartley said: “We recognise that reports of this nature will cause concern in our communities, but our officers are working around the clock and conducting enquiries as part of this live investigation.

“We’re trying to establish the movements of those involved both before and after the disorder and are asking motorists who were driving along Hospital Road, Mill Road and the surrounding areas between 6pm and 9pm on Thursday to check their dashcam footage.



“Our thoughts remain with the family and friends of the victim.”

Anyone with information on Anthony Paul Jones, or the blue Ford Transit van’s whereabouts, has been urged to submit information via the Major Incident Public Portal or contact police quoting log reference 2600255536.

You can also call on 101 or direct message them on Facebook or X social media pages.

Alternatively, you can call Crimestoppers, anonymously, with information on 0800 555 111 or visit online.

News.title: Woman in her 20s dies after car ploughs into parked street cleaner in late-night crash – as ‘uninsured’ driver arrested
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

FATAL CRASH Woman in her 20s dies after car ploughs into parked street cleaner in late-night crash – as ‘uninsured’ driver arrested

A WOMAN in her 20s who was a passenger in a Smart car was killed in a after the vehicle struck a street cleaning vehicle.

Tragically she was pronounced dead at the scene after the horror crash shortly before midnight on Wednesday last week.

Cops arrested the driver, a man in his 20s, on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving and driving over the prescribed limit.

He was also arrested on suspicion of failing to provide a specimen for analysis and causing death by driving while uninsured.





Cops are appealing for witnesses after the fatal smash in Epsom, Surrey, at around 11.40pm, to come forward.

Ththe victim’s next of kin have been informed.

Christ Church Road was closed for several hours while officers carried out their initial enquiries.

The road reopened shortly after 9.45am.



Cops are now urging anyone who was in the area between 11.35pm and 11.40pm to come forward.

Officers are particularly keen to hear from anyone who saw the black Smart car in the moments before the crash.

They are also appealing for anyone with CCTV, dashcam or helmet cam footage which may have captured all or part of the incident.

Anyone with information is urged to contact police.

News.title: Royal Navy drones secretly sent data to China through ‘heartbeat communications’ after years of Beijing spying fears
News.content:
SPY drones used by British special forces have been secretly sending data to China amid concerns over espionage from Beijing.

Cameras in the drones used by elite Navy forces contain components which were made in China and have reportedly been transmitting information back to Beijing.



The K3 Scout surveillance drones have been part of the Royal Marines’ £12million fleet since March.

After finding the breach, the Ministry of Defence has reportedly been forced to remove all internet connectivity from the cameras, the Telegraph reports.



The drones were from major British defence contractor Kraken Technology Group which sourced the cameras from a third party.

The third party is said to have given assurances about the equipment’s security.

After the breach was discovered, an investigation revealed that cameras were sending “heartbeat communications” to an IP address in China.

This data confirms the devices were online and functioning as they should be.

The MoD said no systems were compromised or transmitted externally.

A source said the drones had been part of the UK’s future defence package offered to help secure movement in the Strait of Hormuz.



They added that preparations had already been conducted on the drones and the find was a “major failure to check origins of components and we have lost confidence in the platform.”

A spokesperson for the MoD said: “The first duty of government is national security, and we take the security of our equipment, networks and data extremely seriously.

“A routine cyber vulnerability assessment identified an issue affecting a Kraken Unmanned Surface Vessel sub-system used by the Royal Navy.

“A thorough investigation found no evidence of MOD data or systems being accessed, compromised or transmitted externally.

“Our assurance and testing processes are designed to identify and address potential vulnerabilities early, and we continue to undertake routine security activity across our systems and equipment.”



This comes as the Labour Party tries to maintain relations with the Chinese Communist Party despite the looming threat the country poses.

Last month, a huge Chinese embassy was given the green light after a High Court challenge against the planning permission was dismissed.

The vast complex at Royal Mint Court, near the Tower of London, was approved despite concerns it could lead to terror attacks and the suppression of protests.

The Sun previously revealed that staff at British defence firms were told not to take phones to Wes Streeting’s first speech as Shadow Defence Secretary over fears of Chinese spying.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Streeting spoke at an arms fair packed with Chinese firms – including an electronic warfare specialist that lists signals “cracking” as a flagship service.



Workers at Britain’s List X defence firms – which hold secret government contracts – were advised to leave phones, tablets and other devices outside the exhibition hall where Streeting delivered his keynote address.

News.title: Nigel Farage live: Reform chief to unveil plan to remove foreign nationals from UK prisons to El Salvador jails
News.content:
Reform's nightmare situation as Farage political fortunes suffer

Mirror political correspondent Dave Burke writes inIt's a tricky time for Nigel Farage at the moment.

There are serious questions knocking around about his own and his party's finances, and it's clearly taking a toll. Polls show Reform are slipping while Labour enjoys a 'Burnham bounce'. How long that'll last for remains to be seen, but Mr Farage's personal ratings have also nosedived in recent weeks.

And things aren't looking that brilliant going forward, either. If he wins the farcical Clacton by-election - which he is almost certain to do - he goes back to a heap of problems in Westminster.

A Parliamentary standards probe into an undeclared £5million 'gift' he was given by Thailand-based tech billionaire Christopher Harborne is expected to reopen, and could trigger yet another contest in the coming months.

Last week he decided to try and get on the front foot with announcements on immigration, which is usually his safe space. But that proved to be a disaster.

His not-very-detailed plan to use the Royal Navy to stop small boats was shredded almost immediately by the French government, who said it would be a violation of its sovereignty. And Mr Farage's home affairs chief, Zia Yusuf, was brutally mocked for announcing firms who employ workers with no right to work in the UK would face jail terms under Reform.

The problem for him was that Labour has already brought in such a law. He was branded a "pillock" as a result.

Today Mr Farage is expected to announce plans to send foreign criminals overseas to serve their sentences. How much detail we'll get on how that works remains to be see, but according to reports talks will be held with El Salvador later this year.

Will it disintegrate as fast as last week's policies? The devil will be in the detail, but that scarcely matters for Mr Farage.

At the moment Reform needs headlines that aren't about sleaze, and the party leader will welcome any opportunity to get them.

News.title: Inheritance alert as '£200 mistake' could tear family apart
News.content:
Inheritance alert as '£200 mistake' could tear family apart

Experts have explained how to avoid problems at a difficult time

View 3 Images It can be an upsetting time (Image: Worawee Meepian via Getty Images)

Financial planners are warning of a £200 inheritance mistake that tears families apart and urging Brits to record which possessions they intend to leave to whom and why.

‌



The biggest inheritance rows aren't always over money – they can be over dad's watch, mum's jewellery or grandad's guitar. Financial planners are urging families to have open conversations about treasured possessions while loved ones are still alive, warning that casual promises made years or even decades earlier can easily be forgotten, misremembered or made to more than one person.

‌



Experts said those misunderstandings could leave grieving relatives locked in bitter disputes, even when the items themselves had relatively little financial value. Scott Gallacher, director at Leicester-based Rowley Turton, believes many of these disagreements could be avoided with clearer communication and better record-keeping.

‌



He said: "The biggest inheritance disagreements aren't always about money. They're often about the things people believed had already been promised to them.

"People don't usually set out to create family conflict. These situations arise because life is long. Conversations are forgotten, circumstances change and assumptions build up over decades."

View 3 Images Inheritance can be an emotional subject (Image: Suwatchai Wongaong via Getty Images)

‌



Mr Gallacher said an innocent comment such as, "one day, that'll be yours," could take on enormous significance, particularly if it related to a treasured family heirloom. However, years later, the person making the promise may have forgotten the conversation altogether – or even unknowingly promised the same item to somebody else.

He added: "The argument is rarely about what the object is worth. It's about what it represents."

To help prevent those disputes, Mr Gallacher has created a Promised Gifts Log, allowing people to record which sentimental possessions they intend to leave to specific family members and why.

‌



He said: "The log isn't intended to replace a will or legal advice. It is a practical way to stop an important conversation being forgotten and to give families a clearer record of what was intended."

Rob Mansfield, Independent Financial Adviser at Tonbridge-based Rootes Wealth Management, said writing wishes down was one of the simplest ways to avoid future conflict.

He added: "If it's not written down, it didn't happen, is such a great adage. If your possessions are being divided up, it's because you're no longer with us and so all your family have to go by is any instructions you've left them.

‌



"A promise years ago can easily be forgotten or misremembered. Situations like this can also bring out the worst in some family members and so being as clear as you can and documenting your wishes all help guard against that."

Harvey Dhillon, founder and CEO at Zmartly, said many of the most painful disputes never made it anywhere near a courtroom.

He added: "A will splits money, which divides neatly. It does not split the watch on dad's wrist. That is where families fall out. These rows are more common than the figures suggest, because most never get counted. Ministry of Justice figures show 127 contested probate cases in the High Court in England and Wales in 2025.

‌



"Only the ones that reach the High Court appear at all. Every argument settled in a kitchen, or never settled, is invisible. The reason low-value things cause the worst trouble is that nobody is arguing about the money. They are arguing about who was closest to the person who died. So say it out loud while everyone is in the room, then write it down.

"A log helps. List the item, who gets it, the reason, and the date. The date matters, because the same thing does get promised twice over thirty years. Keep the log beside the will, not instead of it. Only the will carries legal force. Write it down while you can still ask the person what they meant."

Nouran Moustafa, practice principal and IFA at Roxton Wealth, said sentimental possessions often carried far greater emotional weight than their price tag suggests.

‌



She added: "Sentimental possessions can cause more conflict than cash because families are not arguing over market value; they are arguing over memory, identity and what they believed the relationship meant. A £200 watch can carry more emotional weight than a £20,000 investment. The practical answer is to remove ambiguity early.

"Discuss important items openly, record who should receive them and why, and make sure those wishes do not contradict the will. A Promised Gifts Log is a strong idea, but it should include a clear description or photograph of the item, the intended recipient, the date, the reason and confirmation that the decision can be reviewed if circumstances change.

"It should support, not replace, properly drafted legal documents. Families should also revisit the record after major life events. The worst approach is relying on decades-old conversations and expecting grieving relatives to reconstruct someone’s intentions fairly."

‌



View 3 Images Nouran Moustafa (Image: Nouran Moustafa/Newspage)

David Stirling, Independent Financial Adviser at Belfast-based Mint Wealth, agreed that forgotten conversations were often at the heart of family disputes.

He added: "Disputes over sentimental possessions come up more often than people expect and almost always follow the same pattern. A promise made casually over Sunday lunch 30 years ago, genuinely meant at the time, either forgotten or repeated to someone else without realising it. Nobody is being dishonest.

Article continues below

"Life is just long, and the person who could settle it is no longer available to do so. The argument is never really about the object. It is about what the object represents, and that is a much harder thing to divide fairly. The practical answer is to write it down while you still can.

"A letter of wishes alongside a will, or a simple record of what you intend to leave to whom and why, removes the guesswork that causes lasting family damage. The why matters as much as the what. These conversations feel uncomfortable before someone dies, but they feel considerably worse after."

News.title: Wes Streeting gives classy response after radio caller's homophobic rant
News.content:
Wes Streeting gives classy response after radio caller's homophobic rant

Wes Streeting urged followers to 'be strong by being you' after a widely-shared clip showed a caller on LBC being branded a dinosaur after claiming there are 'too many gays in charge'

View Image Wes Streeting has said he is proud to be named the first gay Defence Secretary (Image: Getty Images)

Wes Streeting has hit back after a radio caller's homophobic rant questioning the decision to make him Defence Secretary.

‌



The Labour frontbencher urged followers to "be strong by being you" after a clip of the exchange was widely shared online. The caller, named John, was labeled a "dinosaur" and told he should be ashamed of himself by host Henry Riley.

‌



Mr Riley closed off the exchange by telling John to "give your head a wobble" after he claimed there were "too many gays in charge" and hit out at Mr Streeting.

‌



The Cabinet member, who was appointed to the new role by Andy Burnham, has previously revealed he has faced an "unbelievable" volume of homophobic abuse. He posted on X: "Water off a duck’s back. My message to every single young person who worries about encountering this sort of thing in their lives and careers is simple: we are stronger, they are weaker, and the future is brighter."

'Grotesque' abuse of migrant care workers laid bare in damning report READ MORE :

Content cannot be displayed without consent

In a follow-up post he wrote: "I also want to share something with those struggling with abuse because of who you are or who you love. It might feel hard now, but it gets better. You will build resilience and you will find - in time - strength from your experience. Be proud. Be strong by being you."

‌



During the exchange John said it was a "ridiculous idea to put him (Mr Streeting) in charge of the Ministry of Defence. Asked whether he thought the Defence Secretary was unqualified, he said: "No, it's because he's. gay, and he talks very camp."

Mr Riley responded: "John, you are an absolute dinosaur. You should be ashamed of yourself." The caller insisted Mr Streeting would not be taken seriously, the which the host said: "He's our Defence Secretary. He's one of the most competent politicians we actually have at the moment, whether you like him or not.

"You're seriously saying that because of his sexuality he's not going to be taken seriously? Not by idiots like you." John then whined about Mr Streeting's "camp way of speaking" before stating: "We've got too many gays in charge."

‌



Mr Riley hit back: "Thank God we haven't got any idiots like you in charge, John. Could you imagine what the state the country would be in if we had muppets like you in charge with complete dinosaur views?"

And he finished off by saying: "John, give your head a wobble, mate, yeah?" Mr Streeting was Health Secretary for nearly two years under Keir Starmer before resigning in protest over the former PM's leadership.

He accused Mr Starmer of lacking vision, and was touted as a possible contender for the top job before Mr Burnham re-entered Parliament.

Article continues below

Last week he said he had experienced an "unbelievable volume” of online homophobia since his appointment. Mr Streeting told the Edinburgh Fringe that some “cannot cope with the idea” of a gay Defence Secretary.

He said: "“I am proud of the fact that in my lifetime we’ve gone from gay people not being allowed to serve in the military to a gay defence secretary.

“And in my first week, someone in the MoD said to me, you know, as a gay man, I’m really proud that we have our first gay defence secretary, and it means a lot to many of us who remember the bad old days.”

News.title: Mum told baby boy would likely die – he now asks heart-wrenching question years later
News.content:
Mum told baby boy would likely die – he now asks heart-wrenching question years later

Frank Baziak, eight, from Malahide, was given just a 1% chance of survival as a newborn and now asks his parents 'Will I ever be healthy?' - as his family race to raise €1,000 for a medical report into his care

View 6 Images Frank Baziak has endured a difficult start to life (Image: Supplied)

A little boy told at birth he had just a 1% chance of making it through the night is now eight-years-old — but his fight is far from over. Now, Frank Baziak asks his parents a question they cannot bring themselves to answer: "Will I ever be healthy?"

‌



Frank, who lives in Dublin 13 near Malahide, has short bowel syndrome — a rare and life-limiting condition that the NHS describes as occurring when the small intestine does not work properly or a large portion of it is missing.

‌



In Frank's case, the consequences have been devastating. He has just 35cm of functioning intestine remaining, compared to up to 500cm that a healthy child his age would have. Without enough bowel to absorb the nutrients the body needs, patients like Frank must rely on intravenous feeding — sometimes for life.

‌



According to the NHS, short bowel syndrome can cause severe complications including malnutrition, dehydration, fatigue and a significantly weakened immune system — all of which Frank experiences.

He is fed through a central line and a PEG tube, and must be connected to Total Parenteral Nutrition (TPN) — a method of delivering nutrients directly into the bloodstream — every single day.

View 6 Images He and his family are desperate for answers and a GoFundMe has been set up (Image: Supplied)

‌



Frank's story was first told earlier this year, when his parents Anna and Marcin launched a GoFundMe campaign to fund a specialist medical report. Thanks in large part to the generosity of readers, more than €3,000 (approx £2,500) has already been raised — but time is running out. The family have been told they must secure the remaining €1,000 (approx £850) by the end of September, or their solicitor will be forced to abandon the case entirely.

Anna told us this week: "The initial response to the fundraiser and the story was really amazing, and we are incredibly grateful to everyone who supported us."

She added: "If we don't manage to raise the money by the end of September, all the work our solicitor has done so far could unfortunately come to nothing, as he would have to end his work on the case. It would be absolutely heartbreaking for all of us, but especially for Frank, because more than anything, he wants to finally understand the truth and find out why all of this happened to him."

‌



The family's story is one no parent could ever prepare for.

View 6 Images His first few weeks were particularly frightening (Image: Supplied)

Anna and Marcin, both formerly working as chefs, had dreamed of an ordinary life in Dublin — raising their children and enjoying the simple things. Their eldest, Maja, was born in 2015. Two years later, Frank arrived at the same Dublin hospital, appearing by every measure to be a big, healthy, thriving newborn. He fed well. He slept. He was calm. The family went home filled with joy.

‌



Within days, everything changed.

Frank stopped feeding. He became inconsolable and restless, and his skin began turning a deepening shade of yellow. Anna and Marcin, growing increasingly alarmed, raised their concerns with a community nurse, who they say advised them simply to monitor him. It is a decision that still haunts the family.

"To this day we ask ourselves, what if someone had said, 'please go to the hospital immediately,'" Anna said. "Perhaps our son's life would look completely different today."

‌



The following morning, Frank woke screaming and vomiting a dark green substance. His parents rushed him to hospital, where medics immediately transferred him to Children's Health Ireland at Crumlin. A surgical team was already waiting.

"That was the moment our entire world collapsed," Anna recalled.

View 6 Images Frank Baziak (Image: Supplied)

‌



Frank underwent emergency surgery lasting several hours. Surgeons discovered his intestines had become completely twisted and had turned necrotic — black, without blood supply.

Doctors delivered the news no parent should ever receive: their son had a 1% chance of surviving the night.

"There are no words to describe what we felt at that moment," Anna said. "We were also told that another hour at home could have resulted in our child's death."

‌



Surgeons untwisted and repositioned the intestines during that first procedure. Three days later, a second operation was required, during which 200cm of his 250cm of intestines were removed.

A third surgery followed during his stay in intensive care, leaving Frank with just 35cm of bowel — a fraction of what is needed to sustain life independently.

"From the very first days of his life, our child knew mostly pain," Anna told us.

‌



View 6 Images The parents are determined to remain positive (Image: Supplied)

That pain has never truly left him. His early years were defined by surgeries, injections, tubes, and long, frightening nights alone in hospital. When the family were eventually allowed to go home, the hospital, in many ways, came with them.

Anna and Marcin spent countless hours training with medical staff to learn how to keep their son alive, managing his TPN lines and monitoring him around the clock.

‌



The NHS notes that caring for a child with short bowel syndrome places enormous strain on families, with many parents taking on the role of full-time medical carers. For Anna and Marcin, that has been their reality for eight years.

When Frank was younger, he found it easier to accept his circumstances. Now, the questions have started — and they cut deep. "How much longer will this last?" he asks. "Will I ever be healthy?"

His parents do not have the answers. Frank breaks down in tears regularly, longing to understand why his life looks so different from those of his classmates and friends.

‌



The emotional toll is profound. Anna is clear that Frank's condition is not only a physical burden — it is a psychological one too.

View 6 Images The Baziak family (Image: Supplied)

"The family are increasingly witnessing their son's sadness, frustration and tears as he struggles to comprehend why his life is so vastly different from other children," she said. Yet even amid the heartbreak, Frank continues to surprise his parents with moments of extraordinary courage and joy.

‌



In August 2025, the family welcomed a new baby, Antoni, and Anna said he has served as a reminder "that life can still bring love and goodness".

"We are still trying to live a normal life," she said. "We continue fighting for our children's happiness. We try to smile, even though our hearts have been shattered many times."

The €4,000 specialist medical report the family are fundraising for cannot be carried out in Ireland and receives no public funding. Beyond potentially identifying whether a medical error occurred in the six days following Frank's birth, it could open the door to additional treatment options and provide the family with greater financial support in managing his lifelong care needs.

‌



Most importantly for Anna and Marcin, it would give them something to tell their son. "We want to know that we did absolutely everything possible to fight for his future," Anna said. "And finally, we hope to find at least a little peace."

This week, Anna also revealed that Frank had recently been hospitalised after suffering a severe bout of food poisoning. Because of his compromised immune system and the near-total absence of his intestines, his body is far more vulnerable to infection than most — a reality the family must navigate every single day.

As for the question Frank keeps asking regarding being healthy again, Anna said simply: "That question really captures what he has been going through and how much he wants a normal, healthy life."

News.title: Man taken to court in two-year battle over 90p parking ticket wins £289.50
News.content:
Man taken to court in two-year battle over 90p parking ticket wins £289.50

The company has been ordered to pay him compensation - including the £4.50 it cost him to park at court

View 5 Images John Waters was taken to court by Civil Enforcement Ltd, despite having proof of payment

A man being chased by debt collectors despite proof of parking has successfully defended himself in court and even won compensation. In December 2023, John Waters, 76, entered the Foreman Centre Car Park in Headcorn, Kent, to visit the shops with his wife.

‌



But Civil Enforcement fined him for allegedly keying in only half of his number plate. It started a two-and-half year battle involving multiple letters and hours spent trying to communicate with the company until John got his day in court.

‌



John told the court he had paid 90p to park for an hour and keyed in his registration. When the ticket printed with only the last four digits of his registration, he presumed it was to prevent the ticket being transferred to another vehicle.

‌



View 5 Images The Foreman Centre Car Park in Headcorn

He then returned to his car 36 minutes later and headed home. But a fortnight later the Sittingbourne man was surprised to receive a penalty notice from Civil Enforcement, claiming he had not paid and he was being issued with a £100 fine, reduced to £60 if settled within 14 days.

Armed with a printed copy of his ticket and bank statement, he replied to the letter with his evidence and presumed the fine would be cancelled. A second letter arrived, and John appealed to Civil Enforcement, but the firm rejected his submissions.

‌



Instead, the company said it was prepared to accept the sum of £20 on the basis he had failed to provide his full vehicle registration. Undeterred, the retired chartered surveyor refused to pay, arguing the last four digits of his registration were clearly shown on the parking ticket.

He said: “Paying the £20 is still a 2,000% increase when I’d already paid for parking. I was annoyed that they were seeking, effectively, to extort money from me, when it was unfounded. A lot of people would pay £20, but I basically felt it was a matter of principle. I wasn’t prepared to pay it.”

After the company refused his appeal, the penalty notice climbed to £170 and was passed over to debt collection agencies. Each time he received any correspondence, John always responded, setting out his defence, and even advising the firm he was prepared to present his evidence in county court, and submit a counterclaim to recover his costs.

‌



View 5 Images Headcorn High Street

Two further years passed, with demand letters coming from Direct Collection Bailiffs seeking a payment of £170, which he described as “intimidating”. By the time of the hearing, Civil Enforcement was pursuing John for £277.

He also put forward a counterclaim for the intimidation and anxiety caused to him over the two and a half years he’d been fighting it. Deputy District Judge Chan dismissed Civil Enforcement’s claim against John and upheld the counterclaim.

‌



She ordered the private parking company to pay him £289.50, which included a counterclaim of £250, his court expenses, and the £4.50 spent on parking at the court. John said: “I felt relief really that it reached a conclusion. But I think frustration that they’re [Civil Enforcement] still allowed to keep doing what they’re doing.

“Most people are not aware of their rights really and are intimidated by these parking companies into making payments that are unwarranted.”

In his witness statement, he outlined the precedent set by the case of Parking Eye Limited v Heggie, where the judge ruled that because the motorist had paid for the parking time in full, Parking Eye suffered no financial loss. As a result, the charge was deemed an unenforceable penalty rather than a valid pre-estimate of loss.

‌



View 5 Images John had his day in court

Now the dad’s message to other motorists in a similar position is to keep as much information as possible, including evidence of parking tickets and correspondence, so you can defend yourself if you are subjected to a claim. John said: “Thankfully the judge found in my favour. This effectively means anyone using the car park who pays for a ticket and shows it refers to their car, even if the vehicle registration is not complete, they cannot be liable for any additional penalty charge.”

From the date of the hearing, Civil Enforcement was given 14 days to pay, but by the due date, no funds had arrived in his bank account. John emailed immediately and said he would report the firm to the regulator, British Parking Association, if they did not pay.

‌



The boot finally closed on the parking ordeal when the grandfather received payment, which had Creative Car Park as the reference. He has not been back to the Foreman Centre Car Park. There have been calls to improve the parking machines, after many were stung by fines despite having proof of payment.

View 5 Images John Waters was taken to court by Civil Enforcement Ltd, despite having proof of payment

Motorists said that the number of fines had been deterring people from visiting the town, and businesses subsequently shared concerns over the reduced footfall. Speaking on behalf of the landowner of the Foreman Centre Car Park, property manager Henry Lloyd-Roberts, said he would be contacting Creative Car Park to ask it to formally apologise to Mr Waters.

Article continues below

He said: “I am not familiar with [his] case but am glad he got the correct result and regret that this has caused him stress and anxiety. He has my sincere apologies that this happened at The Foreman Centre. I assure you the landowner is not “happy to let it continue” and whenever a legitimate case is brought to my attention I give it my fullest attention and seek to get suitable redress for the customer.”

Mr Lloyd-Roberts added: “There are a couple of key performance indicators that could certainly be improved, and we are giving them [Creative Car Park] three months from today to do so; otherwise we will have no alternative but to seek an alternative car park management provider.”

Civil Enforcement and Creative Car Park have been approached for comment.

News.title: ‘Ultimate’ airport workout before you taking flight this summer
News.content:
‘Ultimate’ airport workout before you taking flight this summer

Holidaymakers might be able to stop the aches and pains onboard

View 3 Images Some exercises at the boarding gate can help prevent days of recovery after the flight (Image: GETTY)

Countless travellers are heading to the airport in the coming weeks, excited to be making the most of the final summer month. But few will be looking forward to hours in cramped aeroplane seats and the inevitable aches and pains it brings.

‌



However, a handful of movements before you board the plane could help keep this at bay. Experts from JD Gyms have revealed the ‘ultimate’ workout routine to prepare your body for the most physically demanding part of your holiday, whether you’re at the airport or even onboard the plane.

‌



Tip toe and heel walking

Leg muscles are often the first to start cramping up on small plane seats, depending on your height. This can be caused by a lack of circulation while sitting for prolonged periods of time or not having enough leg room.

‌



The experts recommended taking a few minutes before your flight to emphasise some blood flow in your legs to help ward off this ache, saying: “Walking ten steps strictly on your tiptoes, then immediately taking 10 steps walking on your heels and repeating this for 2 minutes can activate your leg muscles.

“This encourages circulation before periods of prolonged sitting, especially before long-haul flights.”

For people with a bit more prep time, the experts recommended adding some time on the stair master into your usual routine to prepare your legs both for the flight and for navigating the airport.

‌



View 3 Images Sitting for long periods of time in airplane seats can lead to a range of temporary physical issues (Image: GETTY)

Glute bridges

The experts said: “Sitting for long hours on a flight or waiting in security queues can cause stiffness in the glutes and hips. Glute bridges can relieve this.

“Lie on your back, push your hips towards the ceiling and hold for two seconds at the top before releasing back down. We recommend three sets of 15 repetitions.”

‌



On the flight

Spending hours in an aeroplane seat quickly leads to stiffness across the body, usually focused on the backs, hips and hamstrings that can take days to shake off after landing.

To mitigate this, the experts suggested taking a walk in the aeroplane aisle or simply standing up every hour or so. While seated, some shoulder rolls and light ankle rolls can also help keep your body mobile despite the restrictions.

View 3 Images Walking and standing during the flight can help alleviate stiffness (Image: GETTY)

Article continues below

At the gym

If you’ve got a few weeks until your getaway, the experts recommended heading to the gym for some specific exercises that can make your holiday a lot easier on your body. They suggested two to three sessions each week with a focus on good form rather than heavy weights could make a “noticeable difference”.

News.title: 'My entitled neighbour kept letting dog bark all day so I got ultimate revenge'
News.content:
'My entitled neighbour kept letting dog bark all day so I got ultimate revenge'

A frustrated man has shared his elaborate revenge plan against his alleged inconsiderate neighbour after their dog would bark all day long. People can't believe how events unfolded

View Image It's reported the dog kept barking all day (stock image) (Image: Getty Images/Johner RF)

From time to time, people run into difficulties with their neighbours, and occasionally things escalate to the point where they start planning payback. It can happen from the tiniest of things, from parking disputes to being left uncomfortable by your nosey neighbours.

‌



That said, one man had to get his own back after reportedly enduring a persistent problem with a nightmare neighbour. The unnamed man turned to Reddit to share what allegedly took place, and it's safe to say it sparked considerable discussion. He'd grown weary of his neighbour's dog barking constantly throughout the day, and he was genuinely exhausted by the situation which was affecting his quality of life in his own home on a daily basis, prompting him to take matters into his own hands.

‌



This isn't the first account of its type to emerge, either. Previously, another person exacted revenge on a neighbour who apparently kept dumping rubbish in their wheelie bin.

‌



How the Neighbour Conflict Escalated Over a Barking Dog

He explained: "A neighbour about three houses away had a dog that it kept chained up outside during the day. When he left the house, the dog would begin barking and not stop for hours at a time.

"It had one of those high-pitched whiny barks and, working from home, I found it impossible to concentrate. After a couple of days of this, I walked around to see what the situation was.

"Saw the dog chained up and looking stressed. I dropped a note in the letterbox just to say I was stressed about the dog and did they realise it sat in the backyard barking all day? No change.

‌



"So I went around to see if I could catch the neighbour, which I did as he was driving out of his driveway. I talked to him about the dog and he said 'that's just what dogs do' and, when I protested, he told me to 'f*** off'.

"Okay, mate. Let's see. So I got my beach fishing rod, removed the hook but left the two large lead sinkers on. At about 2am on Friday night, I walked down and stood behind his side fence (which backed on to bushland).

"I then cast my beach rod so the sinker hit the top of their corrugated iron roof and rattled down. The noise would have been deafening inside that house.

‌



"I reeled the sinkers back in and then recast them again about 10 minutes later. He eventually came out the front and started walking around with his outdoor lights on. I waited for him to go back to bed and I did it again."

Public Reaction

He revealed the neighbour emerged once more, though this time he returned to his property. He also posted another message through his letterbox warning him he'd be "repeating this on random nights until his dog stopped barking".

Following that, it seems the dog's barking ceased. Of course, this isn't something anyone should attempt themselves.

‌



If you're dealing with a similar problem, the best approach is speaking to your neighbour first, then reaching out to your local authority for support if that doesn't resolve matters.

However, people certainly found the tale rather amusing. In reality, many were shocked he'd taken such drastic action.

One person said: "Love this. If a dog is barking its head off then it's in distress."

Article continues below

Another added: "I would have called animal control." To this, the man replied: "Reported to the local council and RSPCA."

A third wrote: "Results." Meanwhile, a fourth also commented: "You are the king."

News.title: Met Office names date when heavy rain will hit UK after days of heatwave
News.content:
Met Office names date when heavy rain will hit UK after days of heatwave

With the mercury expected to hit 36C in East Anglia and the south east this week, the Met Office is warning there will be a 'north south split' with the weather

View 5 Images The Met Office forecast for 7am on Thursday, issued at 5am on Monday (Image: The Met Office)

The Met Office has named the date it expects heavy rain to hit the UK after another heatwave.

Meteorologists are predicting the heatwave across the country from Monday (August 10), with temperatures forecast to climb to 36°C in parts of East Anglia and south-east England by Thursday. The mercury will steadily rise in England from highs between 27°C and 29°C on Monday, 30°C on Tuesday, and between 32°C and 34°C on Wednesday.

It will peak at 36°C on Thursday, according to the Met Office ’s deputy chief forecaster Mike Silverstone.

He said: “After a brief dip on Monday, high pressure will move across the UK before settling to the east, allowing a southerly flow to develop.

“A fairly widespread heatwave is likely across large parts of England and Wales, with hot conditions developing in places. The heat is expected to peak for much of England, Wales, Northern Ireland and Scotland on Wednesday, with up to 34°C possible in parts of central and southern England and southeast Wales. East Anglia and south-east England, however, could see temperatures even higher on Thursday.

View 5 Images Rain will start to sweep across more of the country from 7pm on Friday

“Humidity levels are also expected to increase through the week, which may make conditions feel more uncomfortable, particularly overnight.”

Most of England is subject to a yellow heat health alert from the UK Health Security Agency until Wednesday, but another alert could follow this due to the high temperatures in some parts of the country.

During the heatwave, the Met Office says the public should wear sunscreen, stay hydrated, avoid prolonged exposure to the sun during the hottest part of the day, and check on vulnerable friends, family and neighbours.

View 5 Images By 10pm, clouds cover most of Northern Ireland and western Scotland

However, heavy rain will hit some on Thursday morning as Brits face a ‘north-south split’. While temperatures will pass the 30°C mark everywhere south of Ashington in the north east of England, those further north will see heavy rainfall.

The worst will be in the Highlands of Scotland, where more than an inch of rain is forecast to fall at 7am on Thursday (August 13), according to the forecast issued at 5am on Monday.

That sets off a period of intermittent rainfall across the UK. While it will be relatively dry for most, the weekend will see showers hit 50 council areas of the country - 30 in Scotland, 11 in Northern Ireland, five in England, and four in Wales.

View 5 Images By 1am on Saturday, isolated showers head south to England and Wales

Again, the worst rain will fall in Scotland, where up to 8mm could fall in an hour in the Borders.
