News.title: Travelodge staff gave domestic abuser key to his victim's room
News.content:
Another woman, Jo from Leeds, contacted BBC News following coverage of the Maidenhead attack.

In July, she woke in her room to an unknown man standing at the end of her bed, and screamed for help.

"It was just horrible, it was horrendous. Terrifying. I was shaking so badly," she said.

Her friend who was staying in the room heard him say, "I'm sorry, they gave me this key," she said.

Jo considered staying elsewhere following the reports of the attack in 2022, but was reassured by Travelodge's chief executive Jo Boydell, who previously said: "The safety and security of customers in our hotels is extremely important and we want everyone to be safe, and feel safe, in our hotels."

Jo said: "What happened to us shouldn't have happened. And the assurances [Travelodge] gave are not accurate. The systems are failing."

In response, Travelodge said an investigation found "our updated room access security policies, which were in place at the time, were not correctly followed, which is not acceptable.

"We have retrained the hotel team on our current room security and check-in procedures."

Andy Smith, who has travelled the country with his band and stays in dozens of Travelodge hotels a year, said he had been given keys to other people's rooms recently.

"We went up to the room and there was a guy already asleep in there in a state of undress," he said.

It followed another incident about 18 months ago where another man had gained access to his room by telling reception staff he was checking in under a common name such as "Mr Smith", Andy Smith said.

"I think he just chanced it. Because my name's Smith, I think it's just the pure luck of it. I mean, why wouldn't anyone be asking for ID or anything, like a booking reference or an email address. It beggars belief."

Travelodge responded by saying "any case of an unauthorised person entering a guest's room is a significant cause for concern and we want to be clear that these incidents should not have happened".

News.title: Burnham brings forward ban on 'subscription traps' to ease cost of living
News.content:
Subscriptions will be easier to cancel and companies will be compelled to make it clear when contracts auto-renew at a higher price, Andy Burnham has announced.

The prime minister is also planning to outlaw shops from falsely claiming products previously retailed at much higher prices to advertise supposed deals, which he said tricks shoppers into thinking they are getting better value on purchases.

Burnham will bring forward a package of changes announced under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer to end so-called subscription traps and a crackdown on "pretend prices".

Shadow chancellor Mel Stride branded the measures "reheated" and said the prime minister "has already run out of ideas".

The plans were announced under Sir Keir in April, but are being brought forward by Burnham's government in a bid to give families "room to breathe" amid the high cost of living.

On subscriptions, the government said the changes will mean businesses have "to provide clearer up-front information, regular reminders and a much easier exit to contracts" for customers.

Burnham, who is embarking on a tour of the UK while Parliament is in recess, has promised a series of "everyday fixes" to help people with the cost of living.

He said: "I'm determined to pull every single lever we can to provide people with some room to breathe on the cost of living."

The measures being brought forward are aimed at making it easier for consumers to cancel unwanted subscriptions and stopping people being rolled onto expensive contracts without their knowledge.

They were expected to come into force next spring, but Burnham's government has promised they will now be implemented by January 2027.

When they were announced in April, the government said the plans would save consumers Â£400m a year in total, or up to Â£170 per person.

At the time, the Department for Business and Trade said there are 10 million unwanted, active subscriptions across the UK.

It said that more than 3.5 million people are being "quietly rolled from free or discounted trials into fully costed contracts", while another 1.3 million are caught out by unexpected auto-renewals.

On top of the already planned changes, Burnham is also vowing to end shops' use of "pretend prices". This will stop retailers using "was" prices, made-up discounts or misleading recommended retail prices (RRPs) to highlight deals.

The government will launch a consultation this autumn to decide how the new measures should be implemented.

News.title: Schools in England have new rules on branded uniforms - will the changes save you money?
News.content:
A new law coming into force in September means parents in England should have to buy fewer branded items of school uniform, which the government says will save them money.

From September, uniforms will be limited to three items with a school logo, like a blazer, jumper or sportswear â plus a tie for secondary schools.

Schools are already advised to keep these items to a minimum, meaning many are already within the rules, but about a quarter of schools will need to make changes by the time the law comes into effect.

The government says the changes will save some families "up to Â£50 per child", but schoolwear suppliers say they now face uncertainty in demand for this year's uniforms.

Co-op Academy Belle Vue, in Manchester, is planning to drop the number of its compulsory branded items from seven to three, plus a tie.

It estimates the average cost of the branded parts of the uniform last year was Â£101.94 with a pinafore, and Â£83.95 without â but this year it will cost families an average of Â£53.97.

Next year, when the school switches to a new supplier, it says it will fall further.

The school has decided to get rid of its branded blazer, the branded pinafore, branded shorts and PE jogging bottoms.

News.title: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez says she's freezing her eggs
News.content:
New York Democratic congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has revealed she has decided to freeze her eggs and has shared her first steps in the process on social media.

The 36-year-old posted the clips on Sunday, hours before telling ABC News This Week she had not "ruled out the possibility" of running for president.

In the clips, Ocasio-Cortez shows herself taking an injection and talks through tips she has learnt, before answering questions about costs, clinical procedures, storage and how fertility care works under what she calls the US's "broken" medical system.

In an interview on ABC News she said she wanted to "normalise" conversations about the process.

She said it was important "especially in this political environment".

"This administration is denying reproductive care to women across the country, from abortion rights to the ability to carry out a healthy pregnancy," she said. "I think it's important for us as leaders to have these conversations and share these processes," she added.

In an earlier post on Instagram she said she wanted to share the information even though there was a "political risk" in doing so.

When asked if she would run for president in the 2028 elections after being shown polling reflecting her popularity as a potential candidate, Ocasio-Cortez chuckled and tried to sidestep a direct answer.

"I'm focused on winning the mid-terms, I'm running for Congress right now," she said.

But when pushed as to whether she was open to it and whether it was a realistic prospect, she said: "I haven't ruled out the possibility and I'm very humbled to the tremendous amount of support out there."

"We have a responsibility to remain focused on the midterms and not on our individual aspirations or plans," she said.

After she was asked about a possible Senate run against minority leader Chuck Schumer, the US Senate's top Democrat, Ocasio-Cortez replied that "anything was possible".

The midterms are held every two years and fall in the middle of the president's four-year term of office.

They are due to be held in early November. Votes will be cast for all 435 seats in the US House of Representatives, and a third of the 100 seats in the Senate are up for grabs.

News.title: Infantino has broken trust 'through deception', confederation presidents say
News.content:
Fifa and its president Gianni Infantino have been accused of breaking trust "through deception" in an open letter issued by Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation.

The letter, signed by the presidents and general secretaries, said recent controversy over the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal was fundamentally about "the integrity of the game, and the integrity of those elected to lead it".

FFE would have meant a new company being created to manage commercial and ticketing rights of all Fifa competitions, including the World Cups, with 21% sold off to a private investment company.

It was aborted after widespread criticism from several confederations, led by Uefa which has threatened a boycott of all Fifa competitions.

"When trust is broken through deception, when an individual places himself above the collective that entrusted him with authority, that duty has been abandoned," the letter read.

While the statement did not name Infantino, sources have told BBC Sport that it should be seen as an opportunity for him to resign and leave his position with dignity.

It comes after Fifa issued a statement on Saturday evening which strongly criticised a "concerted and ongoing effort" to "undermine" the organisation and Infantino.

The letter called for a review to be "conducted by a fully independent third party" after Fifa committed to present a report to the Fifa Council in October.

News.title: Could your tattoo stop you from getting a job?
News.content:
Tattoos have been in the cultural mainstream for years. Even the prime minister has got one (a bee, on his bicep).

And there are no signs the trend is starting to fade. More people than ever are going under the needle as a form of self-expression: 40% of British 25-49 year-olds have at least one tattoo, according to a 2024 YouGov poll.

The most popular body part to be inked? The upper arm, says YouGov.

But has that acceptance carried over into the workplace?

News.title: Tech leaders say AI means less work - their staff say they work up to 90 hours a week
News.content:
For years now, executives at companies that are pouring hundreds of billions of dollars a year into developing various artificial intelligence tools have insisted that the technology will ultimately mean people will spend less of their time working.

An engineering director at Google said four years ago that AI would deliver a four-day work week by 2025, external.

Earlier this year, and just one year after that engineering director's prediction, OpenAI took up the challenge, in a manner of speaking. It formally urged companies to start testing out a four-day work week (with no change in pay), claiming that AI will soon be able to speed up so much human labour that the corporate world should prepare itself.

However, a former OpenAI technical employee who left the company last year told the BBC the firm never actually trialled the four-day work week it suggested others should try while they were there.

Instead, the person described what was often a gruelling work culture marked by frequent "crisis meetings", working on weekends, and "super cut-throat" performance reviews that would see colleagues suddenly let go.

"You go in on Saturday or Sunday just to catch up or make sure things aren't broken," the person said.

Other companies have also pushed the idea that AI will effectively reduce the number of hours people need to work, for better or worse.

Anthropic has boasted that its popular coding tool and chatbot Claude is capable of working on its own for seven hours without a break, external, essentially a full corporate workday. Meta's Mark Zuckerberg has said his company is in the middle of the year when "AI starts to dramatically change the way that we work" and that such tools let far fewer employees do more than they ever could have before.

While Meta has since laid off 1 in 10 of its employees, Anthropic's chief executive Dario Amodei has warned that as AI tools inevitably become more productive, it could mean, external even broader job losses.

Despite these claims, workers inside these same tech companies, who are not only developing but using the very AI tools that will purportedly perform at least some of people's work, say they are clocking in far more than the typical five-day, 40-hour work week.

News.title: The team behind Hodgkinson's golden rise and the hunt for a world record
News.content:
The Olympic champion and the world silver medallist over 800m embrace by the side of the track after surviving their latest brutal training session together during an east Manchester downpour.

A short while ago, Keely Hodgkinson lay flat out on the track.

Coach Trevor Painter, aware it may be some time before Hodgkinson can move again, places an opened umbrella beside his star athlete to shield her from the incessant rain, before running for cover.

It requires the assistance of two team-mates to eventually peel her off the ground.

Georgia Hunter Bell, meanwhile, uses the little energy she has left to take herself away to be sick.

Observing it all, Painter jokes he is mostly disappointed that relatively few of their team-mates have suffered the same fate on this occasion, when the cameras are rolling.

This is, after all, what it takes to be part of M11 Track Club, where the emphasis is on fun until the stopwatch starts.

Named after the postcode in which it is based, the near-30 strong international training group continue to create history under the guidance of the meticulous Painter and partner Jenny Meadows, a world medallist who has put herself through all the anguish she now oversees.

There is no doubt in the mind of Hodgkinson, winner of six global medals in as many years as a professional athlete, about the important role of this support system in her monumental achievements.

"I think it's everything," the 24-year-old Hodgkinson tells BBC Sport.

"I probably wouldn't be the person I am without it. We have a very fun approach to training, I love everybody in this group.

"Environment is everything. We have people from all around the world training here. We all get along really well, we're all respective of each other's journey, and we all know that if we want to continue being the best, we've got to train with the best.

"And it works."

News.title: Drought expected to be declared in more parts of England
News.content:
There is no single definition of drought, but it usually refers to a period of prolonged unusually dry weather that can have impacts on people, nature and the environment.

Last month, England and Wales saw the driest July since records began in 1836 - while for southern England, it was the driest month ever recorded.

River levels have continued to fall after less than 10mm of rain across England for the seventh consecutive week.

The Environment Agency has warned that low water levels have resulted in potential navigation issues for boats on the Thames, Lark and Ouse.

Reservoir levels have also continued to decline, with almost all across England below normal and five classed as "exceptionally low", according to the agency.

The National Farmers Union (NFU) has warned that continued dry weather could lead to some food shortages.

NFU president Tom Bradshaw said yields of wheat and oats were "very, very poor" this year and warned livestock farmers have had to use their winter feed rations because they have been unable to grow grass.

The week ahead is forecast to remain mostly dry, with temperatures soaring across much of England and Wales.

Temperatures will peak on Thursday before dropping slightly over the weekend - and for England and Wales, there is no significant rainfall expected in the foreseeable future.

Emma Pinchbeck, chief executive of the Climate Change Committee, said the UK is "not prepared at all" for the prolonged dry weather.

She told Today: "We're seeing right now with the impacts on farming from this drought and the extreme heat we're experiencing, our infrastructure, our agricultural sector and lots of areas of the economy are not really ready for the weather we now have and how that weather will change up to 2050."

News.title: Risk of patient safety 'bonfire' with Health Bill changes, Lib Dems say
News.content:
The Liberal Democrats have urged Andy Burnham to stop the "bonfire of patient safety" as part of the government's plans to modernise the NHS.

Healthwatch England (HWE), an independent body which represents the views of patients at their local health and social care providers, is set to be scrapped under the NHS Modernisation Bill.

The Health Service Safety Investigation Bureau (HSSIB), which carries out patient safety investigations, is also being abolished.

The government says its changes will strip back bureaucracy and improve patient safety.

The Lib Dems warned it risks another Stafford Hospital scandal â where years of abuse and neglect led to hundreds of unnecessary patient deaths.

A Healthcare Commission report found the scandal â one of the biggest in NHS history â involved at least 400 more deaths than expected between 2005 and 2008.

Under the government proposals, Healthwatch's responsibilities will be transferred to integrated care boards (ICBs) and local authorities, meaning they would have to respond to feedback about their own services, rather than being challenged by an independent body.

Separately, HSSIB's functions will be transferred to the government-run Care Quality Commission (CQC), which the Lib Dems argue raises concerns there is no guarantee that staff who raise safety concerns are given anonymity.

Other measures include the abolition of NHS England in a bid to centralise the running of health and social care services under the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC).

The government says this will reduce bureaucracy and allow more resources to be delivered to frontline healthcare services.

News.title: Holiday 'completely overshadowed' by loss of airport luggage
News.content:
Travellers have described struggling to enjoy their holidays, days after hundreds of people flying out of Birmingham Airport were left without their luggage.

While it seems the issues that first emerged on Friday are yet to be remedied completely, the airport said the "vast majority" of baggage was now travelling as planned with passengers, and it was working to reunite others with their luggage.

Louise Fenton said she and her family had had no communication from the airline, holiday company or the airport after their luggage failed to arrive in Gran Canaria on Friday.

She is travelling with three teenagers, and said her daughter, who is autistic, had "struggled enormously" with replacement clothes, and had "barely slept because she is unable to tolerate the alternatives".

"We are staying in a tourist area where the shops are predominantly beach shops, with very limited clothing options, particularly for someone with sensory sensitivities," the mum explained.

"We still have no luggage and, no meaningful information about where it is."

She added the situation had "completely overshadowed" the holiday.

"We have worked hard and saved for this holiday, and we simply don't deserve to have the entire experience taken over by something that isn't our fault."

Speaking to the BBC on Friday and Saturday, travellers variously described the situation as "absolute chaos" and "carnage".

Other flights affected include ones to Turkey, Cyprus, Glasgow and Rome, covering a number of airlines.

News.title: Harry Potter fans force diversion of UK-Ireland power link to avoid Dobby's grave
News.content:
A colleague told him the nature of the calls, and that "apparently, we're going to go straight through Dobby's grave".

"I said, 'Dobby, who's Dobby? I don't know Dobby?'

"I said, 'he's a fictitious character in a fictitious book, the whole thing is fictitious, what are you talking about?'

"[The colleague] said 'no it's very, very serious'."

Ludlam discussed with planners "exactly how to reroute the cable so we wouldn't go anywhere close to Dobby's grave".

He added: "A lot of people were very happy about that, and the project is now going [ahead] and Dobby's happy."

The Bronze Age remains the cable went close to were mentioned in Pembrokeshire council planning documents, external about the power link.

It said archaeological trenches dug near the route of the underground cable "contained the rim of an inverted pottery vessel whose fabric suggests a Bronze Age collared urn circa 1700-1500BC, typically associated with human burial".

The cable diversion is not the first time Dobby's grave has been saved.

In 2022 the National Trust agreed it could remain in place following a consultation, but urged visitors not to leave souvenirs.

Fans were asked not to leave socks on the mock grave, made of pebbles with messages written on them, because the beach was environmentally sensitive.

News.title: Crews tackle heathland fire that spread from van
News.content:
Firefighters have worked through the night after a van caught fire and the flames spread to heathland in the New Forest, creating a smoke plume visible for miles.

The fire broke out on the A31 near Ringwood, Hampshire, shortly after 17:20 BST on Sunday, forcing some motorists to abandon their vehicles.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight Fire & Rescue Service (HIWFRS) said crews in 10 fire engines and 10 off-road vehicles were continuing to work to bring the fire under control "in challenging conditions".

National Highways said the dual carriageway remained closed westbound between the M27 at junction 2 for Ower and the A338 at Ringwood and eastbound between the A338 and M27 junction 1 for Cadnam.

News.title: 'Roll on 2027' as Fleadh 2026 comes to an end
News.content:
The first All Ireland Fleadh in Belfast ended in the early hours of Monday morning with organisers saying they were overwhelmed by the positive response they received from all communities.

It is estimated that there were more than a million people in the city centre during the eight days of the fleadh.

At least 4,000 were still in the grounds of Belfast City Hall at 01:00 BST to hear the closing speeches and final tunes.

Niall McClean, co-chair of the organising committee, told the crowd they were all part of an historic event.

He said: "We've done something that has never, ever happened in this city before. We've brought every single community together â and everybody has absolutely loved it."

McClean added that it has "put a permanent smile on my face. I'm the happiest man in Belfast. Roll on 2027".

"What an incredible week. Everyone I have spoken to has had an amazing time here in Belfast, thousands of people all on a high.

"Belfast has shone, the world has come to our doorstep, bringing the biggest numbers ever seen for a Fleadh Cheoil na hÃireann.

"I'm so proud of our branch and all our members, and what we have achieved together. We dared to dream and those dreams have come true."

To loud applause, he ended by saying: "Well done Belfast, we'll see you next year."

The All Ireland Fleadh returns to the city from 1 to 8 August 2027.

News.title: Parents fear being left behind in screening for rare condition after Jesy Nelson campaign
News.content:
Parents of children with a rare genetic condition say they fear Wales is being left behind as other parts of the UK introduce routine screening for newborns.

After widespread campaigning, including by former Little Mix star Jesy Nelson, testing for spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) will happen in England and be trialled in Scotland but not in Wales.

Warren Davies, whose three-year-old daughter Ophelia-May has SMA type 2, external, said it felt like the Welsh government was "playing God because they have the opportunity to effect change and are choosing not to".

The Welsh government said it had followed UK National Screening Committee (NSC) guidance that had not recommended routine newborn screening for SMA.

Newborn screening for SMA is also not in place in Northern Ireland, external.

News.title: Banksy works cost public almost £150,000
News.content:
Three artworks by street artist Banksy have cost taxpayers almost Â£150,000 in cleaning operations and security so far, with the bill expected to rise.

The largest single cost relates to a mural painted on the Royal Courts of Justice in September 2025, where removal efforts and security have so far cost more than Â£85,000.

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) says it has spent Â£50,000 trying to remove paint from the wall of the Grade II-listed building in Carey Street. A further Â£35,300 was spent on overtime and security costs.

The spending was disclosed to the BBC through Freedom of Information requests and is likely to reignite debate over whether Banksy's work is vandalism or valuable public art.

Banksy, who emerged from Bristol's graffiti scene in the 1990s and became one of the world's most famous street artists, is known for murals and installations that often appear overnight and attract large crowds.

The latest costs relate to a mural depicting a judge in a wig battering a protester with his gavel, which appeared on the Royal Courts of Justice in London on 8 September 2025.

Banksy claimed the image as his own work, by posting it on his website and Instagram account.

News.title: Do solar panels perform better in a heatwave? An expert explains
News.content:
With parts of the UK facing yet another spell of extreme heat, many solar panel owners will be watching their generation apps closely. Hot, bright weather can look like ideal conditions for home solar, especially if you’re running fans, air conditioning or other appliances during the day.

But while long summer days can help solar panels produce plenty of electricity, heat itself does not make panels work better. In fact, very high temperatures can slightly reduce the efficiency of the solar cells. The good news for most UK households is that this drop is usually modest, and a well-designed system can still perform strongly during a heatwave.

However, heatwave generation will still depend on cloud cover, roof orientation and local conditions. A hot but hazy or stormy afternoon may not produce as much electricity as a cooler, clearer day.

Get a quote for solar panels on your home

Use our comparison tool to get a range of free quotes from leading solar panel installers across the UK.

But solar panels don’t work better simply because it’s hotter. They need sunlight, not heat. In fact, very high temperatures can slightly reduce how efficiently panels convert sunlight into electricity.

For most UK households, though, this drop in efficiency is usually modest. Even during extreme heat, solar panels can still perform strongly, and evidence from Britain’s hottest day on record suggests that heatwaves can still deliver some of the year’s highest solar generation.

If you’re considering installing a system before the hottest months of the year, it’s worth comparing solar panel quotes from trusted UK installers so you can see how system size, panel type, battery storage and roof layout could affect your likely generation.

How do solar panels perform when it’s hot?

Modern solar panels are designed to operate across a wide temperature range. According to trade body Solar Energy UK, most panels are built to work from around -40C to 85C, but they generally perform best when the solar cells are closer to 25C or below.

That can feel counterintuitive. After all, the hottest days are often the sunniest. But solar panels don’t like heat in the same way humans do. Strong sunlight increases the electrical current a panel can generate, yet as the panel warms up, its voltage drops, and power is essentially current multiplied by voltage. In practice, that means bright sunshine can still deliver great generation, but higher panel temperatures shave a little off the top.

Air temperature vs solar panel temperature

One important detail is that it’s the temperature of the solar cells inside the panel that matters most, not the headline temperature on the weather app.

Solar panels are rated in laboratory conditions (often called “standard test conditions”) at 25C. Out on a roof, panels can run significantly hotter than the surrounding air because they absorb solar radiation. While wind and airflow under the panels can cool them, on a still, sunny day it’s common for the panels themselves to be far warmer than the ambient temperature.

How much power do solar panels lose in a heatwave?

The impact of heat is usually described using a panel’s temperature coefficient – a number on the datasheet that indicates how much the panel’s power output falls as its temperature rises above 25C.

As a rule of thumb, for every degree above 25C, solar panels can lose around 0.34 to 0.5 percentage points of power output, depending on the model and the quality of the cells.

To see what that means in the real world, consider Britain’s all-time temperature record of 40.3C, set on 19 July 2022.

If you used the air temperature alone as a rough guide, the difference between 25C and 40.3C is 15.3C. On that basis, a good modern panel would be operating at roughly 5 per cent below its optimum rating.

In reality, panels can be hotter than the air temperature in full sun. But even at the top end of many manufacturers’ operating ranges – around 85C – the loss implied by typical temperature coefficients is still usually in the region of 20 per cent compared with the 25C test condition.

That sounds large, but it’s worth keeping in perspective. First, it’s a comparison to an ideal laboratory reference point. Second, it’s a “moment in time” penalty at a particular panel temperature, not a promise that your annual solar yield will fall by 20 per cent.

For most homeowners, the bigger financial question is how this annual generation compares with the upfront cost of solar panels, rather than what happens during one unusually hot afternoon.

You may also be able to reduce the upfront cost through solar panel grants and funding, including 0 per cent VAT, local schemes or support such as ECO4 if you meet the eligibility criteria.

Heat doesn’t just affect solar panels: the inverter matters, too

If you notice your system output dropping more than the panel maths suggests on very hot days, it may not be the panels at all.

Solar systems rely on an inverter to convert the electricity generated by the panels (DC) into the form used in your home (AC). Inverters generate heat while they operate, and many are designed to protect themselves by reducing output if they get too hot, a behaviour sometimes described as thermal derating or throttling.

That’s one reason installers usually try to position inverters in a cool, well-ventilated place out of direct sunlight. Poor airflow around an inverter – or a unit installed in a hot loft space – can make a bigger difference during a heatwave than the panel temperature coefficient alone.

What happened on the UK’s hottest day on record?

Britain’s record-breaking heat in July 2022 provides a useful real-world test.

According to estimates from Sheffield Solar’s PV Live modelling, cited by Solar Energy UK, solar generated 66.9GWh of electricity over the course of 19 July 2022, supplying around 8.6 per cent of the UK’s power needs that day. Over the previous seven days, solar had provided around 9 per cent.

In other words, even on the hottest day the UK has ever recorded, the national solar fleet still supplied a meaningful share of electricity, and the evidence suggests only a small drop-off in performance.

How to tell if your panels are ‘good in the heat’

If you’re comparing solar panels – or just trying to understand your existing system – a few details can help. These are also useful details to check when comparing the best solar panels, because headline wattage is only one part of long-term performance.

Temperature coefficient (Pmax): the closer this figure is to zero, the less performance falls as panels heat up.

NOCT (Nominal Operating Cell Temperature): a clue to how warm a panel tends to run under typical real-world conditions.

Inverter operating temperature / derating behaviour: some inverters reduce output at high temperatures – good siting and ventilation can minimise this.

Verdict: Do solar panels work in a heatwave?

Solar panels can still work well in a heatwave, but they do not become more efficient simply because it is hot. In fact, very high temperatures can slightly reduce panel efficiency because heat lowers voltage.

For most UK homes, however, this reduction is usually modest. Longer daylight hours and strong summer sunshine often mean solar panels still generate plenty of electricity overall, even if each panel operates a little less efficiently than it would on a cooler, brighter day.

That means a heatwave is not usually a cause for concern about your solar panels underperforming. The bigger lesson is that system design is key. Panels need good airflow, inverters should be kept out of extreme heat where possible, and homeowners should look at generation over days and weeks, rather than judging performance by a single hot afternoon.

As UK summers become hotter and heatwaves more common, understanding this balance will become more important. Solar panels need sunlight, not heat, but a well-designed system should still be able to make strong use of long, bright summer days.

Plug-in solar panels will become legal in Great Britain from 27 August, opening the way for supermarkets, DIY chains and electrical retailers to begin selling the small-scale solar systems to the public.

Lidl, B&Q, Currys and Amazon are among the household names that have been working with the government on plans to bring plug-in solar to the British market. Asda, Screwfix and Wickes have also taken part in talks about the technology, while Iceland was named in an earlier government announcement.

However, shoppers may not find plug-in solar panels on shelves as soon as the regulations change. Retailers must first source products that meet the government’s new safety requirements, and most of the companies involved have yet to announce a product range, price or firm launch date.

Here is what we know so far about where plug-in solar panels could be sold.



Will Lidl sell plug-in solar panels?

Lidl was one of the first retailers publicly linked to the rollout.

In March, the government said Lidl and Iceland were working with ministers, alongside solar equipment manufacturer EcoFlow, to bring plug-in solar products to the UK.

The prospect immediately raised the possibility of solar panels appearing in Lidl’s famous middle aisle. Similar balcony solar kits are already available through Lidl in parts of Europe, where the technology is more established.

However, a UK launch does not appear to be imminent. The Independent understands that Lidl is still in the early stages of exploring the technology and has not confirmed a launch date.

The supermarket has also yet to reveal which product it might stock or how much a system would cost.

Early reports suggested that a Lidl system could cost around £400.



Will B&Q sell plug-in solar panels?

B&Q has given one of the clearest indications that it plans to sell the devices.

The DIY retailer joined a government roundtable on plug-in solar in June, alongside Amazon, Asda, Currys, Screwfix and Wickes.

B&Q chief executive Graham Bell said the retailer was working with the government and suppliers to ensure any products it offered were safe, compliant and straightforward to install.

“We look forward to making plug-in solar available to our customers as soon as possible,” he said following the roundtable.

B&Q already sells portable solar panels and battery generators. These products can power compatible appliances or charge a portable battery, but they are not the same as plug-in solar panels designed to feed electricity into a home through a mains socket.

The retailer has not yet announced a product, price or launch date.



Will Currys sell plug-in solar panels?

Currys was also named by the government as one of the flagship retailers supporting plans to bring plug-in solar to British homes.

The electrical retailer took part in the June discussions, although it has not yet announced which products it might carry or when they could become available.

Michelle Gorringe-Smith, director of new categories at Currys, said the company was “delighted to be working with the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero to bring plug-in solar panels to the market.”

Currys would be a natural outlet for the technology because it already sells a wide range of domestic electrical products and some portable energy equipment. Nevertheless, its participation in government talks should not be treated as confirmation that a particular kit will be available from 27 August.



Will Amazon sell plug-in solar panels?

Amazon has publicly welcomed the introduction of self-installed plug-in solar systems.

“This is a fantastic opportunity to make renewable energy more accessible to people around the UK,” John Boumphrey, Amazon’s UK and Ireland country manager, said in the government’s announcement following the retailer roundtable.

“Enabling households to generate their own power with self-install plug-in solar panels is a practical step that supports household budgets and delivering against net zero goals.”

Amazon already lists products described as balcony solar kits, microinverters and portable solar panels. Buyers should be cautious, however, because products designed for other European countries will not automatically comply with the new British rules.

A device appearing in Amazon search results does not necessarily mean it is approved for connection to a UK mains socket. Shoppers should look for clear confirmation that the complete product meets the government’s UK plug-in solar specification rather than relying on an adaptor or buying individual components separately.

Amazon has not yet announced a dedicated range of compliant products or confirmed when they might become available.

What about Iceland, Asda, Screwfix and Wickes?

Iceland was named alongside Lidl in the government’s original March announcement. It has not yet confirmed whether plug-in solar panels will be sold in its supermarkets, through its website or through another retail arrangement.

Asda, Screwfix and Wickes attended the government’s June roundtable but did not make individual public commitments to stock the products.

Screwfix and B&Q are both owned by Kingfisher, although that does not necessarily mean they will sell the same products or introduce them at the same time.

For now, these retailers are best described as being involved in discussions rather than confirmed sellers.

Will EcoFlow sell plug-in solar panels?

EcoFlow is a manufacturer rather than a high-street shop, but it could be one of the first recognisable brands to launch a compliant system.

The company already sells balcony solar products in Europe and was named by the government in March as one of the manufacturers helping to bring the technology to Britain.

EcoFlow’s UK communications representative said at the time that making the systems available in shops would improve access to solar for people living in flats and rented homes.

However, consumers should not assume that an existing European EcoFlow product can simply be connected to a British socket. Any system sold for that purpose will need to comply with the technical and electrical requirements introduced for the British market.

When will plug-in solar panels go on sale?

The legal changes come into force in Great Britain on 27 August, but it’s not a guaranteed nationwide retail launch.

As The Independent previously reported, only products that comply with the government’s interim specification will be covered by the new exemption.

Compliant plug-in solar devices will have a maximum rated output of 800W, with one device permitted per electrical circuit. The new rules apply to solar generation and do not cover plug-in batteries that draw electricity from the home, store it and feed it back later.

Retailers will need to make sure their products, plugs, microinverters, cables, mounting equipment and instructions meet the required standards. This could mean that the first compliant products arrive gradually rather than appearing in every participating shop on the day the law changes.

How much will plug-in solar panels cost?

The government’s final impact assessment uses an estimated retail cost of approximately £400 to £600 for a complete system, with £500 as its central assumption.

Government modelling also suggests that a compliant 800W system could save a household around £70 to £110 a year. The higher figure is based on panels facing south at a 30-degree angle, while a vertically mounted east- or west-facing system could save closer to £70.

These figures are illustrative rather than guaranteed. Actual savings will depend on shading, location, energy prices, the direction and angle of the panels and how much electricity the household uses while the system is generating.



What should shoppers check before buying?

Consumers should wait for products that clearly state they are compliant with the new British electrical requirements.

An imported balcony solar kit, portable panel or power station is not necessarily suitable for feeding electricity into a home through a mains socket. Buyers should also check whether they need permission from a landlord or freeholder and whether the proposed mounting position is secure, unshaded and permitted under local planning rules.

B&Q, Currys, Amazon and Lidl are among the most likely places to eventually offer plug-in solar products, but none has yet published a confirmed range, price and launch date. Shoppers should therefore treat claims that a particular system will be available from 27 August with caution unless the retailer has confirmed it directly.

Nichols, the owner of soft drinks brand Vimto, has acquired healthy beverage maker VitHit in a deal worth €75 million (£64 million), created by former professional rugby player Gary Lavin.

Mr Lavin, who played for Leinster and Harlequins, will step down following the sale of the business. He launched the brand in Dublin 25 years ago as a healthy alternative to sugary sports drinks.

The brand has expanded into 13 overseas markets, generating revenues of more than €26.5 million (£22.7 million) last year and delivering underlying profits of €4.1 million (£3.5 million).

London-listed Nichols described the acquisition as a "strategic milestone" for the group, confirming plans to accelerate sales growth for the VitHit brand.

Mr Lavin said: “Since launching VitHit more than 25 years ago, our ambition has always been to build a distinctive health and wellness drinks brand with broad consumer appeal.

“We are proud of what the team has achieved and consider Nichols the ideal partner to support the next stage of the brand’s development.”

The VitHit healthy drink brand founded by former professional rugby player Gary Lavin has been bought by Vimto owner Nichols for €75 million (£64 million)

Nichols will keep VitHit’s Dublin office and said it would be “supported by its management team, some of whom will step away after a smooth transition, while the chairman and founder, Gary Lavin, will step down from day one”.

Nichols chief executive, Andrew Milne, said: “With its established market position, alignment with our asset-light operating model, proven profitability and significant headroom for growth, VitHit perfectly fits the acquisition profile we have been looking for and is fully aligned with our long-term growth strategy.

“Nichols is ideally placed to accelerate VitHit’s development through our commercial capabilities, customer relationships, route-to-market expertise and international infrastructure.

“A significant opportunity exists to expand distribution across the group’s existing customer base.”

North Korea is preparing to send as many as 50,000 soldiers to support Russia’s war against Ukraine, Volodymyr Zelensky claimed, a much bigger deployment than anything Pyongyang had committed thus far.

The Ukrainian president said Moscow and Pyongyang had agreed to station between 30,000 and 50,000 North Korean troops on Russian territory, an escalation from earlier deployments that he described as first hundreds and then thousands of men.

Neither Russia nor North Korea confirmed any such agreement, and it was not immediately clear how Ukraine had formulated its assessment.

“North Koreans appear on the territory of the Russian Federation from time to time," Mr Zelensky said in an interview with the Ukrainian television service United News on Saturday.

“At first, we were talking about hundreds, then thousands, and now a decision has been made for 30,000 to 50,000 North Koreans to be deployed on the territory of Russia."

Pyongyang is thought to have sent 16,000 soldiers and deminers to Kursk, the Russian region partly seized by Ukrainian forces in 2024, since late that year, along with shipments of ballistic missiles.

The figures Mr Zelensky gave would represent a commitment on a much larger scale. He had said last month that preparations to receive North Korean troops had been underway since June in Voronezh, a region bordering Ukraine.

North Korean leader Kim Jong Un meets Russian president Vladimir Putin

He said the arrangement would give North Korea something more valuable than the manpower it was sending.

"North Korea will build up its capabilities in fairly modern warfare, will receive licences from Russia and will receive all kinds of military tools from them. We understand this clearly," he said, adding the troops were gaining combat experience and were not preparing for peaceful circumstances.

Mr Zelensky argued that this made the arrangement a problem for Asia rather than just for Europe, and urged Seoul to work more closely with Kyiv, particularly on air defence, where Ukraine has clear gaps, and on drones.

South Korean law limits what Seoul can supply to countries at war to non-lethal aid.

“They have a legal restriction under their constitution," Mr Zelensky said of South Korea. "But we would like to have this cooperation and are counting on it. Our diplomats are in contact."

Mr Zelensky cited Russia's use of North Korean missiles against Ukrainian targets, including one strike last month that he said killed a family, as evidence of what Pyongyang stood to learn.

Ukraine's military intelligence agency said last week that North Korea was preparing to send a missile unit of about 90 soldiers to Voronezh with six launchers and 120 missiles to operate as part of Russia's 112th missile brigade. Andrii Cherniak, a representative of the agency, told Reuters that North Korea had already supplied 40 KN-23 and KN-24 short-range ballistic missiles and Moscow and Pyongyang were expected to settle the details of the deployment at talks next month.

The two countries signed a mutual defence treaty in June 2024, committing each to come to the other's aid if attacked.

North Korea has since become one of Russia's most important suppliers of munitions and men, purportedly in exchange for food, fuel, cash and military technology.

Britain, which has trained Ukrainian troops and supplied air defence missiles, has sanctioned a number of North Korean officials over the deployments and joined a group of countries monitoring sanctions enforcement against Pyongyang after Russia vetoed the continuation of a UN panel that previously did the job.

Ben Jones, a star of The Dukes of Hazzard and a former American politician, has died, aged 84.

The actor was best known for playing bearded mechanic Cooter Davenport on all seven seasons of the hit US series, which ran from 1979 until 1985 on CBS.

Jones’s wife, Alma Viator, shared the news in a Facebook post on Sunday (9 August), writing that he died from a “massive heart attack”.

“I lost the love of my life today,” she said. “He was home resting in his favourite chair waiting for the Braves to come on and whoop the Yankees. Ben had the most amazing rich full life. He loved and was loved by so many. He will be missed. I love him so so much.”

open image in gallery Jones with the cast of 'The Dukes of Hazzard'

Born in Tarboro, North Carolina, Jones began his acting career in the theatre in the early Sixties – touring in productions of Summer and Smoke and Desire Under the Elms across the US before landing a role in 1975 action comedy Moonrunners.

He later took on small parts in films including Smokey and the Bandit and The Lincoln Conspiracy, before being cast in The Dukes of Hazzard as the lovable mechanic Cooter. The hit series followed cousins Bo (John Schneider) and Luke Duke (Tom Wopat) in the fictional Georgia county of Hazzard as they cooked up various get-rich-quick schemes while evading corrupt county commissioner J.D. “Boss” Hogg (Sorrell Booke).

After the show came to an end in 1985, Jones pivoted into politics – becoming a member of the US House of Representatives for Georgia’s fourth district in 1989. He had previously lost to incumbent Pat Swindall but won in a rematch after the latter was indicted for perjury.

During his time in the House of Representatives, Jones was a Democratic whip and was re-elected in 1990, but lost his seat in 1993 after the electoral district boundaries were redrawn. He later ran for office again in 1994 and in 2002, but lost both times.

After leaving politics, Jones reprised the role in two follow-up Dukes of Hazzard films in 1997 and 2000, and also took on small roles in films Primary Colors and Meet Joe Black. Alongside his wife, Jones set up a Dukes of Hazzard museum and themed store next to the Shenandoah National Park in Virginia before releasing 13 albums as Cooter’s Garage Band.

His Dukes of Hazzard co-star Tom Wopat paid tribute to the star on social media, writing on Instagram that the show had “lost another integral part of their cast”.

“Ben Jones was a fine friend and a fierce advocate of all the best things we can offer in the entertainment business,” he posted on Instagram. “He will be sorely missed... Denver Pyle frequently said to Ben, 'I'm not your Uncle Jesse!' But I feel like we lost a Duke cousin today.”

Jones is survived by his wife, Viator, whom he married in 1992, and his children, Rachel and Walker.

News.title: Faithful dog leads best friend’s funeral procession
News.content:
A 15-year-old collie-spaniel cross named Bo led the funeral procession for his owner, Graham Price, 74, who was laid to rest in South Wales on Tuesday, August 4.

Price shared an unbreakable bond with Bo, whom he had owned since the dog was a puppy.

For more than 20 years, Price played bass guitar with Crazy Cavan ’n’ the Rhythm Rockers, a Welsh rockabilly band closely associated with the Teddy Boy movement.

Formed in 1970, the band built an international following and continued touring and recording until the death of its frontman, Cavan Grogan, in 2020.
