Ecuador Illegal Mining: A Billion-Dollar Criminal Economy

Illegal gold in Ecuador generates an estimated US$800 million to US$1.3 billion a year, according to the country’s security policy framework. Other reporting, citing the FACT Coalition, puts the figure at up to US$1 billion annually.

The Defence Ministry said on 4 August that operations from January to July 2026 caused about US$20 billion in losses to criminal economies. That includes more than US$4 billion from illegal mining and more than US$14 billion from narcotics.

The Organized Crime Observatory counted fewer than 60 illegal mining points before 2018. By 2024, that number had jumped to over 652, showing how rapidly the sector has expanded.

Azuay and the Amazon: Where the Gold Flows

Azuay province is the epicentre, with pressure points in Camilo Ponce Enríquez, Sígsig, Pucará, and Santa Isabel. Camilo Ponce Enríquez is a key hub because it combines extraction, artisanal work, and processing plants.

In the Amazon, illegal mining operates in at least nine of Ecuador’s 71 protected areas. Seven of those are in the rainforest region.

The Napo, Calera, and Amarillo rivers show contamination above legal limits, the government found. The Santa Bárbara River basin in Azuay is also under pressure.

More than 500 hectares in the Yutzupino area were impacted by mining between January 2017 and December 2024. This damage adds to the environmental toll in the region.

Armed Groups and the Gold Supply Chain

Criminal organisations have penetrated the gold supply chain from mine sites to processing plants to smuggling routes, authorities say. Groups now control unauthorised extraction sites, processing facilities, and smuggling networks.

Los Lobos are a central trafficking partner of Mexico’s CJNG, with ties to European drug traffickers and FARC dissident factions, InSight Crime reports. A Los Lobos-financing network was targeted in Azuay and El Oro, with one suspect moving about US$3.2 million between 2023 and 2025.

Los Choneros could receive US$1 million per month from illegal gold, according to a reported official estimate. This shows how gold has become a parallel income stream to cocaine for major gangs.

Noboa’s Crackdown and the Investment Dilemma

President Daniel Noboa’s government has elevated illegal gold mining to a national security threat. The Plan Nacional de Seguridad Integral 2025–2029 treats it as a priority and calls for coordinated action by the armed forces, police, and mining regulators.

Operations have seized machinery, explosives, fuel, and ore, and closed storage centres. In February 2026, Environment Minister Inés Manzano suspended mining in Napo and restricted processing plants in El Oro and Loja over contamination concerns.

Noboa says the mining cadastre will reopen progressively from late 2026 to restore order and attract investment. Critics warn the push to accelerate extractive investment risks weaker environmental safeguards and insufficient consultation.

What This Means for You

If you live in or invest in Latin America, this is a warning about operating environment risk. Legal mining projects face competition from criminal operators who undercut costs and corrupt officials.

The environmental damage also raises long-term liabilities. Contaminated rivers affect water supplies and agriculture, which can hurt property values and community relations.

For investors, the reopening of the cadastre offers opportunity, but due diligence on security and environmental compliance is now essential. The line between legal and illegal mining is dangerously thin in Ecuador.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened in Pucará, Azuay province? Police found eight dismembered bodies on 9 August in two mass graves inside an illegal gold mine. The victims were buried about two meters deep with hands tied, with injuries including dismemberment and decapitation. How much money does Ecuador illegal mining generate? Estimates range from US$800 million to US$1.3 billion a year. The Defence Ministry says illegal mining caused over US$4 billion in losses to criminal economies from January to July 2026. Which armed groups are involved in illegal mining? Los Choneros and Los Lobos are the main groups. Los Choneros could earn US$1 million a month from gold, while Los Lobos partner with Mexico’s CJNG and European traffickers. What is President Noboa doing about illegal mining? Noboa has declared illegal mining a national security threat. His government is seizing machinery, suspending mining in contaminated areas, and plans to reopen the mining cadastre from late 2026 to attract legal investment.

Sources: Ecuador’s National Police; Primicias; El Universo; Reuters

World.title: Chile Probes China-Linked Telecom Espionage
World.content:
Chile · Technology

Key Facts Ongoing probe — Chile’s civil police and prosecutors are investigating possible cyber-espionage against telecom firms.

— Chile’s civil police and prosecutors are investigating possible cyber-espionage against telecom firms. Named carriers — Entel, Movistar and Telmex are cited as alleged targets of the suspected intrusions.

— Entel, Movistar and Telmex are cited as alleged targets of the suspected intrusions. US alert — Former US Ambassador Brandon Judd reportedly warned Chilean officials about possible attacks in February.

— Former US Ambassador Brandon Judd reportedly warned Chilean officials about possible attacks in February. Timeline — Suspected accesses reportedly ran from September 2024 to April 2025.

— Suspected accesses reportedly ran from September 2024 to April 2025. Alleged actor — Investigators are looking at ’Lilac Typhoon’, a Microsoft label for a China-linked threat group.

— Investigators are looking at ’Lilac Typhoon’, a Microsoft label for a China-linked threat group. Legal basis — Chile’s Law 21.663 and the National Cybersecurity Agency now mandate telecom incident reporting.

Police and prosecutors investigate possible cyber-espionage against Entel, Movistar and Telmex, after a US warning. No breach is confirmed yet.

The Chile cyberattack story is an ongoing investigation, not a confirmed breach, and it is rattling the country’s telecom sector. Police and prosecutors are probing possible cyber-espionage against the biggest phone and internet companies, including Entel, Movistar and Telmex. The probe, reportedly tagged ’Lilac Typhoon’ or ’Tifón Lila’, follows a warning from US authorities. If you live in or invest in Chile, this matters because telecoms hold your calls, messages and data. A real intrusion could mean widespread privacy fallout.

The investigation is being led by the civil police, under instructions from the Metropolitan Center-North Prosecutor’s Office. Reports from 8 and 9 August 2026 say the case is framed as possible ’sabotaje informático’, or computer sabotage. The alleged activity reportedly involved malicious programs designed to access equipment and transfer information.

The suspected accesses run from September 2024 to April 2025. That is a long window of potential exposure. No verified list of stolen records has been published. No company has confirmed a data breach.

For residents and investors, the stakes are clear. Telecom networks are essential services under Chilean law. A compromise could expose personal communications, billing details or network infrastructure. The investigation is a reminder that critical infrastructure is a prime target for state-linked actors.

The civil police and Metropolitan Center-North Prosecutor’s Office are leading the probe, which reportedly covers suspected accesses from September 2024 to April 2025. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

How The Case Surfaced: Chile cyberattack

The case came to light through a US diplomatic channel. Reports say former US Ambassador Brandon Judd delivered a written notice to then-security minister Luis Cordero earlier in 2026.

That notice mentioned possible attacks on electronic devices in Chile. It was then referred to the civil police.

El Dínamo first detailed the investigation on 8 August 2026. Emol followed on 9 August with reports of congressional concern.

Deputies are urging clarification of the alleged espionage. The specific US alert document has not been named publicly.

The timing fits a broader pattern. US agencies have increasingly shared threat intelligence with Latin American governments.

Chile, as a regional tech hub, is a natural recipient.

What Was Targeted

The reporting names Entel, Movistar and Telmex as alleged targets. These are three of Chile’s largest telecom operators, covering mobile, fixed-line and internet services.

One account also mentions Brotec Construcción, but that firm is not a telecom operator. The suspected activity reportedly aimed at national computer systems and telecom company information.

Attackers allegedly used malicious programs to access equipment and transfer data. Exactly which datasets were exfiltrated remains unconfirmed.

CrowdStrike research on telecom intrusions shows common targets. These include mobile subscriber information, call metadata and text messages.

That is a general pattern, not proof of what happened in Chile.

Company Responses

None of the named companies has issued a public statement about this investigation, according to the supplied sources. Entel, Movistar and Telmex have not confirmed or denied any intrusion.

They are also not commenting on the probe’s details. That silence is typical in an ongoing investigation.

Companies often wait for police findings before speaking publicly. Under Chile’s new cybersecurity law, they would be required to report confirmed incidents to regulators.

The lack of confirmed breach means customers have no specific action to take yet. Still, changing passwords and enabling two-factor authentication are sensible precautions.

Chile’s Cybersecurity Push

Chile has been building a stronger cyber-defence framework. Law 21.663, published on 8 April 2024, created the National Cybersecurity Agency.

The law imposes mandatory incident reporting for essential services, including telecoms. The agency completed its first qualification of Operators of Vital Importance on 24 July 2026.

That list covers entities whose disruption would have serious impact on the country. Telecom operators are central to that category.

The law gives the agency supervisory and sanctioning powers. Companies that fail to report incidents can face penalties.

This investigation will test how well the framework works in practice. For expats and investors, the framework offers some reassurance.

Chile is moving toward international standards on cyber-resilience. But the alleged espionage shows the threat is real.

What It Means For You

If you live in Chile, your phone and internet data could be at risk. A successful espionage operation could expose call records, messages or personal details.

The investigation is still early, so there is no evidence your data was taken. For firms operating in Chile, the lesson is to review security protocols.

Telecoms are a prime target for state-linked groups. The alleged actor, ’Lilac Typhoon’, is associated with the Chinese People’s Liberation Army as a concealment layer.

Investors should watch for regulatory fallout. If a breach is confirmed, expect scrutiny of telecom security practices.

That could mean higher compliance costs, but also a stronger sector overall.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the Chile cyberattack confirmed? No. Chilean police and prosecutors are investigating a possible cyber-espionage case against telecom firms. No breach has been officially confirmed. Which companies are named in the probe? Entel, Movistar and Telmex are named as possible targets. No company statement has been issued about the investigation. What is ’Lilac Typhoon’? It is a Microsoft label for a threat actor associated with China. Investigators are examining possible links to this group. What should I do if I’m a customer? There is no confirmed breach, so no urgent action is needed. Still, change passwords and enable two-factor authentication for safety.

Sources: Chile’s Fiscalía Metropolitana Centro Norte; the investigative police (PDI); a US cyber advisory; La Tercera; Reuters

World.title: US Bets US$150M on Guyana Bauxite to Break China’s Grip
World.content:
Guyana · Economy

Key Facts Deal size — US$85.5M equity plus US$64.5M private co-investment, totalling US$150M.

— US$85.5M equity plus US$64.5M private co-investment, totalling US$150M. Target asset — First Bauxite (FBX) mine in Guyana, plus new calcination facilities.

— First Bauxite (FBX) mine in Guyana, plus new calcination facilities. US strategy — Reduce reliance on Chinese-controlled refractory-grade bauxite.

— Reduce reliance on Chinese-controlled refractory-grade bauxite. Official visit — Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau in Guyana Aug 9–12, 2026.

— Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau in Guyana Aug 9–12, 2026. Next step — Brown-fused alumina plant to be built in the United States.

— Brown-fused alumina plant to be built in the United States. Source split — White House says ’over US$85M’; Kaieteur News details US$150M package.

Washington’s first major critical-minerals equity stake in Guyana targets refractory-grade ore and a new alumina plant on US soil.

Guyana bauxite is the story. The United States is putting real money behind its critical-minerals talk. A US$150 million package — including a US$85.5 million equity stake from the Department of War — will buy and expand the First Bauxite (FBX) mine in Guyana. This is the first big US government equity move in the country’s bauxite sector. It aims squarely at cutting dependence on Chinese-controlled supply of refractory-grade bauxite. The investment comes as Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau visits Georgetown from Aug. 9 to 12, 2026, to meet President Irfaan Ali and cabinet members. Energy and critical minerals are the top items on the agenda.

A bauxite mine in Guyana’s Berbice region, where the US-backed expansion will add new calcination facilities and secure refractory-grade supply. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What the US$150M Package Actually Buys: Guyana bauxite

The money splits two ways. The Department of War’s Economic Defense Unit and the Office of the Assistant Secretary of War for Industrial Base Policy are putting in US$85.5 million for an equity stake in Strategic Bauxite USA.

Private co-investors add US$64.5 million. Together, that’s US$150 million aimed at buying and expanding the FBX mine in Guyana.

They’re also funding new calcination facilities in Guyana. Further down the line, a brown-fused alumina plant would rise in the United States.

Brown-fused alumina is critical for refractories — the heat-resistant linings in steel furnaces and cement kilns. China controls most of the global supply.

Washington sees that as a weakness.

The White House fact sheet, released Aug. 9, 2026, confirms the broad strokes.

It says the Department of War is investing over US$85 million in ’Standard Bauxite’ — a name that doesn’t match Kaieteur News’s ’Strategic Bauxite USA’. The difference is notable.

Both sources agree on the strategic goal: secure refractory-grade bauxite supply chains outside Chinese control.

This deal also sends a message to other nations in the region. The US is ready to back its words with actual investment in hard assets.

Why Guyana, Why Now

Guyana has the right kind of bauxite. The refractory-grade ore there is high quality and relatively easy to access.

China has dominated this market for years, and the US wants a reliable alternative. Guyana is politically stable, close to US markets, and open to foreign investment.

For the US, this is about supply security. Refractory-grade bauxite is essential for making steel and cement, which are foundational for any economy.

If China decides to restrict exports, US industry would feel the pinch. This deal is a hedge against that risk.

The timing also matters. Deputy Secretary Landau’s visit is a clear signal that the US is serious about deepening ties with Guyana.

The country is already a growing oil producer, and now it’s becoming a critical minerals partner. That two-pronged relationship is rare in the region.

The choice of Guyana is no accident; its reserves are vast and its government is cooperative. This makes it a natural fit for US strategic goals.

What It Means for Investors and Expats

If you invest in Latin America, this deal is a template. The US government has now put equity — not just loans or grants — into a mining project in the region.

That changes the risk picture. A US government-backed mine in Guyana is a different asset than an unbacked one, especially with China’s role in critical minerals under scrutiny.

For expats living in Guyana, watch for knock-on effects. Infrastructure spending around mining towns, new logistics demand, and a possible influx of US technical staff could shift property and service markets.

The calcination facilities won’t be built overnight, but the project pipeline is real.

The brown-fused alumina plant in the US is a long-term signal. It means the US is willing to invest in downstream processing now, with the mine as the upstream anchor.

That vertical integration is rare for US government investments abroad. It could attract private capital into Guyana’s mining services sector.

For local businesses, this could mean new contracts and more jobs. But it also brings the risk of rising costs if demand outstrips supply.

Discrepancies and Open Questions

The numbers don’t fully line up across official sources. The White House says ’over US$85 million’ into ’Standard Bauxite’.

Kaieteur News reports US$85.5 million into ’Strategic Bauxite USA’ with US$64.5 million in co-investment. The difference could be a typo or a change in corporate name.

Either way, the total package is US$150 million per Kaieteur, and the White House doesn’t dispute that figure.

One oddity: the Office of the Assistant Secretary of War for Industrial Base Policy — that’s a new entity under the Department of War, created after the 2025 reorganization. It has a narrow goal: make sure the US military has access to critical materials.

Bauxite for refractories fits that goal because blast furnaces need those linings.

The Guyana government hasn’t officially commented on the deal, despite the investment being announced. Kaieteur News noted that silence.

That’s unusual for a transaction involving a sovereign’s mineral resources. Watch for a statement from the Ministry of Natural Resources in the coming days.

If Guyana pushes back, the deal could stall.

For now, the investment is announced, not closed. Legal and regulatory approvals in both countries are pending.

The visit by Deputy Secretary Landau could be the platform for a formal signing or at least a public endorsement. Expect more details by Aug.

12, when he leaves Georgetown.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Guyana bauxite deal worth? Kaieteur News reports the total package at US$150 million: a US$85.5 million equity investment from the US Department of War plus US$64.5 million in private co-investment. The White House fact sheet says only ’over US$85 million’, so the full figure isn’t officially confirmed. What will the money be used for? It will buy and expand the First Bauxite (FBX) mine in Guyana. It also funds new calcination facilities in Guyana and eventually a brown-fused alumina plant in the United States. Why is the US investing in Guyana bauxite? To reduce reliance on Chinese-controlled sources of refractory-grade bauxite. This grade is essential for making refractories used in steel and cement production. China dominates supply, and Washington sees that as a strategic risk. Who is the US official visiting Guyana? Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau. He is in Guyana from Aug. 9 to 12, 2026, and will meet President Irfaan Ali and cabinet members. Energy and critical minerals are the focus.

Sources: US White House and Department of War statements; Kaieteur News; Office of the President of Guyana; Reuters

World.title: US Venezuela Trade Jumps 113% To US$9.5bn In H1 2026
World.content:
Venezuela · Economy

Key Facts Trade jumps — US–Venezuela trade hit US$9.528 billion in the first half of 2026, up 113% on a year earlier.

— US–Venezuela trade hit US$9.528 billion in the first half of 2026, up 113% on a year earlier. Oil permits — Washington widened its oil licences in February 2026, letting Repsol join Chevron in Venezuela.

— Washington widened its oil licences in February 2026, letting Repsol join Chevron in Venezuela. Two rates — The street dollar trades near 841 bolivars, against an official rate of about 758.

— The street dollar trades near 841 bolivars, against an official rate of about 758. Wide gap — That leaves roughly a 13.5% gap between the official and street exchange rates.

— That leaves roughly a 13.5% gap between the official and street exchange rates. Bond pause — A new US licence on 3 August pushes back dealings in a PDVSA bond until 17 September.

Sanctions fail to slow the rebound. Oil licences broaden, while the bolivar’s parallel rate runs 13.5% above official.

Trade between the US and Venezuela rebounded hard in the first half of 2026. Bilateral commerce reached US$9.528 billion, up 113% from a year earlier, according to the US Bureau of Economic Analysis. The numbers landed on 8 August, and they show the sanctions regime is not stopping the flow of goods. For US investors and expats watching Latin America, this is a signal that engagement is deepening. The Venezuela trade surge touches energy, food imports, and the daily reality of a bolivar that trades well above official levels.

Venezuela trade charts show a 113% rise in H1 2026, while the parallel bolivar hit 841 per dollar on 10 August. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

Venezuela Trade Jumps 113%

The Bureau of Economic Analysis reported the figures on 8 August. The US$9.528 billion total covers exports and imports in both directions, a dramatic reversal from the declines of the prior two years.

The jump was driven largely by higher energy shipments, which rose after Washington expanded oil licences in February 2026. Agricultural machinery and chemical inputs also contributed, as US exporters took advantage of easing restrictions to meet Venezuelan demand for essential goods.

US goods heading south include machinery, agricultural products, and chemical inputs, with exports benefiting from the licence expansions that allowed more crude to flow north. Venezuela’s exports to the US are dominated by oil, though volumes remain limited by licence conditions that cap production and require specific approvals.

The growth is notable not just for the raw number but for the change in direction: two years of decline have reversed sharply, and the pace is far faster than most analysts predicted at the start of 2026.

Oil Licences Are The Engine

Chevron has kept operating under US Treasury licences, with its Venezuela oil output running at about 280,000 barrels per day under its existing authorisation. In February 2026, the US Treasury broadened permissions to include Repsol and other energy firms, allowing them to engage in selected oil and gas activities that had previously been off-limits.

This widening allowed additional crude volumes to reach US refineries, directly boosting the trade surplus and giving Venezuela a new source of hard currency.

These licences authorise selected oil and gas activities, but they are not permanent. Washington can change or revoke them as policy shifts, which is a key risk for companies like Chevron and Repsol that have committed capital to the country’s ageing infrastructure.

The licences also cover the import of diluents and other inputs needed for Venezuela’s heavy oil production, making them even more critical to the supply chain that feeds the trade numbers.

The latest action is General Licence 5Y, issued on 3 August 2026. It delays authorisation of transactions involving the PDVSA 2020 8.5% bond until 17 September 2026, replacing GL 5X.

This gives bondholders and the market a clear window, preventing a sudden move that could disrupt financial flows. The delay also signals that the US is in no hurry to force Venezuela into default, keeping the door open for further financial engagement and reducing immediate downside risk for investors holding Venezuelan assets.

The Bolivar’s Two-Tier Reality

On 10 August 2026, the parallel dollar traded near 841 bolivars, according to a rate tracker updated that same day. The official BCV rate sat at about 758 bolivars, with multiple Venezuelan outlets citing 757.54 Bs/USD, a 0.11% increment from the previous day.

That gap has widened over the past month as the central bank slowed its intervention in the foreign-exchange market, which had previously helped keep the spread narrower. The official rate is adjusted daily, but it lags behind street movements, creating a persistent arbitrage opportunity.

That is a black-market premium of roughly 13.5%, which is a substantial cost for anyone using official channels. Other trackers show slightly different figures, such as 855.16 Bs or 863.89 Bs, because they snapshot different moments in a fast-moving market with multiple sources.

The trend is what matters — the premium is creeping up, and it has not been this wide since the first quarter of the year, when the central bank faced similar pressure on reserves.

For anyone converting money in Venezuela, the gap matters. You lose around 13 cents on every dollar if you use official channels, which is a significant hit for expats receiving remittances or companies repatriating profits.

That premium drives everyday transactions toward the parallel market, where rates are set by supply and demand rather than central bank policy. It also complicates accounting for foreign firms, which must decide which rate to book their local income at, nor is there a clear international standard for which rate to apply in financial statements.

Why This Matters For You

If you live in Latin America or invest here, Venezuela trade flows affect regional supply chains, from energy pricing to the availability of goods in neighbouring markets. US dollars moving into the country ease import pressures and shape currency stability, as they provide a buffer for the bolivar and allow the government to fund essential purchases.

More dollars flowing in means the bolivar is less likely to slide further, but the parallel premium suggests the market is not fully convinced that the regime’s policies are sustainable.

The oil licences also influence global crude prices, as more Venezuelan barrels mean more supply, with the effect being modest so far but growing as volumes increase. This is particularly relevant for consumers in Brazil and beyond, where fuel prices are sensitive to shifts in global supply.

The expansion to Repsol and other firms in February was a clear signal that Washington wants to keep the flow going, despite the political risk involved.

Watch the 17 September bond deadline. If the licence is extended again, expect markets to hold steady, with little disruption to Venezuela-linked assets.

If not, expect volatility in bonds and equities tied to PDVSA, as well as a potential impact on the parallel dollar rate. For expats sending money home or investors holding PDVSA paper, the date is a key marker that should guide your next move.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did US–Venezuela trade rise 113%? The US Bureau of Economic Analysis reported US$9.528 billion in bilateral trade for H1 2026. Broader US oil licences and higher energy shipments drove most of the growth. What is the current parallel dollar rate in Venezuela? On 10 August 2026, the parallel rate was about 841 bolivars per US dollar. The official BCV rate was about 758 bolivars, implying a 13.5% premium. Are US sanctions on Venezuela still in place? Yes, but the US Treasury has issued targeted licences. February 2026 expansions added Repsol and other energy firms. The licences remain revocable at any time. What is General Licence 5Y? Issued on 3 August 2026, it delays authorisation of transactions involving the PDVSA 2020 8.5% bond until 17 September 2026. It replaces the earlier GL 5X.

Sources: US Bureau of Economic Analysis; Banco Central de Venezuela; US Treasury oil licences; Reuters

World.title: Vaca Muerta Nears Records, But US$20 Billion Gap Looms
World.content:
Argentina · Energy

Key Facts June output — Argentina pumped 914,900 barrels per day nationally, near its all-time high.

— Argentina pumped 914,900 barrels per day nationally, near its all-time high. Shale star — Vaca Muerta alone delivered 633,946 barrels per day in the same month.

— Vaca Muerta alone delivered 633,946 barrels per day in the same month. Global share — The country is approaching roughly 1% of world oil production.

— The country is approaching roughly 1% of world oil production. Ready to export — Analysts at BBVA reckon Argentina already has about 250,000 barrels a day it could sell abroad.

— Analysts at BBVA reckon Argentina already has about 250,000 barrels a day it could sell abroad. Export goal — YPF projects US$50 billion in Vaca Muerta exports by 2031.

— YPF projects US$50 billion in Vaca Muerta exports by 2031. Infrastructure gap — US$15–20 billion more is needed for pipelines, ports and terminals.

— US$15–20 billion more is needed for pipelines, ports and terminals. Tech tug-of-war — US pressure and Chinese tech collide over Huawei gear near the basin.

Argentina’s shale heartland is pumping near-record crude. Yet a missing US$20 billion in infrastructure could stall the boom just as Washington and Beijing circle.

Vaca Muerta is fuelling Argentina’s oil boom to near-record levels. National output hit 914,900 barrels per day in June, just shy of the magic million milestone, with the shale basin itself pumping 633,946 barrels daily. That puts the country on track for about 1% of world production, a rare leap for a nation long known for gas shortages. The boom is real, but so is the bottleneck. Without up to US$20 billion in new infrastructure, this momentum could stall. For anyone living or investing in Latin America, this is the region’s sharpest energy story right now.

Pump jacks dot the Vaca Muerta landscape in Neuquén, where output hit 633,946 bpd in June but export pipelines remain a constraint. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

Vaca Muerta’s Record Output, But Not Quite One Million

The numbers, from sector monitor an oil-sector monitor ALyC via Infobae, are striking. National crude output hit 914,900 barrels per day in June 2026.

Vaca Muerta, the Patagonian shale powerhouse, contributed 633,946 barrels of that, according to Ámbito. That is a near-record, but not the 1 million bpd some headlines hint at.

Argentina still has room to grow. The basin’s May shale output was 626,077 bpd, per Economies.com, showing steady momentum.

The world’s total production is vast, so even 915,000 bpd is just under 1% of it. The gap to the magic million is narrowing, but the infrastructure needed to sustain further growth remains the critical constraint.

Looking ahead, Vaca Muerta’s potential is immense. Developers are drilling faster and completing wells more efficiently.

Yet the surface logistics — pipelines, pumps, and port capacity — have not kept pace. The subsurface is rich; the surface is the new frontier.

Analysts at BBVA Research note that Argentina’s oil boom is now a story of connecting the basin to the world. The current exportable surplus of 250,000 barrels per day already needs better evacuation routes.

Every additional barrel of production requires a corresponding investment in midstream capacity.

It also offers aeronautical services, such as passenger, aircraft landing, parking charges,…

The US$20 Billion Infrastructure Challenge

Every barrel needs a pipeline, a port, and a terminal. BBVA Research warns that Argentina needs between US$15 billion and US$20 billion in extra investment for this midstream network.

That includes transport lines, compression stations, and export ports. The current surplus is already meaningful, with BBVA estimating a 250,000 barrel-per-day exportable surplus.

But moving that oil to global buyers requires infrastructure that is not fully built yet. The Vaca Muerta Oil Sur (VMOS) pipeline, a US$3.2 billion project, offers some relief with a 377,400 bpd capacity.

It is not enough on its own. Additional pipelines and port expansions are in planning, but financing remains a challenge.

The cost of inaction is high. Without the needed investment, production growth could plateau.

The industry is already feeling the pinch, with some operators slowing drilling programmes due to evacuation bottlenecks. The midstream gap is now the single biggest threat to the boom.

Argentina’s government is courting private capital, including from the United States and China. But geopolitical tensions over technology and trade are complicating the picture.

The infrastructure investment needed is vast, but the potential returns are equally large, with YPF projecting US$50 billion in exports by 2031.

The next two years will be pivotal. If the midstream network expands in time, Vaca Muerta could become a top-tier global exporter.

If not, the boom may peak earlier than expected. The world is watching.

YPF’s Big Bet on Export Riches

Argentina’s state-controlled energy giant YPF sees a huge prize ahead. It projects Vaca Muerta could generate US$50 billion in exports by 2031.

That figure, reported by EnergyNow, would transform Argentina’s trade balance. Energy exports already reached US$11.1 billion in 2025, and the country is becoming a dependable supplier.

But those export goals depend on solving the logistics puzzle. As BBVA notes, the constraint has shifted from the subsurface to the surface.

It is no longer about drilling wells; it is about moving the oil. YPF is investing in its own infrastructure, including the VMOS pipeline, but it cannot go it alone.

The company is also partnering with international investors to expand port capacity. The prize is substantial, but so is the risk of failure.

YPF’s projections assume that infrastructure keeps pace with production growth. That will require coordination between the public and private sectors, as well as regulatory stability.

The government has shown willingness to support the sector, but execution remains the key challenge.

If YPF succeeds, Vaca Muerta could rival other major shale plays in the United States. If not, the country risks squandering a once-in-a-generation opportunity.

The stakes could not be higher.

US-China Tug of War Over Huawei Tech

The energy boom now has a geopolitical subplot. CALF, a Neuquén utility, signed a contract with Huawei for fibre-optic and digital infrastructure.

The project sits near Vaca Muerta itself. US officials allegedly warned that executives’ visas could be restricted if the deal proceeded.

CALF says a US embassy official made that threat. China’s embassy called it interference in Argentina’s affairs.

The dispute also touches YPF, whose monitoring centre would use Huawei technology. This adds a layer of tension to an otherwise pure energy story.

The Huawei dispute is part of a broader US-China rivalry over technology and influence in Latin America. The US is wary of China’s growing presence in critical infrastructure, while China views such projects as part of its Belt and Road Initiative.

Argentina is caught in the middle.

The immediate impact on oil production is minimal, but the long-term risk is real. If geopolitical tensions escalate, they could deter investment in the very infrastructure needed to sustain the boom.

Both Washington and Beijing are courting Argentina, but with conflicting demands.

For now, the energy sector is pressing ahead, hoping that diplomacy will prevail. The industry is closely watching the outcome, as any disruption could affect the flow of capital and technology.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Vaca Muerta’s current oil output? Vaca Muerta produced 633,946 barrels per day in June 2026. National output was 914,900 bpd the same month, according to the an oil-sector monitor monitor. How much infrastructure investment does Vaca Muerta need? BBVA Research estimates US$15 billion to US$20 billion is needed for pipelines, compression, terminals, and ports. YPF projects about US$130 billion in cumulative investment through 2031. Is the US-China dispute affecting oil production? Not directly. The dispute centres on a Huawei-CALF fibre project near the basin. It adds political risk, but production has not been interrupted. What are Argentina’s export prospects from the shale boom? YPF projects US$50 billion in exports by 2031. Currently, the country has a 250,000 barrel-per-day exportable surplus, per BBVA Research.

Sources: Oil & Gas sector monitor via Infobae; YPF; BBVA Research; Argentina’s Energy Secretariat

World.title: Argentina Jobs Crisis Worsens as Formal Work Vanishes
World.content:
Argentina · Economy

Key Facts Jobs vanishing — More than 235,000 formal private jobs have gone since Milei took office in late 2023.

— More than 235,000 formal private jobs have gone since Milei took office in late 2023. Half off-book — 44.2% of workers now have no registered contract, the highest share in two decades.

— 44.2% of workers now have no registered contract, the highest share in two decades. More jobless — Unemployment has climbed to 7.8%, up from 5.7% when Milei started.

— Unemployment has climbed to 7.8%, up from 5.7% when Milei started. State cuts — About 130,000 government jobs have also disappeared since December 2023.

— About 130,000 government jobs have also disappeared since December 2023. Credit tightening — Banks are lending less as more borrowers fall behind on payments.

— Banks are lending less as more borrowers fall behind on payments. Precarious work — People who lose steady jobs are mostly landing in informal, unprotected ones.

— People who lose steady jobs are mostly landing in informal, unprotected ones. No rescue — The Central Bank has ruled out any government bailout for households in debt.

More than 235,000 formal private-sector jobs have disappeared since Milei took office. Informality has hit a two-decade high, and the credit market is feeling the squeeze.

Argentina jobs are disappearing fast under Javier Milei, and it is starting to hit ordinary wallets. More than 235,000 formal private jobs have gone since he took office in late 2023, on official social-security records. Nearly half of all workers, 44.2%, now work off the books — the most in twenty years. That matters for you: shaky work means banks lend less, so credit is drying up for shoppers and small firms alike.

Job seekers line up outside an INDEC labour office in Buenos Aires, August 2026, as formal employment hits a two-decade low. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

The Argentina Jobs Numbers Behind the Headlines

The 235,000 figure is a cumulative loss, not a single-day event. It covers the stretch from Milei’s election in November 2023 to April 2026, as counted by researchers from the University of Buenos Aires and the national research council, using Social Security records.

Other official data paint an even broader picture. The Ministry of Human Capital, as summarised by El País, counts almost 400,000 fewer formal salaried jobs overall — 250,000 in the private sector, 130,000 in the public sector, and 17,400 in domestic work.

Unemployment is also climbing. The national statistics agency says 7.8% of the workforce was jobless in Q1 2026, compared to 5.7% when Milei began his term, according to the Buenos Aires Herald.

The informal sector is soaking up the displaced. Private studies cited by Análisis Digital say the bulk of new jobs created in the last year were informal, without pension or health contributions.

The trend is not just a statistic; it is reshaping the labour market’s very structure. According to Sebastián Menescaldi, associate director at EcoGo, ’the quality of employment is deteriorating: the fall in registered salaried employment is not being offset by better conditions elsewhere, but by precarious activities.’

This shift has deep roots. For decades, Argentina’s formal labour market has been shrinking relative to the informal sector, but the acceleration under Milei’s austerity policies is notable.

The report from the University of Buenos Aires and the national research council highlights that most job losses in the private sector were in construction, manufacturing, and commerce, sectors that are highly sensitive to economic downturns.

The regional distribution is also uneven. According to the same report, the provinces most affected include Córdoba, Santa Fe, and the city of Buenos Aires, where formal employment dropped by more than 8% on average.

In contrast, some provinces with strong agricultural or energy exports have seen less severe losses.

Why Credit Is Drying Up

Here is the trap. The cash economy soaks up people who lose formal jobs, but it locks them out of banking.

Informal workers have no stable income proof, so banks won’t lend to them.

Rising arrears are braking credit recovery across the board. The Buenos Aires Herald reports that high defaults are ’putting a brake on the recovery of consumer credit’.

Borrowers who fall behind are being shut out of the financial system, which further slows lending. And there is no state lifeline coming — the Central Bank dismissed a household-debt bailout as a matter between private parties.

For consumers, that means tighter credit cards and fewer personal loans. If you’re an expat relying on a local credit line, expect higher rejection rates and steeper interest.

The squeeze reaches past consumer credit. Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) that rely on formal workers for collateral or income verification are also facing more difficulties in securing financing.

A recent survey of small firms found that 60% had less access to bank loans in the first half of 2026.

Without a formal contract, many workers also lose out on pensions and private health cover. The government saves money now, but the longer-term bill is more poverty and inequality.

Banks, still bruised by past crises, are lending mostly to people with formal jobs. That leaves nearly half the workforce shut out, split off into a cash economy the banks won’t touch.

Why This Matters for Your Money and Your Future

If you live in Argentina or invest here, the jobs crisis is not just a statistic. It shapes everything from property demand to the peso’s stability.

When fewer people have steady pay, they spend less. That slows the economy and dents company profits, so tread carefully with local shares and bonds that depend on Argentines shopping.

For expats, the rise in informality means a tighter job market if you’re seeking local employment, and a less predictable business environment if you’re hiring. The days of easy formal contracts are on hold.

The good news? Similar crises have eventually reversed when structural reforms took hold.

But that’s a long-term play, not a quick fix. Watch the labour data closely — it’s the best early sign of recovery.

The political climate also adds a layer of uncertainty. With midterm elections scheduled for late 2026, the Milei administration faces growing pressure to address the jobs crisis.

However, any new spending could conflict with austerity measures, potentially leading to a stalemate that prolongs the slump.

On a brighter note, some sectors are showing resilience. Agricultural exports, energy, and technology services have generated formal employment in regions less affected by the recession.

For example, the province of Neuquén has benefited from Vaca Muerta shale oil, creating thousands of formal jobs despite the national downturn.

For expats considering relocation, the key is to understand that the formal labour market is currently not an easy entry point. Many are instead choosing to work remotely for foreign companies, which shields them from the local contraction.

But if you plan to invest locally, assess the risk closely.

The consumer credit market is likely to remain subdued for the rest of 2026. Banks are expected to keep their lending criteria tight, and interest rates remain high.

If you are in debt, consider consolidating or refinancing where possible, though options are limited.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many formal jobs has Argentina lost under Milei? More than 235,000 formal private-sector salaried jobs were lost between November 2023 and April 2026, per a study from the University of Buenos Aires and the national research council. Including public sector and domestic work, the total is almost 400,000, according to Ministry of Human Capital data cited by El País. What is the current informality rate in Argentina? The national statistics agency’s household survey shows 44.2% of workers were informal in Q1 2026, the highest in recent records. That means nearly one in two workers lacks a registered contract. How does informality affect access to credit? Informal workers often have no proof of stable income, so banks reject them for loans. Rising arrears among formal borrowers also brake credit recovery, as the Buenos Aires Herald reports. Will the state bail out households in debt? No. The Central Bank called any state debt-forgiveness a matter between private parties and dismissed a bailout. That leaves consumers and investors to face the squeeze alone.

Sources: INDEC household survey; a University of Buenos Aires and Conicet labour study; El Economista; Buenos Aires Herald

World.title: Bolivia IMF Deal: What US$1.9bn Means for You
World.content:
Bolivia · Economy

Key Facts Deal size — The IMF’s Extended Fund Facility is US$1.9bn over 36 months, announced 29 July 2026.

— The IMF’s Extended Fund Facility is US$1.9bn over 36 months, announced 29 July 2026. Extra cash — Up to US$5bn more could come from other multilateral lenders, but nothing is locked yet.

— Up to US$5bn more could come from other multilateral lenders, but nothing is locked yet. Bolsín gone — The old fixed exchange-rate mechanism ends, replaced by a more flexible regime.

— The old fixed exchange-rate mechanism ends, replaced by a more flexible regime. Fuel crunch — Diesel shortages and falling gas exports helped push Bolivia to the IMF.

— Diesel shortages and falling gas exports helped push Bolivia to the IMF. Still pending — The IMF Executive Board and Bolivia’s Congress must both approve the deal.

— The IMF Executive Board and Bolivia’s Congress must both approve the deal. Key figures — President Rodrigo Paz and Economy Minister José Gabriel Espinoza lead the reforms.

A staff-level agreement could unlock billions more and reshape the boliviano, fuel prices and investor rules. Here’s what changes.

Bolivia IMF agreement has been reached at staff level, a US$1.9 billion Extended Fund Facility that is not yet a done deal. The 36-month program, announced on 29 July 2026, still needs approval from the IMF Executive Board and Bolivia’s Congress. If approved, the deal could unlock up to US$5 billion in additional financing from other multilateral lenders. That extra money matters more than the headline figure, as it is the bridge that could carry Bolivia through its worst economic crisis in decades. For investors and expats, the real story is what comes next. The old bolsín cambiario exchange-rate mechanism is finished, replaced by a more flexible regime with limited central bank intervention. That shift changes how you should think about the boliviano, fuel prices and getting dollars out of the country. Here is a practical guide to what this Bolivia IMF program means for anyone living in or invested in Bolivia.

The Banco Central de Bolivia building in La Paz, where officials confirmed the end of the bolsín cambiario on 30 July 2026. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

Bolivia IMF Deal: What It Actually Covers

The Extended Fund Facility is the IMF’s main tool for countries with serious balance-of-payments problems, and Bolivia qualifies on all counts. The country is dealing with falling natural gas exports, a severe shortage of foreign currency and persistent diesel fuel shortages, according to Reuters and official statements.

The US$1.9bn figure is the IMF’s own commitment, not the US$5bn total that some headlines have suggested. That larger number is the expected extra financing from other lenders like the World Bank and the Inter-American Development Bank, which an IMF program typically unlocks.

Think of the IMF deal as a seal of approval; other multilaterals are far more willing to lend when the IMF has signed off on a country’s reforms. The staff-level agreement is a strong signal, not a guarantee, as final approval could take weeks.

Why the Boliviano and Fuel Markets Are Shifting

Bolivia’s crisis did not come from nowhere. Natural gas exports, once the backbone of the economy, have fallen sharply as reserves deplete, resulting in a shortage of dollars that made it hard for importers to pay for fuel and other essentials.

Diesel shortages have been a recurring problem, hitting transport and agriculture hardest. The IMF program is designed to fix these imbalances, but the medicine is bitter: expect fuel subsidies to be phased down, which means higher prices at the pump.

Expect the exchange rate to become more market-driven, which means the boliviano could weaken further against the dollar. For anyone earning in bolivianos and spending in dollars, the trend is clear.

Budget for a weaker currency and higher local prices, while those earning dollars could see opportunities. A more realistic exchange rate makes Bolivian assets cheaper for foreign buyers, from real estate to mining ventures and export businesses, if the reforms hold.

What Investors and Expats Should Watch Next

The IMF program is only the beginning of a longer adjustment. The US$5bn in potential additional financing is contingent on Bolivia meeting program targets, including fiscal consolidation and exchange-rate reforms.

For investors, that means watching three things: the pace of fuel subsidy cuts, the central bank’s intervention policy and the government’s handling of dollar liquidity. Each will signal whether the reforms are real or just paperwork.

For expats, the practical effects are more immediate: if you hold local currency, consider how much you need in the short term and how much you can convert to dollars, and if you run a business, factor in higher input costs and a weaker exchange rate. If you are paid from abroad, your purchasing power in bolivianos will likely rise.

The IMF deal is not a rescue; it is a framework for Bolivia to rescue itself, and the difference is crucial.

There is also the question of timing. The IMF’s Extended Fund Facility typically disburses in tranches, tied to quarterly reviews, so Bolivia will not see the full US$1.9bn at once.

The first disbursement might come within weeks of board approval, but subsequent tranches depend on meeting fiscal targets and structural benchmarks. That means the programme could stall if the government backtracks on subsidy reform or if the central bank resorts to heavy-handed intervention.

For investors, a useful proxy is the central bank’s net international reserves, which have been dwindling; a sustained rebuild would signal credibility, while a continued slide would suggest the old habits are back.

The Bottom Line for Latin America

Bolivia’s IMF breakthrough is a regional signal. It shows that multilateral lenders are willing to support countries that confront hard truths, even if the politics are messy.

For anyone invested elsewhere in Latin America, the lesson is simple: countries that move toward flexible exchange rates and realistic fiscal policy get financed, while those that cling to artificial stability get cut off. Bolivia just chose the first path; the next six months will show whether it can walk it.

The Bolivia IMF story is not over with this staff-level agreement; it is the opening act. The real drama will unfold in the corridors of the central bank and parliament, but for now, the direction is clear: fewer subsidies, a floating boliviano and a more open economy.

That is a profound change for a country that once nationalised its gas industry and railed against the IMF. If the program succeeds, Bolivia could rewrite its economic narrative; if it fails, the consequences could be severe.

Either way, the world is watching.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the IMF deal final? No. It is a staff-level agreement announced on 29 July 2026. The IMF Executive Board and Bolivia’s Congress must still approve it. How much money could Bolivia actually get? The IMF program itself is US$1.9 billion. Up to US$5 billion in additional financing could come from other multilateral lenders, but only if the program is approved and reforms are implemented. What happened to the bolsín cambiario? The traditional fixed exchange-rate mechanism has ended. The central bank now uses a more flexible regime with limited intervention, which means the boliviano will be more market-driven. Will fuel prices go up? Very likely. The IMF program typically requires phasing down fuel subsidies. Expect higher diesel and gasoline prices as part of the adjustment.

Sources: International Monetary Fund; Banco Central de Bolivia; Bolivia’s Economy Ministry; Reuters

World.title: Strange Balloon-Like Object Spotted Over Costa Rica
World.content:
A mysterious white object seen high above several parts of Costa Rica over the weekend triggered a new round of speculation online, with residents sharing photos and videos from communities stretching from the Central Valley to the Pacific coast. Sightings were reported Saturday, August 8, from areas including Quepos, Pérez Zeledón, Acosta, Grecia and Heredia.

Additional reports came from Alajuela and Cartago, with witnesses describing a white, roughly circular object that appeared to be floating high in the sky. By today, the object had a likely general explanation but still no publicly identified owner. The National Meteorological Institute (IMN), said the object does not belong to the agency.

Based on its visible characteristics, however, the institute said it appears to be some type of balloon. That distinction leaves an important part of the mystery unresolved: who launched it, where it came from and what it was carrying. High-altitude balloons are commonly used for weather observations, atmospheric research, communications, photography and other scientific work.

Weather balloons can carry a radiosonde, a small instrument package that measures atmospheric conditions such as temperature, humidity and pressure while its movement can also be used to calculate wind speed and direction.The radiosonde is technically the instrument suspended beneath the balloon, rather than the balloon itself.

Costa Rica has seen a remarkably similar episode before. On February 2, 2023, a large white balloon was visible from numerous parts of our country, including the Pacific, Central Valley and Caribbean. The object initially puzzled authorities. Neither the IMN nor the University of Costa Rica said it belonged to them, and Civil Aviation officials said at the time that they had no record identifying who had launched it.

University of Costa Rica researchers initially examined images and said the object appeared consistent with the type of balloon used to carry atmospheric instruments. But the mystery did not end there. Several days later, China acknowledged that one of its balloons had passed through Costa Rican airspace and formally apologized to Costa Rica for the incident. Chinese officials described the aircraft as a civilian device used for research and said it had deviated from its intended route because of weather conditions.

The incident unfolded at the same time that another Chinese high-altitude balloon crossed the United States, setting off an international dispute before the U.S. military shot it down off the coast of South Carolina. U.S. officials described that balloon as a surveillance platform, while China maintained that it was a civilian research aircraft that had gone off course.

Costa Rica had another unexplained balloon-like object only a month later, in March 2023. That object was spotted over La Unión, and Civil Aviation, the IMN and university researchers again said they did not know who had launched it. The object seen over Costa Rica this weekend has not been connected to those earlier events, and there is currently no evidence suggesting it came from China or served any surveillance purpose.

For now, the most that can be said with confidence is that it appears to be a balloon, it does not belong to Costa Rica’s national weather service, and its origin remains publicly unidentified.

World.title: Costa Rica Targets Luxury Car Tax Evasion After Ferrari Case
World.content:
A Ferrari declared for a fraction of its real value has become the poster case for a customs loophole that Costa Rica’s vehicle importers say is bleeding Costa Rica of millions in tax revenue. The Asociación de Importadores de Vehículos y Maquinaria, (Aivema), is warning that luxury vehicles worth well over one hundred thousand dollars have been declared at Customs for as little as fifteen hundred dollars, and the Ministry of Finance has confirmed similar cases of its own.

Among the examples Hacienda has publicly cited is a Toyota Land Cruiser with a real market value near one hundred forty thousand dollars that was declared at only twenty thousand, a gap that allowed the importer to avoid roughly twenty six million colones in taxes. In a separate case, a Ferrari’s undervaluation created a tax shortfall of more than sixty seven million colones, or roughly one hundred thirty five thousand dollars.

The heart of the problem traces back to a policy shift Hacienda made in 2024. Import taxes on vehicles used to be calculated against a government table of minimum market prices. Under the new system, importers simply self-declare a vehicle’s value, and Customs calculates taxes from that figure. In practice, many importers have been declaring numbers far below what the vehicles are actually worth.

One widely cited case involved a two thousand twenty five BMW X6 M declared at just over seven thousand dollars despite a real Costa Rican market value near one hundred ninety five thousand dollars. The shift has coincided with a sixteen percent drop in tax revenue collected from vehicle imports, and Aivema’s leadership says the government has known about the problem for roughly a year without implementing a fix.

The issue surfaces as part of a much larger fiscal enforcement campaign. Costa Rica recently unveiled a package of twenty four measures aimed at strengthening tax collection and cracking down on evasion and smuggling without creating new taxes. Hacienda Minister Víctor Julio Carvajal has said tax evasion costs the country more than two point six billion colones annually and has described vehicle undervaluation as theft on a large scale.

Three related bills are moving through the legislative pipeline, including one that would let Hacienda set maximum taxable values by decree, one targeting the sale of fraudulent electronic invoices worth an estimated seven hundred billion colones in circulation, and one meant to speed up judicial collection on roughly four hundred billion colones in unresolved tax debt.

The undervaluation problem also intersects with organized crime investigations already underway. Following raids connected to the so called Lusso case, prosecutors seized twenty one luxury vehicles worth a combined two point seven million dollars, including two Ferraris tied to the alleged leader of a criminal network, several of which were found circulating without registration or tax payment.

Separate audits have found undervaluation of import declarations reaching as high as sixty eight percent of a luxury vehicle’s real value, a pattern investigators now treat as a potential red flag for money laundering rather than simple tax avoidance.

Aivema is pushing for Hacienda to restore a verification mechanism for declared vehicle values and has reminded the ministry that it retains the legal authority to audit declarations and collect any unpaid taxes retroactively.

World.title: Costa Rica Faces Strong Winds, Saharan Dust and Heat
World.content:
Strong trade winds, Saharan dust and unusually hot conditions will affect several parts of Costa Rica today, with gusts potentially reaching 95 km/h (59 mph) in higher elevations. Wind speeds of 40 to 70 km/h (25 to 43 mph) are expected across the Central Valley, northern Pacific, mountain ranges and occasionally the far north of the Northern Zone.



The strongest gusts, ranging from 80 to 95 km/h (50 to 59 mph), are forecast for mountainous areas. Drivers should exercise particular caution on exposed roads and mountain passes, especially when operating motorcycles, high-profile vehicles or vehicles carrying unsecured loads. Strong gusts may also bring down branches and affect lightweight outdoor structures.

The windy conditions coincide with a new mass of Saharan dust moving across Costa Rica. The dust began arriving through the Caribbean on Saturday and is expected to cover more of the country on Sunday. Its presence will reduce atmospheric moisture, bringing sunnier skies, fewer widespread showers and higher daytime temperatures.

Liberia could reach 36.5°C (97.7°F), while Nicoya may reach 35.9°C (96.6°F). People spending time outdoors in Guanacaste and other hot areas should limit prolonged exposure during the middle of the day, drink water regularly and avoid leaving children or animals inside parked vehicles.

San José is forecast to reach approximately 26.7°C (80.1°F), with an overnight low near 18.8°C (65.8°F). Partly cloudy conditions are expected across the Central Valley, although light drizzle remains possible in higher areas. Despite the drier air, rain has not been ruled out completely. Cloud cover may increase over the southern Pacific during the afternoon, followed by greater cloudiness over the Caribbean at night. Isolated showers are possible in both areas.

Saharan dust can produce hazy skies and reduce visibility. It may also aggravate symptoms among people with asthma, allergies and other respiratory conditions. Those who are sensitive to airborne particles may want to reduce strenuous outdoor activity if the haze becomes noticeable.

The windy, dry pattern is expected to extend into the beginning of the week. Tropical Wave No. 30 is forecast to approach Costa Rica on Monday, although its potential to generate heavy rain appears limited because it will move through an atmosphere with relatively low moisture.

World.title: João Fonseca Builds Momentum Ahead of Cincinnati Open With Montreal Run
World.content:
João Fonseca is beginning to find his form at exactly the right time. The 19-year-old Brazilian defeated former world No. 2 Casper Ruud 7-6(6), 6-3 at the National Bank Open in Montreal, giving one of Latin America’s fastest-rising tennis players another significant victory just days before the Cincinnati Open.



Fonseca followed an opening win over Stefanos Tsitsipas with an increasingly confident performance against Ruud, overcoming an uneven start before taking control from the baseline. The result sends him into a Sunday showdown with defending Montreal champion Ben Shelton and provides another indication that Fonseca could arrive in Cincinnati as considerably more than a young player worth watching.

He may arrive as one of the dangerous players nobody particularly wants to see nearby in the draw.

Fonseca Finds a Way Against Ruud

The victory over Ruud was not as straightforward as the score eventually suggested. Fonseca struggled early on serve and fell behind 4-2 in the first set before breaking back immediately. He then recovered from 5-3 down in the tiebreak to take the opening set. From there, the match changed.

The Brazilian began dictating more points with the aggressive baseline tennis that has quickly become his trademark. He broke Ruud early in the second set and did not face another break point on his way to the victory. It was Fonseca’s fourth win against a Top 20 opponent this season and improved his career record against Ruud to 2-0.



The other victory came at Roland Garros earlier this year, when Fonseca defeated the Norwegian during his breakthrough run to the quarterfinals in Paris. Perhaps more important than another highly ranked scalp was the way Fonseca adjusted after the difficult opening That ability to solve problems during matches has become increasingly important as his level of competition has risen.

Strong Return After Wimbledon

Montreal is Fonseca’s first tour-level tournament since Wimbledon, where his run ended in the third round. Any questions about rust have disappeared quickly. His first match back came against former world No. 3 Stefanos Tsitsipas, and Fonseca won 7-6(3), 7-5. Even that match required some composure.



Fonseca failed to serve out the contest at 5-4 in the second set but responded by winning eight of the next nine points. Two matches later, he is still in Montreal without having dropped a set. The combination of victories over Tsitsipas and Ruud is particularly encouraging because they required Fonseca to handle different styles and different moments of pressure.

Those are precisely the kinds of situations that become increasingly important during the North American hard-court season.

Ben Shelton Provides the Next Test

Fonseca’s next challenge will be considerably more difficult. He faces American Ben Shelton on Sunday evening for a place in the Montreal quarterfinals. The match is scheduled for no earlier than 6 p.m. in Montreal, or 4 p.m. in Costa Rica. Shelton, ranked No. 10, is the defending champion and the highest-ranked player remaining in the tournament.

Like Fonseca, he has not lost a set during his first two matches. The two have met once before. Shelton defeated Fonseca in three sets in the quarterfinals in Munich earlier this year. That match was played on clay, making Sunday’s hard-court meeting a different test.

Shelton’s left-handed serve is particularly dangerous on a court where the ball is bouncing high, while Fonseca’s ability to attack from both wings gives him the kind of power needed to prevent the American from controlling points. It will also be Fonseca’s sixth match against a Top 10 player this season.

He has already faced Jannik Sinner, Carlos Alcaraz, Alexander Zverev and Novak Djokovic in addition to Shelton. Few teenagers receive that level of experience so quickly.

Cincinnati Comes Next

Whatever happens against Shelton, Fonseca’s Montreal performance changes the context surrounding his arrival at the Cincinnati Open. Fonseca is currently listed at No. 27 in the Cincinnati player field, placing him firmly among the strongest Latin American entrants in Mason.



Argentina’s Francisco Cerúndolo, Tomás Martín Etcheverry and Sebastián Báez, Peru’s Ignacio Buse and Chile’s Alejandro Tabilo are also part of a substantial regional presence in the men’s tournament. But Fonseca is increasingly becoming the player who attracts the most attention.

Part of that comes from age and potential. Part comes from the way he plays. Fonseca is willing to attack early in rallies and possesses enough power off both sides to push established players behind the baseline. When the first serve is working, he can shorten points considerably.



The more interesting development this season, however, has been his ability to survive when everything is not working. That was visible against Tsitsipas. It was even clearer against Ruud.

No Longer Just a Prospect

Fonseca has spent much of the past two seasons carrying the label of Brazilian tennis’ next major prospect. That description is becoming outdated. At 19, he has already won ATP titles, reached a Grand Slam quarterfinal and defeated some of the best-known players in the sport.



His run at Roland Garros included one of the biggest victories of the season when he came from two sets down to defeat Novak Djokovic before beating Ruud in the following round. Those performances raised expectations considerably. They also changed the standard by which Fonseca is now judged.

Reaching a Masters 1000 tournament and playing competitive tennis is no longer particularly surprising. The question is increasingly how far he can go. Montreal is providing another answer.

A Player to Watch in Cincinnati

The Cincinnati Open main draw begins August 13 at the Lindner Family Tennis Center in Mason, Ohio, one of the final major stops before the US Open. For Fonseca, Cincinnati represents another opportunity to test his rapidly developing hard-court game against an elite field before traveling to New York.

A week ago, he would have arrived with questions about his form following a break from tour-level competition. Those questions are disappearing. Straight-set victories over Tsitsipas and Ruud have replaced them with another one. How much further can João Fonseca go?

Ben Shelton will provide the next answer Sunday night. Cincinnati comes immediately afterward.

World.title: FIFA Defends Gianni Infantino Amid Leadership Crisis
World.content:
FIFA has accused critics of waging a “concerted and ongoing effort” to undermine the organization and its president, Gianni Infantino, as the crisis surrounding his leadership continues to deepen. The governing body issued a strongly worded statement Saturday defending Infantino following the collapse of a controversial proposal to bring private investors into FIFA’s World Cup commercial business.

The plan triggered fierce opposition from several major football organizations and has left Infantino facing boycott threats, calls for his resignation and growing questions about his bid for another term as FIFA president. Infantino, who has led FIFA since 2016, is seeking reelection at the organization’s congress in March 2027. FIFA’s 211 member associations will ultimately decide whether he remains in office.

European football’s governing body UEFA has emerged as one of his strongest critics. Despite FIFA abandoning the private investment proposal, UEFA has said the decision alone is not enough to restore confidence in Infantino’s leadership. The dispute has escalated to the point that European football officials have threatened to boycott FIFA competitions, including World Cups.

New Allegations Add to Pressure

Infantino faced another controversy Friday after The Telegraph reported allegations involving his time as UEFA general secretary between 2009 and 2016. The British newspaper alleged that Infantino used his influence to help secure the promotion of a female UEFA employee with whom he was reportedly involved in a personal relationship.

Infantino has categorically denied the allegations. The Telegraph also reported that the employee later received a six-figure payment when she left UEFA, along with approximately €50,000 ($57,800) toward an MBA program. UEFA has acknowledged that a payment was made to the former employee and that expenses connected with an MBA program were also covered.

FIFA did not specifically identify the Telegraph report in its Saturday statement but pushed back strongly against recent coverage surrounding its president. “Recent reporting has included unsubstantiated assertions and demonstrably false claims concerning FIFA and its president,” the organization said. FIFA added that speculation and insinuation should not be treated as fact and said it would challenge inaccurate or misleading reporting.

FIFA Warns Against Attempts to Remove Infantino

FIFA also emphasized that any effort to replace Infantino must follow the organization’s statutes and established election procedures. “Those who do not have the support of FIFA’s Member Associations should not seek to achieve through allegation, insinuation or misinformation what they cannot achieve through FIFA’s established democratic processes,” the organization said.

FIFA’s leadership reaffirmed its support for Infantino during a crisis meeting in Morocco earlier this week. The organization also apologized to its 211 member associations for mistakes in the way the private investment proposal was handled, acknowledging that members should have been more involved in the process.

That apology has done little to settle the dispute. UEFA has said it has lost confidence in Infantino, while Norwegian Football Federation president Lise Klaveness went further Friday and publicly called for him to resign. Klaveness, one of Infantino’s most outspoken critics in international football, said he no longer has the institutional trust necessary to lead FIFA.

Her name has also been mentioned as a possible future candidate for the FIFA presidency, although she has played down speculation about running.

Infantino Retains Support Outside Europe

Despite the growing pressure in Europe, Infantino continues to receive significant backing elsewhere. The Confederation of African Football has publicly supported his leadership, while South American governing body Conmebol has rejected attempts to remove him outside FIFA’s established electoral process.

Infantino traveled to Cali, Colombia, on Friday for the inauguration of newly elected right-wing President Abelardo de la Espriella, where Conmebol president Alejandro Domínguez reiterated his support. Domínguez said Infantino’s work at FIFA should not be ignored and called for disagreements within world football to be resolved through dialogue.

The competing statements highlight a widening divide within international football ahead of the 2027 FIFA presidential election. For years, Infantino appeared to be heading toward another term with relatively little resistance. The collapse of the private investment plan and the increasingly public confrontation between FIFA and UEFA have now turned what once looked like a straightforward reelection campaign into one of the most serious leadership crises of his decade in charge.

World.title: Costa Rica Reports Renewed Increase in COVID-19 Cases
World.content:
COVID-19 has once again become the most widely circulating respiratory virus detected in Costa Rica, as health officials urge residents to take basic precautions amid an increase in cases and hospitalizations. The latest epidemiological surveillance places COVID-19 ahead of rhinovirus and parainfluenza among respiratory viruses currently circulating here.

During epidemiological week 29, covering July 13 through July 19, Costa Rica recorded 126 confirmed COVID-19 cases, up from 94 the previous week. That represents an increase of about 34%. Hospitalizations also climbed, with 29 COVID-19 patients receiving hospital care compared with 18 the previous week, an increase of roughly 56%. Five deaths associated with COVID-19 were reported during the same epidemiological week.

The figures remain far below the levels Costa Rica experienced during the height of the pandemic, and there is currently no national health alert for respiratory illnesses. However, the change in circulation has prompted renewed attention as several respiratory viruses spread simultaneously.

Costa Rica has recorded more than 771,000 cases of respiratory illness so far this year, a broader figure that includes illnesses caused by multiple viruses rather than COVID-19 alone. Children, older adults and people with chronic health conditions remain among those considered most vulnerable to complications from respiratory infections.

Health authorities are recommending many of the familiar measures used to reduce respiratory infections: keeping vaccinations current, washing hands regularly, covering coughs and sneezes and choosing well-ventilated spaces when possible. People experiencing respiratory symptoms are also being encouraged to avoid crowded activities and limit close contact with vulnerable relatives or friends until they recover.

The renewed circulation of COVID-19 comes during Costa Rica’s rainy season, when respiratory illnesses can become more noticeable as people spend more time indoors and several viruses circulate at the same time. For residents and travelers, the latest numbers do not signal a return to pandemic-era restrictions. There have been no announcements of renewed mask mandates, travel requirements or widespread restrictions connected to the current increase.

Instead, the emphasis remains on individual precautions, particularly for people at greater risk of serious illness. Health officials continue to monitor COVID-19 alongside influenza, rhinovirus, parainfluenza and other respiratory illnesses to identify changes in circulation and hospital demand.

World.title: Three-term Mayor Rigo Vellos defeats Shajarie Rogers in heated PUP convention in Corozal Town
World.content:
Three-term Mayor Rigo Vellos defeats Shajarie Rogers in heated PUP convention in Corozal Town

By Jose Luis Cruz: Three-term Mayor Rigoberto ‘Rigo’ Vellos has emerged victorious in Sunday’s heated PUP convention in Corozal Town. Vellos defeated Shajarie Rogers against all the odds to remain as the PUP’s mayoral candidate for Corozal Town.

At the close of polls today, officials reported that over 3,400 people had casted their votes. Tensions, which were already high prior to today’s convention, rose to more than once as voting progressed and the vote counting began.

Earlier tonight Breaking Belize News reported that unofficially Vellos was victorious and that the Vellos team for councilors were also leading but that the split ballots remained to be counted

According to PUP Chairman Henry Charles Usher Vellos received 1,790 votes to seal the victory.

World.title: BTL – From Beginning to End: Ashcroft Gets The Last Laugh?
World.content:
BTL – From Beginning to End: Ashcroft Gets The Last Laugh?

The views expressed in this article are those of the author and not necessarily those of Breaking Belize News.

By Adam Flowers: From the very beginning in 1988, when the Esquivel-UDP first opened BTL to public shareholding, perennial Belizean boogeyman Lord Michael Ashcroft slowly sank his fangs into the company; and now nearly 40 years, several administrations, half a billion dollars and countless controversies later including this latest; he is taking one last bite of the BTL pie and having the last laugh.

After tooth and nail, BTL was finally nationalized in 2009; at an enormous gross nationalization-related outlay to Belize of roughly $564 Million. And even that figure does not necessarily represent the complete bill. Once years of accumulated interest, legal and arbitration expenses, tax concessions and other costs arising from the wider BTL saga are considered, contemporary estimates placed the overall cost closer to $700 Million. Opposition parliamentarians were already warning by 2017 that the final figure could approach $700 Million, though no single audited Government accounting has established $700 Million as an exact final nationalization cost. More than half the big B. The cost associated with liberation from Ashcroft’s near-total control of Belize’s telecommunications sector; only now to once again intertwine itself with Ashcroft-linked interests through the Speednet acquisition through 2030 for almost another $100 Million.

And are we surprised that the maturity of the amortization schedule coincides with the year in which the next general election cycle would culminate in 2030, if the current term runs its full course?
