Others have also questioned why, if prosecutors had sufficient evidence, the girls were arrested only 10 months after the murder. Some have asked whether the arrests were prompted by Eka Kupatadze’s campaign, and whether political influence may have played a role.

Those questions also remain unanswered.

Timeline of Giga Avaliani's case – read more 1 October 2025 – The attack

Giga Avaliani, a 28-year-old mathematics teacher, was attacked outside his home in Tbilisi. 24 October 2025 – Death

After spending 23 days in a coma, Giga Avaliani died. November–December 2025 – First arrests

Four minors were arrested: Aleksandre Gabashvili, Giorgi Rikadze, Demetere Chikovani and Ani Naskidashvili. April 2026 – First convictions

Tbilisi City Court found Aleksandre Gabashvili and Giorgi Rikadze guilty and sentenced each to 10 years and six months’ imprisonment. Demetere Chikovani was sentenced to six years and nine months’ imprisonment. He was later convicted over separate violent offences committed at a different time, increasing his total sentence to nine years and nine months. June 2026 – Another conviction

The court sentenced Ani Naskidashvili to five years and three months’ imprisonment for failing to report the crime. July 2026 – Another arrest

Giorgi Malania was arrested. According to prosecutors, he was charged with aiding and abetting the intentional infliction of grievous bodily harm committed by a group. His trial is still under way and no verdict has yet been delivered. August 2026 – Two more arrests

Two more minor girls were arrested: Nia Imnadze, Giga Avaliani’s former student and the girlfriend of the principal convicted defendant, and Anastasia Beruashvili, described as a friend of Nia Imnadze and the girlfriend of the second convicted defendant.

Broader picture

From the outset, the Giga Avaliani case came to represent more than a single criminal investigation.

It exposed a range of systemic problems, most notably a lack of public trust in investigative authorities. The case also highlighted shortcomings in Georgia’s juvenile justice system, as well as concerns over the protection of the rights of both victims and defendants.

Many observers questioned the release of footage showing Nia Imnadze’s arrest, particularly as it was made public by her lawyer. Some argued that the video was intended to generate public sympathy for his client.

“Unfortunately, public trust in the justice system – the police, the Prosecutor’s Office, the courts and other institutions – is now so low that victims, defendants and lawyers increasingly see shaping public opinion as the only way to obtain justice. They then seek to use public pressure to their advantage,” lawyer Londa Toloraia wrote.

In her view, this reflects a profound crisis affecting both citizens and the justice system itself.

“You no longer trust the state, even when it may actually be making a lawful decision.”

Toloraia also raised a number of questions about the arrests of the two girls: What evidence were they based on? Why did they take place 10 months after the murder? And why were they carried out at night, when Georgian law restricts procedural actions during nighttime hours, particularly in cases involving minors?

“How much influence does public opinion have over the justice system? A great deal. It is extremely difficult to withstand public pressure. And where institutions are fully politicised, it becomes virtually impossible to make a decision that is unpopular with the public,” she argued.

She stressed that legal standards must be upheld even when dealing with those accused of serious crimes – especially when the defendants are minors.

The Avaliani case has also exposed a darker side of public reaction. Following Nia Imnadze’s arrest, social media was flooded with hostile comments directed at both her and her family. Many users described her as the main culprit and called for severe punishment. Others went further, posting comments about the suffering they believed awaited her in prison.

A second group of social media users expressed concern about the tone of those comments. Toloraia addressed the debate in a lengthy social media post.

“Children are not born criminals. Before demanding that they be lynched, we should first ask why they became who they are,” she wrote, adding that juvenile crime in Georgia has reached one of its highest levels in recent years. She argued that the state’s response has focused on opening a “special prison” for children rather than preventing youth crime. A state in which parents who have lost a child must seek justice through public mobilisation, while institutions make decisions according to fluctuations in public pressure, is a broken state,” Toloraia concluded.

World.title: Odesa in summer 2026: Life between sea and war. VIDEO
World.content:
Beaches, bomb-damaged homes and explosions in broad daylight. In the summer of 2026, Odesa is caught between its traditional seaside resort atmosphere and the constant threat of Russian attacks. While some people relax by the sea and stroll through the city centre, others sift through the rubble left by the latest strike.

JAMnews visited Odesa to show what life in the city looks like today.

Odesa and the surrounding region remain frequent targets of Russian strikes. Residential neighbourhoods, critical infrastructure and port facilities have all come under attack.

Russia has carried out combined attacks using drones and missiles, seeking to overwhelm Ukraine‘s air defence systems.

The impact of these attacks is visible across the city. Residential buildings have been damaged, windows blown out and flats destroyed. Strikes have also hit Odesa’s historic centre, including heritage buildings and universities.

Ports in Odesa Region, along with the logistics hubs and warehouses that support them, are also regularly targeted. Attacks on port infrastructure have disrupted Ukraine’s transport network and Black Sea export routes.

The strikes often occur in broad daylight, when the streets are busy, cafés and shops are open, and beaches are filled with residents and visitors. At any moment, the familiar sounds of the city can be interrupted by explosions, air defence fire or the buzz of attack drones.

On several occasions, missiles have been intercepted directly over the coastline while beaches were crowded with people.

Today, it is possible to spend the day at the beach and the night in a bomb shelter.

World.title: “Russia’s annexation of Georgia’s regions would not go unanswered” – embassies on 18th anniversary of August war
World.content:
France, Germany, Italy, Britain: Russia’s annexation of Georgia

France, Germany, Italy and the UK issued a joint statement marking the 18th anniversary of the 2008 Russo-Georgian war, reaffirming their support for Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.

18 years after the Russian aggression, we reaffirm our full support to the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Georgia within its internationally recognized borders. We welcome Republic of Naoero’s decision to withdraw its recognition of the so-called independence of Abkhazia and South Ossetia.

We urge states that have established diplomatic relations with these entities to follow this example,” the statement said.

August 7, 2026 marks 18 years since the start of the Russo-Georgian war over South Ossetia. In the 2008 war, 412 Georgian military personnel and civilians were killed, along with 365 people on the Ossetian side. Some 20,000 ethnic Georgians were displaced. Georgia also lost control of 125 more villages in the Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia).

The independence of South Ossetia and Abkhazia is recognized by Russia, Nicaragua, Venezuela and Syria.

August 7, 2026 marks 18 years since the start of the Russo-Georgian war over South Ossetia. In the 2008 war, 412 Georgian military personnel and civilians were killed, along with 365 people on the Ossetian side. Some 20,000 ethnic Georgians were displaced. Georgia also lost control of 125 more villages in the Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia). The independence of South Ossetia and Abkhazia is recognized by Russia, Nicaragua, Venezuela and Syria.

France, Germany, Italy and the UK condemned Russia’s military presence in Abkhazia and South Ossetia.

ЭWe reiterate our condemnation of Russia’s ongoing military presence in the occupied breakaway regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia in violation of international law as well as Russia’s obligations under the six-point agreement of 12 August 2008.

Russia’s ongoing militarization of Georgia’s occupied territories poses a serious threat to the security of Georgia and to regional and European stability,” France, Germany, Italy and the UK said.

The statement also referred to rulings by the European Court of Human Rights.

In October 2025, the court found Russia responsible for a number of violations in the occupied regions, including the use of excessive force, ill-treatment, unlawful detention and restrictions on movement between Georgian-controlled territory and areas occupied by Russia.

“We urge Russia to implement the rulings of the European Court of Human Rights relating to this situation and to fully fulfil the commitments it made on August 12 and September 8, 2008,” the statement said.

The four countries also expressed concern over recent developments in South Ossetia.

They said the so-called “Agreement on Deepening Alliance and Cooperation,” signed by Moscow and the de facto authorities in South Ossetia on May 9, 2026, further violates Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and is incompatible with international law.

“This is a clear violation of international law. This document, as well as the appointment of a Russian citizen to head the region raise concerns on a possible full-fledged annexation of the region, which would not go unanswered,” the statement said.

Support for the Geneva International Discussions, co-chaired by the EU, OSCE and UN, was reaffirmed.

They said it is the only format that allows the parties to work towards a peaceful resolution of the conflict.

The statement also stressed the importance of the EU Monitoring Mission in Georgia and said its work would continue to be supported in the future.

News in Georgia

World.title: Former championship winning team cut from A-Leagues
World.content:
Western United has had its A-Leagues participation agreement terminated, effectively ending any flicker of hope of the troubled club making a return.

United has essentially been an A-Leagues club in name only for more than a year amid varied financial woes, which included not paying players and staff.

The club was placed into hibernation by the Australian Professional Leagues (APL) in September 2025, with A-League Men and Women players having to scramble to continue their careers elsewhere.

Ownership West Melbourne Group avoided a wind-up order from the Australian Tax Office in January by settling a $15.5 million tax debt.

Football Australia declined to reinstate the Tarneit-based club's licence in May and United again won't participate in either the ALM or ALW.

West Melbourne Group have another wind-up hearing in the Federal Court on Tuesday and on Monday the APL officially terminated their participation agreement in the A-League competitions.

Western United won the A-League Men's grand final in 2022. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

"Since the club was placed into conditional hibernation in September 2025, the APL has been in close consultation with Western United as they've worked through financial, governance and legal matters to try and rebuild the club," APL chair Stephen Conroy said in a statement.

"The APL board has since taken the decision to terminate Western United's club participation agreement.

"The club was in breach of a number of its obligations under that agreement, including its obligation to comply with the Football Australia National Club Licensing Regulations.

"It's been a difficult period for everyone connected to Western United — and we want to acknowledge the management, staff, players and especially the fans — who have given so much to the club and will no doubt be hurt by this news."

Sadness after Western United licence removal Western United fans have expressed their disappointment and sadness after the team was stripped of its A-League licence late last week.

AAP understands United still owes some of its former players and staff money.

United was granted a licence in 2018, off the back of grand promises to build its own stadium, entered the A-League Men ahead of the 2019-20 season and won the ALM championship in 2021-22.

A women's team followed in 2022-23 and reached the grand final in their first season.

United has consistently been defiant and adamant it will return to the A-Leagues.

When put into hibernation, the club claimed it wasn't a "step back".

Western United finally opened their small Ironbark Fields ground in 2024. It saw just one season of A-League football. (Getty Images: MB Media/Santanu Banik)

After the tax debt was paid in January, the club declared its ambition to seal a "strong return to the A-Leagues".

Despite the latest development, the club on Monday broadcast plans to return in a year's time under new ownership.

"Over recent months, we have worked closely with the APL on a pathway that gives the club the best opportunity to survive, rebuild and return to the A-League under new ownership," United said in a statement on Monday.

"This creates an opportunity for new custodians, new investment and a fresh start.

"The objective must now be to preserve Western United's identity in Melbourne's west and work towards a return to the A-League for the 2027-28 season.

"This should not be the end of Western United. It should be the reset that allows the club to rebuild and return stronger."

AAP

World.title: Trial begins in case of man accused of Bogie triple murder
World.content:
A man accused of murdering three people and attempting to murder another person on a rural Queensland property has pleaded not guilty at the opening of a three-week Supreme Court trial in Townsville.

Darryl Valroy Young, 63, is charged with three counts of murder and one count of attempted murder.

Police say Maree and Mervyn Schwarz were killed in a shooting incident in the rural north Queensland community of Bogie on August 4, 2022. (Supplied)

The court heard Mr Young is accused of murdering Mervyn Schwarz, Maree Schwarz and Graham Tighe by using a firearm to shoot each of them in the head at a property in Bogie, north-west of Mackay, on August 4, 2022.

Mr Young is also accused of attempting to murder Ross Tighe during the same incident.

Police say Graham Tighe was also shot dead during the incident on a Bogie cattle property on August 4, 2022. (Facebook)

Mr Young appeared in the courtroom wearing a long-sleeve navy button down shirt and black pants.

He listened to proceedings in the courtroom through earphones that were connected to a listening device.

A jury of 12 people, six men and six women, and an additional three men empanelled as reserve jurors, heard opening statements by the crown.

Mr Young's lawyer told jurors he denied ever seeing the Schwarzs or the Tighes on the day they were shot. (ABC News: Carole Howlett)

Brother to give evidence

Prosecutor David Nardone told jurors that Ross Tighe would give evidence in the trial and explain that on August 4, 2022, he, his mother, his brother and his stepfather were shot at the gate of Mr Young's Shannonvale Station.

"The man that Ross Tighe saw wielding the rifle is the accused Darryl Valroy Young," Mr Nardone.

"The most important witness you will hear from in this trial is Ross Tighe, it is the evidence of Ross Tighe that you will receive first when that begins tomorrow."

Prosecutor David Nardone (right) is appearing on behalf of the crown. (ABC News: Chloe Chomicki)

Missing cattle accusations

Mr Nardone said Mr and Mrs Schwarz and Ross Tighe had been visiting Graham Tighe who lived at Sutherland Station in August 2022 to assist with mustering cattle.

He said Graham Tighe received a call from his neighbour, Mr Young, on August 3, 2022.

"Darryl Young angrily accused Graham Tighe of selling calves that belonged to him," he said.

He said two people at Graham Tighe's home overheard the phone call in which Mr Young asked the family to attend the front gate of his property at 8am the following morning.

He said once the family arrived Mr Young began to level accusations once again before arming himself with a rifle.

"The accused Darryl Young walked back to his ute and said something like, 'I'll end this once and for all'," Mr Nardone said.

The Supreme Court trial, being held in Townsville, is expected to run for three weeks. (ABC North Queensland: Tom Major)

The crown prosecutor detailed gunshot wounds suffered by Mr and Mrs Schwarz and the Tighe brothers.

He also described a desperate struggle by Ross Tighe to seek help while critically injured.

Mr Nardone told jurors that both Ross Tighe's evidence and ballistic testing from police would support the crown case that Mr Young used a rifle, which he was not licensed to carry, to shoot Mr and Mrs Schwarz and the Tighe brothers.

He also said that jurors would be shown photos from trail cameras at the gate of Mr Young's property which Ross Tighe said were missing on August 4, 2022.

"You will be asked to infer that the trail cameras usually at that gate were taken down hours before the killing," Mr Nardone.

Defence lawyer Anthony J Kimmins (right) is representing Mr Young. (ABC News: Chloe Chomicki)

Defence says neighbours were friendly

Defence lawyer Anthony J Kimmins told jurors that Mr Young denied ever having a phone call about missing cattle with Graham Tighe on August 3, 2022 or meeting with the family at the gate of Shannonvale Station on the following morning.

"He is accused of slaughtering three members of one family and attempting to slaughter a fourth," Mr Kimmins said.

"He has been given nicknames; the beast of Bogie, the butcher of Bogie.

Mr Young silently watched on as the crown and his defence lawyer gave opening statements on Monday. ( ABC News: Carole Howlett)

"The fact that he is accused of committing these offences does not prove anything, nor do the nicknames.

"Darryl Young is presumed to be innocent of each and every one of these offences."

Mr Kimmins said Mr Young and his neighbours worked collaboratively and had reinstated 8 kilometres of fence line between the properties weeks before the alleged shooting.

He asked jurors to consider the working relationship between the two families and whether missing cattle was a plausible motive for the "slaughter or attempted slaughter of a family".

Mr Kimmins said throughout the trial the defence would challenge other aspects of the case including whether other persons had a motive to kill.

He said the defence would also question how Ross Tighe suffered a gunshot to the abdomen when he was supposedly running away from gunfire.

The trial continues.

World.title: My Brilliant Career cast reflects on 'defiant' Netflix adaptation
World.content:
My Brilliant Career is a story that has been with actress Philippa Northeast for some time.

Northeast rediscovered the 1901 Miles Franklin novel as a teenager after her mother first read it to her when she was a child.

"I was [about] 10, and illiterate," Northeast told ABC News.

"[I was] way too young to be having this book read to [me] … but what it did establish in me from a young age is this is a really important book to my mum."

Northeast says her mother was overcome with emotion when she got the role. (Supplied: Netflix)

Northeast (Territory, The Newsreader) plays Sybylla in the upcoming Netflix series, a young woman who wants to be a writer, while her family is determined to marry her off.

She breaks every convention as she looks for a story that will allow her to write her way to independence.

The tension comes when she falls in love. Will she marry, or risk it all for a creative life?

"To see a woman living life on her own terms, I think, has been a saving grace for a lot of people," Northeast says.

"And that's been more than iconic; it's so incredibly essential, and that was the case with my mum."

Northeast was speaking to ABC News at an intimate luncheon celebrating the series, which is out on Thursday.

She says when she landed the role of Sybylla, there was one person she knew she had to call straight away.

"I called mum, because I knew it was special, and she hung up on me immediately," Northeast said.

"And then she rang back later to say that she just had to cry in the car and have her own moment with the information I'd given her."

'It will bust your heart open'

My Brilliant Career has been adapted for stage and screen before, including Gillian Armstrong's 1979 film starring Judy Davis as Sybylla and Sam Neill as suitor Harry Beecham.

There was an outpouring of tributes when Neill died suddenly last month. He was 78.

In the Netflix adaptation, Harry is played by Christopher Chung (Slow Horses, Blitz).

Christopher Chung takes on the role of Harry Beecham. (Supplied: Netflix)

Kate Mulvany (Hunters, Elvis) takes on the role of Augusta, Harry's aunt, who brings him up when he is orphaned as a boy.

"Sam was a dear friend of mine," Mulvany told ABC News.

"And I had the enormous privilege of calling him when I got the role and saying, 'Hey, I'm playing your aunt, can you believe that?'

" And he immediately wanted to know who was playing Harry Beecham, and he was so thrilled when Chris was cast, he was a big Slow Horses fan. "

Kate Mulvany says she relayed messages between "the two Harrys". (Supplied: Netflix)

Mulvany says the two would send messages to each other, often via her.

"I was the very happy middle person in the Chris Chung/Sam Neill sandwich, getting to relay the messages between the two Harrys, between the two eras," Mulvany said.

"And I'm so sad that Sam won't get to see this iteration of My Brilliant Career, but he was very present in the shooting.

"He was texting constantly and wanting to know all the gossip, and I think he'd be really proud of what Chris brings to Harry Beecham."

Mulvany says the series is "a celebration of rebellion".

"It's got a real rebel heart to it," she says.

"It's got a feminist rebel heart, but every single person has a bit of Sybylla in them, no matter who you are.

Mulvany says in the era of AI, the series tells the story of an artist standing up for her craft. (Supplied: Netflix)

"And in the era of AI, and jobs being taken from artists, this is a pure artist standing up for her craft and saying, 'I want to do this; let me do this.'

" It's also romantic, and sexy and dramatic and sad, and it will bust your heart open. "

A world expanded

Miah Madden (Paper Dolls, The Clearing) plays Betty, a young First Nations woman who is new to the story in this iteration of the narrative.

Miah Madden's character Betty is introduced in the Netflix adaptation. (Supplied: Netflix)

"I think that this series has a lot of potential to be able to reflect a period of Australian history that has been told before, but we are broadening that perspective to include a true reflection of that time," Madden told ABC News.

"And I think that Australian audiences and the Australian population are ready for a story like this.

"I think it's definitely a correction of the original text because I think these perspectives — these First Nations, Chinese, queer perspectives — have always been there and it's wonderful for us to be defiant and showcase those stories."

Shari Sebbens, a stage director and actress (The Sapphires, The Office), is an associate producer on the show and says Liz Doran, who adapted the story for the small screen as a writer and one of the executive producers, was determined to include other cultures and stories.

Shari Sebbens says there's a defiance in the Netflix production. (Supplied: STC/Prudence Upton)

"Liz wanted to make sure there was First Nations representation because I think it's really odd when we tell Australian stories, especially this early — this is set around Federation — and you can't tell that story without First Nations presence or at least acknowledging First Nations absence," Sebbens told ABC News.

"So, in that way I think the defiance in this production lives in the expansion of Miles Franklin's world, which I know when you read the book, people will say there was racism that was of its time, but it's still of this time.

"That racism that existed then is the racism that exists today; it hasn't evolved."

Sybylla is described as a "shockingly modern" young woman. (Supplied: Netflix)

Sebbens says My Brilliant Career still resonates 125 years on because women are still coming up against glass ceilings, no matter their cultural background.

"One hundred and twenty-five years is a long time," Sebbens says.

"It's also a blip in the long line of societies and cultures that have existed, and women's roles have changed so much because the patriarchy decided to take over, but I think that's what it is.

" It's about women today still being okay to want something and want it out loud and want it with all their heart and being met with resistance at so many points in their life. "

My Brilliant Career will stream on Netflix globally from this Thursday, August 13.

World.title: Woman cleared of Cassius Turvey's murder avoids jail for driving with no licence
World.content:
A woman found not guilty of murdering Perth school boy Cassius Turvey has avoided being sent to jail for driving without a licence.

WARNING: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains an image of a person who has died, used with the permission of their family.

Cassius Turvey was chased down and beaten with a metal pole while walking with friends after school in Perth's east in October 2022. He died in hospital ten days later.

Aleesha Gilmore stood trial for the 15-year-old's murder along with three other men. She was found not guilty, but was convicted of assaulting a teenager and unlawfully detaining two others in the days before the attack.

Court sketch shows Aleesha Gilmore, in a blue jacket, at the sentencing trial for the murder of Cassius Turvey. (Supplied: Anne Barnetson)

She was handed a 15-month prison sentence for those offences in June 2025, suspended for two years with strict community conditions.

On Monday, Gilmore appeared before the Supreme Court via video link from a secure location for driving without a licence, an alleged breach of her conditional suspended imprisonment order.

Opportunity for rehabilitation

State prosecutor Benjamin Stanwix told the court Gilmore lost her licence in December 2025 after police found she was driving under the influence of alcohol.

The court was told Gilmore blew over 0.08 — with a blood test showing her alcohol level at 0.098.

She was fined and disqualified from holding a licence for seven months at the time, but was convicted in June of driving without a licence and given a further nine-month disqualification.

Warren Pearce says the court ruling went against the intentions of the Act. (ABC News: Briana Shepherd)

Mr Stanwix told the court even though driving without a licence breaches the terms of a suspended sentence, the state was not asking for an immediate term of imprisonment as that would not give Gilmore the opportunity for rehabilitation.

He said the state did not take that position lightly and told the court he did not want Gilmore to leave with the impression the state was "a soft touch".

Gilmore's lawyer, Simon Freitag, said Gilmore had been following the terms of her suspended sentence, which include attending counselling and taking part in programs.

Mr Freitag said his client had managed to get some cleaning work until they asked for a police check, and was now actively looking for FIFO work.

Cassius Turvey grew from shy boy into a leader A memorial plaque for Cassius Turvey in his community of Midland, east of Perth, sits as an enduring reminder of the legacy he left behind: "gentle giant", "huggable teddy bear", and a "young leader".

No immediate imprisonment

Chief Justice Peter Quinlan said he was satisfied it would be unjust to order a term of immediate imprisonment, considering Gilmore was half way through her suspended sentence, but that she needed to stay on the "straight and narrow".

He told Gilmore she was not responsible for the death of Cassius Turvey but said her notoriety meant her name would probably always be associated with that.

"I appreciate given your notoriety it makes it more difficult for you to obtain work," he told Gilmore.

"But that's not a reason to give up."

Gilmore was fined $500, to be paid on top of the $1,000 she was already fined for driving without a licence.

World.title: Victorian health watchdog issues warning over alleged fake doctor
World.content:
Victoria's health watchdog has issued a warning about a Melbourne woman accused of pretending to be a doctor and charging $20,000 to use unapproved medicines to treat a man with a chronic illness.

The state's Health Complaints Commissioner has issued an interim prohibition order against Assma (Sarah) Samadi, banning her from providing any health service in Victoria, alleging she may have contravened the code of conduct under the Health Complaints Act.

The Victorian Health Complaints Commissioner also made a public warning about the case, after an investigation was launched on August 5.

Do you know more? Contact Antonia O'Flaherty at Oflaherty.Antonia@abc.net.au or on antoniaoflaherty@protonmail.com

Commissioner Bernice Redley said it was alleged that Ms Samadi, an unregistered health practitioner, offered treatment to an individual she was not qualified to provide and unlawfully supplied unapproved medications to treat a chronic illness.

It's alleged Ms Samadi charged more than $20,000 for the treatments and represented herself as a medical practitioner, the commissioner said.

"The Commissioner reasonably believes that Ms Samadi may have contravened the Code of Conduct as set out in Schedule 2 of the Health Complaints Act 2016, and that it is necessary to publish this warning statement to avoid an imminent and serious risk to the life, health, safety or welfare of a person or the public," a statement from Ms Redley said.

"Members of the public are encouraged not to engage with Ms Samadi in relation to the provision of any general health service."

The interim prohibition order against Ms Samadi will also remain in place.

The Victorian Health Complaints Commissioner has issued an official warning after a woman allegedly provided unapproved medication to a man. (Health Complaints Comissioner)

The health watchdog urged anyone with concerns about the matter to contact the Health Complaints Commissioner on 1300 582 113 or online.

Police charged Ms Samadi last month with trafficking steroids, possessing drugs and common assault in Melbourne's Bayside.

After executing two search warrants, police allege they found a stash of cocaine and significant quantities of prescription medicines including testosterone, synthetic anabolic steroids, painkillers and human growth hormone.

She was granted bail and is set to appear in Moorabbin Magistrates Court on October 19.

Police also arrested a 39-year-old man from Brighton East and he was also charged for the same offences, including two counts of trafficking steroids along with possessing cocaine, a drug of dependence and a schedule 4 poison.

He was granted bail to appear in court on the same date.

World.title: Nine boys charged with 70 offences over alleged Kimberley crime spree
World.content:
Police have charged nine boys with a combined 70 offences over a string of vehicle thefts in Western Australia's far north.

Police allege the boys trespassed several houses across Derby, 2,200 kilometres north of Perth, between 1am and 4:30am on Friday last week.

The boys allegedly stole a tray-top ute, a Toyota LandCruiser, a quad bike and four motorcycles over the course of the morning.

The group were arrested and all vehicles recovered and returned to the owners.

There were no reports of injuries.

Derby Police arrested the boys after the string of break-ins and thefts in the early hours of August 7. (ABC Kimberley: Erin Parke)

The 70 charges include several counts of stealing and attempting to steal a motor vehicle, as well as trespassing.

Seven of the boys are due to face the Derby, Broome and Perth Children's courts at various dates this month, while two teenagers were issued with cautions.

'Resilient community' under pressure

Derby Police officer-in-charge Nathan Smith said the group had allegedly been the driving force behind a recent spike in offending around the town.

"Every sub-district has certainly bubbles where there's increases in crime and this is just one that's happened in Derby," Senior Sergeant Smith said.

" For the most part, we're a resilient community that has been subject to an increase off the basis of a young group that were like-minded in their attitude on the night. "

Senior Sergeant Nathan Smith thanked the community for help in reporting and resolving the incidents. (ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson)

He said the close-knit nature of Derby's community, including residents looking out for each other and being mindful of suspicious behaviour, had played a key role in resolving the incident.

"It's a safe place to live, it's a safe place to come and visit and travel through," Senior Sergeant Smith said.

"We take this very seriously."

Community solutions

Youth crime in the Kimberley has been in the spotlight across the past week, after a viral video of a separate alleged car theft in Kununurra.

A long-awaited on-country youth facility in the Kimberley welcomed its first cohort of young men earlier this year.

The Wala Kooral-bi Centre, 120km south of Derby, offers an on-country diversion program for boys aged 14 to 17.

Eight teenagers have been housed at the facility since May, with the Marlamanu Project offering an alternative to sending juveniles south to Perth's controversy-plagued Banksia Hill Detention Centre.

The Wala Kooral-bi Centre opened this year. (ABC News: Andrew Seabourne)

"Those community led solutions are the ones that increase our ability to distract and prevent this cohort from continuing this behaviour," Senior Sergeant Smith said.

"We're really supportive of Marlumanu and the work they are doing.

"We want to make sure that's a program that continues to operate because I think it's a needs basis in community."

'Community safety a priority'

Shire of Derby-West Kimberley chief executive Tamara Clarkson said the incident was a disappointing one for the town.

"Community safety is obviously a priority of the shire, but it is a police matter," she said.

Tamara Clarkson says incidents like the one last week are not common. (ABC Kimberley: Anthony Pancia)

"Always ensure that you are locking vehicles, your windows and doors, hiding keys never leaving them available."

Ms Clarkson urged people to report anything concerning to police.

"This is definitely a rarity for Derby," Ms Clarkson said.

"We've worked hard with our community to ensure that safety in priority."

World.title: Coalition calls on Albanese to apologise to Japan's PM over melon gesture
World.content:
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is facing pressure to apologise to his Japanese counterpart over a gesture he made about two melons she gifted him, which his office insists was not a crude joke.

In an interview last month, Mr Albanese gestured to his chest when recalling the melons during an exchange with Bush Deep podcast host Nikki Osborne, who asked how the fruit had been smuggled into the country.

The incident resurfaced this morning after former Australian ambassador Shingo Yamagami criticised the exchange in The Australian, labelling it "insulting", ignorant and a betrayal of the "close relationship" between Australia and Japan.

Anthony Albanese is facing backlash from another gaffe during his appearance on the Bush Deep podcast last month. (Supplied: YouTube)

The former Ambassador suggested Mr Albanese was making a quip about Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's body, but a spokesperson for Mr Albanese told The Australian, "this assertion is wrong".

The comment has not been supplied to the ABC despite multiple requests.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said it was beneath the office of the prime minister, and demanded Mr Albanese apologise.

"They were insulting, and the prime minister should make a personal apology. He's done it through a statement. I mean, the hypocrisy of Labor and the foreign minister on this topic," Mr Taylor said.

Angus Taylor has called on Anthony Albanese to apologise. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

The gaffe occurred during the same podcast that landed Mr Albanese in hot water when he said he would shag Kylie Minogue during a game of "shag, marry, date". He later apologised for those comments.

While Mr Albanese was condemned by several female parliamentarians at the time, including Shadow Communications Minister Sarah Henderson, the main focus was on Minogue and not Ms Takaichi.

Liberal Deputy Leader Jane Hume added to the criticism, calling the comments "grubby" and "inappropriate".

Labor ministers defend PM

Senior cabinet ministers have again been forced to defend Mr Albanese's appearance on the podcast.

Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek today deflected criticisms and disagreed with Mr Yamagami's interpretation.

PM apologises for shag comment Anthony Albanese made the comments during a game of "shag, marry, date" on the Bush Deep podcast.

"We have an excellent relationship with Japan. Japan is a very important strategic and economic partner … and I think the former ambassador is wrong in his interpretation," she told Sunrise.

Health Minister Mark Butler reiterated Australia's strong economic and security ties with Japan.

"It's very close. It involves constant communication between our two countries, two at the highest level. I know Prime Minister Albanese feels the deepest respect for that relationship," he told reporters.

The federal Transport Minister Catherine King argued the comments were being blown up by the opposition.

Comments 'unfortunate' but not Japan's primary concern

While officials may have winced in private, nobody in the Japanese government has publicly commented about Mr Albanese's gaffe.

Ms Takaichi's first visit in May solidified Australia's place as a critical energy partner for Japan, and an increasingly important security partner as well.

When the episode first came out, officials in the Japanese government told the ABC they were not focused on the exchange and that Tokyo would not comment on a minor episode, particularly given the scale of cooperation between the two countries.

The episode has also drawn little attention so far in the Japanese press, aside from one scathing opinion piece in the English-language Japan Times which lambasted Mr Albanese and accused him of rank sexism.

Shingo Yamagami says it shows cultural ignorance and is insulting to the partnership between Japan and Australia. (Perth USAsia Centre: Kelly Pilgrim-Byrne)

But one member of the Australian business community with close links to Japan said the exchange "had absolutely not gone unnoticed" among Japanese elites, even if they were publicly silent about it.

In his criticism, Mr Yamagami pointed out that Ms Takaichi has already copped sexist and derogatory attacks from Chinese state media, but it was not expected from Japan's strategic partner.

Innuendo aside, the former diplomat also highlights that Mr Albanese's comments ignore the cultural significance of crown melons, which are intensely cultivated luxury fruits in Japan.

Australia and Japan sign agreements on energy, defence and critical minerals Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and his Japanese counterpart Takaichi Sanae agreed to bolster cooperation on energy, defence and critical minerals.

In the face of an "increasingly dangerous" geopolitical climate, he urged the prime minister to show greater focus.

"So, prime minister, please enjoy Japan's sweet and juicy melons without thinking about a woman's anatomy, and instead focus on what our two countries must do together," he said.

Mr Yamagami had a fraught relationship with Labor when he was in Canberra and was particularly angry when Foreign Minister Penny Wong urged him, while she was still in opposition, to pull back his public criticisms of China.

World.title: What have we learnt from Origin Energy's data breach?
World.content:
Three weeks ago, Origin Energy told 900,000 former and current customers that their information had been exposed in a data breach.

The major cybersecurity data leak made headlines and raised the alarm that the threats were becoming more prevalent.

It also showed that anyone with their information online could be vulnerable, according to Curtin University Associate Professor in AI and Cybersecurity, Mihai Lazarescu.

"There is no such thing as 100 per cent security," he said.

Associate Professor Lazarescu, who has worked in cybersecurity for over 16 years, said whenever anyone put information online, there was a chance it could be compromised.

That included commonly used details, such as email addresses and first and last names.

"Never give your full name and date of birth because that is identifiable evidence," he said.

How did Origin Energy compare to Australia's biggest data breaches?

Origin's breach affected hundreds of thousands of customers, but it wasn't technically the largest.

Australian companies such as Canva, Optus, and Qantas had data breaches that affected millions of customers.

Canva Read more Australian online design tool Canva suffered a data breach impacting 137 million of its users in 2019. A cybercriminal identified as Ghosticplayers breached Canva's defences but was stopped by Canva when it detected malicious activity in its systems.

Access to usernames, real names, email addresses, country data, encrypted passwords and partial payment data of users was leaked. Latitude Read more In March 2023, Latitude, the Australian personal loan and financial service provider, was affected by a data breach that impacted more than 14 million people from Australia and New Zealand. The Latitude breach was one of Australia's largest breaches in recent history.

The attack occurred when one set of employee credentials was stolen, allowing access to Latitude's customer data, including full names, physical addresses, email addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, driver's licence numbers and passport numbers.

Much of the information was data stored from 2005, which drew questions on why companies continue to store customer records beyond the required seven-year time frame. Optus Read more In September 2022, the Optus data breach impacted 9.8 million customers. The security incident brought up questions about Australian data security policies and how companies handled them.

Cybercriminals believed to be working for a state-sponsored operation breached Optus's internal network, compromising personal information and impacting up to 9.8 million customers, almost 40 per cent of the population.

Personal data included names, birth dates, addresses, phone numbers, passport information, driver's license numbers, government ID numbers, medical records & Medicare card ID numbers. Medibank Read more In December 2022, Medibank, the Australian health insurance giant, was the victim of a data breach affecting the personal details of 9.7 million customers. The attack was believed to be linked to a well-known ransomware group based in Russia, the REvil ransomware gang.

The privacy breach was first discovered when REvil posted on a dark web blog a folder that contained 6GB of raw data samples, indicating that they had larger amounts of data to release, and demanded a $10 million ransom. The data included names, birthdates, passport numbers, medical claims data, and medical records. Qantas Read more In July 2025, up to 6 million Qantas customers were affected when the Australian airline confirmed a data theft incident that impacted a significant portion of its customer base. Data compromised included names, email addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, and frequent flyer numbers.

The breach was reportedly attributed to a cyber attack targeting the airline's call centre. Origin Read more In July 2026, Origin Energy, Australia's largest energy retailer with more than 4.8 million customers, announced that the information of 900,000 current and former customers was accessed during a data security breach. The energy provider confirmed it first became aware of a potential security threat in early July but initially did not believe it credible.

The company said it was still working to determine the total number of people affected and would notify impacted customers.

While there is no indication full payment card details were compromised, experts say the stolen information remains highly valuable and are urging affected customers to remain cautious about unsolicited emails, text messages and phone calls long after the breach.

The information included names, dates of birth, phone numbers, home addresses and email addresses, as well as the last four digits of some credit cards and the last three digits of some bank account numbers.

What does the Origin breach reveal about cybersecurity?

Associate Professor Lazarescu said the fact that a power company was potentially breached should have been expected, given how easy data could be accessed online.

"It will get worse," he said.

"99 per cent of people have no understanding of how difficult it is to protect data.

"It requires both the technical and administrative aspects of security to be perfect."

He said the only way to be fully protected online was to be "checking all the time", from bank statements to which information was given online.

Recent data from the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) showed most of the leaked customer information in data breaches included contact details, financial details and identity information.

Associate Professor Lazarescu said social media was also one of the easiest ways for criminals to access data.

"You see people posting online with photos with specific locations, timing. These are not secure," he said.

"When you have criminal groups that are very well organised and make a lot of money out of what they do, these are not beginners.

" I've seen groups that were based in Europe where there were 11-year-olds coding. "

Associate Professor Lazarescu said having data leaked could not only put people at risk of being hacked but, in worst-case scenarios, their data could be sold on the dark web to criminal groups.

"It could create a situation that's expensive and complicated to fix," he said.

He said serious discussion should be taking place that outlined to customers what the risks of data leaking could entail and the potential consequences if security measures failed.

Hidden costs of data leaks

The severity of a data breach depends on the sensitivity of the data and the nature of the exposure, rather than just the total number of people affected.

Charles Sturt University computing professor Yeslam Al-Saggaf said the Origin data breach was "more concerning" than the Canva breach, despite fewer customers being affected.

"The value of data is low as these students don't have credit cards, don't have car loans, mortgages, and don't have driver's licences," Professor Al-Saggaf said.

Origin Energy confirms hack Energy company Origin has confirmed that there has been unauthorised access and disclosure of some customers' data, a day after it announced it was investigating a "potential" breach.

"Whereas in the Origin data breach financial details of individuals and businesses have been compromised."

He said when individuals' and businesses' financial details were published online, it exposed them to a range of risks, such as losing money through payment redirection attacks and identity theft.

He said businesses and individuals could also face a situation with additional costs and an increase in insurance premiums.

Cyber insurance providers have noted the increase in cyber attacks and, in turn, are raising premiums.

According to a 2025 report by the Australian Signals Directorate's Australian Cyber Security Centre, the Australian Cyber Security Centre responded to 1,200 cybersecurity incidents in the last financial year, an 11 per cent increase.

The average self-reported cost of a cyber incident for a small business had risen to 14 per cent, while medium businesses have seen a 55 per cent increase.

Cyber-hacking number one cause of data breaches

The Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) received 1,205 data breach notifications in the 2025 calendar year, representing an 8 per cent increase from 2024, according to OAIC data.

Cyber hacking remains the primary cause of data breaches reported to the OAIC.

Of the data breaches notified in 2025, the majority were attributable to malicious or criminal activity.

Health service providers were the most commonly affected, accounting for 19 per cent of the total.

How can we protect our data from being leaked?

The Australian government said it had revised its cybersecurity policies to strengthen resilience against nation-state threat actors amid the rise in cyber attacks.

In 2025, the OAIC launched a new Notifiable Data Breaches (NDB) statistics dashboard to keep the public informed on the volume and type of data breaches occurring.

Professor Al-Saggaf said "people are becoming numb to the drama of data breaches", and people who remained naive to cybersecurity were most at risk.

"They happen every day in Australia because Australians are trusting, affluent, speak English, and some are not technically savvy," he said.

"We need to improve our literacy with respect to cybersecurity hygiene practices."

AI has changed what criminals can do with your stolen Origin data The theft of names, addresses and phone numbers may seem less serious than stolen bank details, but cyber experts say AI is changing what criminals can do with that information.

He advised using a strong, unique password that differed for each account, or using a password manager, to help protect individuals.

He said enabling multi-factor authentication could provide an additional layer of verification, and using secure payment methods on secure websites could also help avoid potential security risks.

But as scammers started to integrate artificial intelligence into their operations, he warned regular security measures would need to be strengthened.

"AI is going to make impersonation more sophisticated, so use more than one method to communicate with your close contacts if they ask for financial assistance, and keep an eye on bank balances and credit card statements," he said.

World.title: ‘Bizarre display of gutter politics’: WA One Nation leader returns serve to premier’s broadside
World.content:
PoliticsWAOne Nation ‘Bizarre display of gutter politics’: WA One Nation leader returns serve to premier’s broadside Michael Philipps August 10, 2026 — 6:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

West Australian Premier Roger Cook has launched a scathing attack on One Nation for promoting “people who are convicted rapists, people who have charges pending, people who have been accused of sexual assault” as the battle for a looming byelection in Perth’s south heats up. However, One Nation’s WA leader Rod Caddies returned serve, accusing Cook of “desperate and bizarre tactics” ahead of the vote in Secret Harbour, sparked by the resignation of former minister Paul Papalia in July. WA Premier Roger Cook. AFR Speaking at a press conference on Monday, Cook was asked to comment on a 2021 podcast featuring Labor’s candidate for Secret Harbour, Georgia Tree, who was working for federal Brand MP Madeleine King at the time. On the episode of the In the House & In the Senate podcast, Tree spoke of Labor having potential “skeletons in the closet” in the aftermath of Brittany Higgins’ allegations that she was raped in Parliament House in Canberra.



On Monday, Cook defended Tree’s appearance, and said her comments showed she stood up for her community. “She doesn’t take bullcrap,” Cook said. “She calls it out when she sees it, and she was making a comment about the people who don’t have a voice, the people who are voiceless. “She was providing a voice to those people, so I’m proud of the comments that she made.” Cook added that Tree’s stance stood in contrast to One Nation.



“[One Nation] are the people who promote people who have been charged or convicted of outstanding arrest warrants for sexual assault,” Cook said. Related Article One Nation Pauline Hanson opens up on domestic violence, prison and racism claims “They promote as their campaign leader someone who is a convicted rapist. “So when it comes to standing up for women, I back Georgia Tree any day.” In April, One Nation leader Pauline Hanson said she had fired Sean Black, who was rehired by the party as its national campaign after he was jailed in 2018 for raping and violently assaulting a woman.



In March, South Australian One Nation candidate Aoi Baxter was dumped on the eve of the election after it was revealed he was wanted in the UK for allegedly failing to appear in court over sexual touching charges. Cook said a lot had changed in parliament since he was first elected in 2008. “A lot has changed in relation to the culture, not only of all parts of Parliament, but certainly on my side of politics,” he said. “We are promoting women today, and as a result of that, our party is much stronger. “It stands in contrast to the sort of people that One Nation are putting up, people who are convicted rapists, people who have charges pending, people who have been accused of sexual assault.



“They are the sort of people that they are promoting, and that is the sort of person that [WA Liberal leader] Basil Zempilas is trying to get up in Western Australia by directing Liberal Party preferences to One Nation.” WA One Nation leader Rod Caddies. Trevor Collens However, Caddies said he wouldn’t be “pulled down into the gutter” by the premier. “All sides of politics are noticing Labor and the premier’s desperate and bizarre tactics,” Caddies said. “Their attempt to use weasel words to imply nefarious things about my candidate or me shows the premier’s lack of moral standards and character, and I won’t be pulled down into the gutter with him.



“It is interesting to see the premier endorse his candidate’s podcast comments; he seems to agree there are skeletons in his party’s closet, and perhaps he and his candidate should open up about what they are.” Caddies said it was disappointing to see the government behave this way. “We are on opposite sides of politics, but even I was still expecting certain basic standards of behaviour,” he said. “We expected a robust campaign that pulls no punches, not this bizarre display of gutter politics.” Tree said she stood by her comments on the podcast, adding that she had always been outspoken, and would always fight for what is right – particularly when it comes to women’s experiences in the workplace.



“I led a sit-in in Federal Parliament in 2021 to stand up against ‘don’t ask, don’t tell’ culture and sexual harassment in the workplace,” she said. Related Article Updated

Public transport WA Labor and Liberals battle it out over Karnup train station promise “I was backed and fully supported by my boss at the time, Minister Madeleine King. Just as I have been ever since I spoke out on this issue.” Tree added that since 2021, there had been great shifts within the Labor Party. “Both the federal and WA Caucus is now made up of more than 50 per cent women,” she said.



“This is one of the reasons why I am running, we need to see more young women entering politics to fight for change and not be afraid to stand up, speak out and take their seat at the table.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: KPMG chair-elect admits to sending ‘naive, embarrassing and wrong’ email
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesWhistleblowers KPMG chair-elect admits to sending ‘naive, embarrassing and wrong’ email Colin Kruger Updated August 10, 2026 — 6:30pm ,first published 3:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

KPMG’s chairman-elect Michael Ebeid has issued a grovelling apology for dismissing allegations from a whistleblower that have rocked the consultancy as he fights to win his job on a permanent basis. And in a bigger issue for the consultancy, documents released by parliament on Monday showed that two major law firms that reviewed the whistleblower’s claims early in the saga failed to take basic steps, such as interviewing people involved or checking staff emails. KPMG’s incoming chairman Michael Ebeid issued a grovelling apology to Senator Deborah O’Neill. Getty Images But in March, Ebeid had emailed his colleagues on the KPMG board accusing Labor’s Senator Deborah O’Neill of airing “completely false” allegations when she read out the whistleblower’s claims that top staff at the firm had misused confidential client information. Those allegations have since been substantiated. Ebeid, who has essentially been functioning as the chairman of the firm that is trying to recover from its top executives’ misuse of clients’ confidential audit documents, needs to get the backing of KPMG partners in a vote that concludes on Wednesday.



Related Article Big four accountants KPMG directors flee as whistleblower scandal worsens On Monday, documents released by O’Neill’s parliamentary committee, which is investigating the scandal, revealed Ebeid’s personal apology to O’Neill for the March email. “What I wrote was wrong,” Ebeid told O’Neill on Saturday, according to one document. “I described statements about the whistleblower’s allegations made by you to the Senate as false. I described the firm’s process as thorough. Events since have shown that neither was true, and that the concerns you raised on the whistleblower’s behalf have helped uncover serious wrongdoing and I can only thank you for that.” He said he thought he was being helpful, based on his knowledge at the time. “However, with what I know now, my email was naive, embarrassing and wrong on every level,” Ebeid wrote. And in a fresh issue for the embattled firm, the committee also released documents that KPMG had battled to keep hidden under claims of legal professional privilege. The committee said it was in the public interest to release these documents ahead of another public grilling this Friday.



The legal documents were the reports from two law firms, Allens and Ashurst, and relate to their work on the whistleblower complaints. KPMG had initially used the reports from the law firms to claim that the whistleblower’s complaints were unsubstantiated while refusing to make the actual documents public. A fresh investigation by Allens has led to a purge of KPMG’s most senior people as some of the most serious allegations have now been substantiated. “The Ashurst and Allens processes were central to the claim that KPMG had undertaken comprehensive internal and external investigations prior to the speech given by Senator Deborah O’Neill on 24 March 2026,” the committee – chaired by O’Neill – said in a statement. It said the committee had found there was a “compelling public interest” in examining the results of the law firms’ investigations at its next hearing, allowing it to publish the previously legally privileged documents. KPMG’s new chief executive John Sams told partners that the parliamentary committee informed the firm of its intentions to publish the documents on Friday.



“We acknowledged the Committee’s role and the importance of scrutiny and transparency, while noting that the reports reflect a point in time and do not correctly represent the current status of the investigations,” he said. One of the documents was a report submitted to KPMG in December last year by Allens that said all the whistleblower’s allegations were unsubstantiated. This includes the claim that KPMG’s Lendlease audit team stole confidential board papers and shared them internally to help win multimillion-dollar external audit tenders for Westpac and Dexus. Given the credibility of the KPMG executives involved, Allens said it was “disproportionate and unnecessary” to search staff emails to check what they had said was correct. A subsequent investigation by Allens confirmed that senior partners had illicitly accessed sensitive Lendlease board documents and kept them in a work locker, and led to the immediate expulsion of former chief operating officer Eileen Hoggett.



Another document released was an Ashurst report from February last year. At the committee’s public hearing last month the law firm described its work for KPMG as legal advice. This report also cleared KPMG personnel of any wrongdoing “based on the material reviewed”, but the report contained a significant caveat. “In coming to these conclusions we have not had the benefit of speaking directly to any of the individuals concerned and assessing their credibility,” Ashurst’s lawyers wrote. Ashurst and Allens, two of Australia’s largest law firms, declined to comment. Since May, the firm has lost its chief executive Andrew Yates, chairman Martin Sheppard, and Hoggett after she lied the board documents. KPMG audit partner Kim Lawry also resigned from her senior roles last month after Westpac requested that she be removed from its audit “to ensure there is no distraction”.



KPMG independent board member Patty Akopiantz quietly left the firm’s regional board last month, following former NSW premier Mike Baird’s exit in September, and fellow independent director Jane Hemstritch is expected to resign once replacements have been found.
