World.title: Rising use of AI at home will undermine value of HSC
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

NSW Education Minister Prue Car is right to request a ban on unsupervised HSC take-home assessments. The HSC only has value if it reflects a student’s own knowledge and thinking, and with more than 1000 cheating cases last year, it’s clear that AI is being widely used to do students’ work, rather than assist with learning (“HSC take-home ban to fight surge in AI”, August 10). Anyone who has used AI knows it is an excellent learning tool, but there is a big difference between using AI to better understand a topic and using it to write an assignment. If schools fail to protect the credibility of the HSC, universities and some employers will increasingly rely on their own entrance tests and interviews. That would make the HSC a less valuable credential for everyone. John Kempler, Rose Bay NSW Deputy Premier and Education Minister Prue Car. Rhett Wyman A radical overhaul of the HSC assessment procedures is long overdue. Because the HSC is a high-stakes examination, cheating has always been problematic. However, increasing misuse of AI by unsupervised HSC students is the catalyst for a moratorium on take-home assessment tasks. While take-home assessment tasks have played an important part in HSC coursework, there is no way of knowing with certainty who is completing any task that is taken home by students. While all HSC candidates must pledge to submit only their own work, those pledges cannot prevent students from collaborating with their parents, older siblings, tutors, coaches and others. This has been the case for years. A return to supervised HSC assessment tasks would be an effective measure in equipping our school-leavers with a robust credential that accurately reflects their attainments. Irene Buckler, Glenwood It’s not just the use of AI at home that is the danger here. Any student with an ounce of drive and desire for success will ask anyone (or anything) for help in securing a better mark than would otherwise be had with a supervised assessment. When doing an assignment at home, it’s always been easy to get information and answers simply by asking a knowledgeable person, like a parent, or even by opening an Encyclopaedia Britannica. Forgoing supervision is an invitation to the student to find as much help as possible – which is why take-home tasks should be permanently banned if we are trying to find out what the student can actually do for themself and by themself. So, don’t blame the availability of AI for students using it, blame the policy of allowing take-home tasks. Mia David, Wollongong The plagiarism scandals at Harvard and Cambridge universities involving senior academics highlight the need for accountability and the importance of safeguards to support integrity. The NSW Higher School Certificate is an internationally recognised credential, and the move to safeguard its integrity, and to deal with concerns relating to the growth of AI, are to be applauded. What is also needed is a mandatory short course in ethics and ethical understanding for all learners embarking on their HSC journey that addresses the values that underpin the roles of learning, responsibility and the importance of personal achievement. Rod Leonarder, Roseville Silencing the media Pauline Hanson’s spiteful standoff with the ABC, The Age and The Guardian shows how much the relationship between our politicians and the media has changed. Back when the news was still in black-and-white, journalists would stand as Robert Menzies entered the room for one of his rare press conferences. While the questioning of the prime minister could then be quite sharp, the tone of those exchanges was always mutually respectful. Accredited reporters doing their job were not excluded or attacked. Today, Hanson bans representatives of outlets she dislikes and impugns their motives, yet suffers no consequences. This is only possible because journalism is no longer a specifically unionised trade. The once independent Australian Journalists Association is extinct. Along with its demise went a tradition of solidarity. Had the old AJA been confronted by Hanson’s tactic, they would have responded with a “one out, all out” boycott. One Nation would not be reported until its ban on individual outlets was lifted. It is a matter of regret that the media is now so fragmented, and its workers so gotcha-driven and insecure, that they have ignored this obligation to support their colleagues. David Salter, Hunters Hill



Pauline Hanson has banned certain journalists from One Nation press conferences. Eamon Gallagher Rather than being reactive to One Nation’s toxic rhetoric, the PM should argue for the real benefits of 80 years of post-war migration (“To rein in Hanson, her political foes must stop making One Nation’s case”, August 10). This includes offsetting a low fertility rate and an ageing population. He could reflect on the leadership and courage shown by Bob Hawke and Paul Keating on sometimes unpopular policies. Tony Simons, Balmain PM’s risky gamble It is difficult to find words to accurately describe the pathetic and timid response to gambling advertising reform. Anthony Albanese is clearly more concerned with protecting the gambling industry and their broadcasting mates than the welfare of ordinary people (“Albanese, Taylor hedge their bets on gambling reform deal, spooked by One Nation”, August 9). To put this in perspective, when cigarette advertising was banned it was, according to broadcasters, an end-of-life experience. They survived. When alcohol advertising was banned it was also an end-of-life experience. Again, the companies survived. Banning s will make life more difficult for gambling companies and broadcasters, but they will also survive. For the sake of all Australians, Albanese needs to grow a spine and stand up to the gambling and broadcasting industries. Ross Hudson, Mount Martha (Vic) Reading the latest article on reforms to gambling advertising reminds me that as a country, we have been in this situation twice before – once involving tobacco and once involving alcohol. It’s clear that with these two interventions, the doom and gloom scenarios did not eventuate. Why would it be different with gambling? Remember, it was never about banning the product, only its advertising.

Graham Hansen, Denistone Voters have had enough of the misery that online gambling is causing Australians. Albanese seems unwilling to enact legislation to remove this scourge from our society. His assertion that his government has done more than any other to curb online gambling fools no one because everyone knows that previous governments have done nothing. Ian Adair, Hunters Hill Photo: Vintage Wilcox: September 2024



Sink the subs With the decision that Australia had “dispatched up to 130 tradespeople to help with production bottlenecks” (“Very real risk of no subs at all: Turnbull”, August 10), not only have we provided billions in upfront payments for subs that may not arrive, but we are sending highly trained tradespeople. This back-of-the-envelope agreement by Scott Morrison should never have been endorsed by Anthony Albanese the day after his election as PM, but it must be ended. It will no doubt be at an awful cost to us, but it’s better than continuing. Our investment in Australian, unmanned, remote-controlled submarines needs to be increased instead. Bill Johnstone, Blackheath Stamp out duty With the correction now taking place in the housing market, which may be good news for potential buyers and particularly those entering the market for the first time, one of the remaining obstacles to mobility in the market has to be stamp duty (“The Sydney suburbs with the deepest property downturns”, August 8). I understand it accounts for up to 22 per cent of state taxes, but with sales declining, this must surely have a negative effect on state revenues. Stamp duty is certainly a huge disincentive for those considering downsizing, which might otherwise free up living space for those who need it more. In addition to this, there is a distinct lack of suitable (smaller) property for downsizers to move into. A partial solution might be to reform and significantly lower the rate of stamp duty. This would not reduce the amount of stamp duty collected to fund public services, as, in the context of downsizing it is not now being collected at all. Better that a state government collects some tax than none at all. I have the feeling that this issue is ideological rather than pragmatic. Time for the discussion to be taken up and taken seriously. Shaun Davies, St Peters Calling it Chris Rivers’ letter highlights the serious issue of jobs being sent offshore (Letters, August 10). The other matter arising from this is the old chestnut from consumers: “I cannot understand the person who answers the phone”. My problem arises because I am hard of hearing and, despite having hearing aids, I simply cannot understand many accents. One of the worst offenders is Telstra. On many occasions, I have tried to speak to someone in Australia for the above reason but was not even able to be transferred back to Australia from the overseas call centre. Years ago this was happening and Telstra fixed it for a while, but unfortunately, it’s now worse than ever. So really it’s a double whammy, both for Australian employees and Australian consumers. It’s just not good enough. Christine Helby, Forbes



Profits and loss In addition to the penalty issued to the gardener who cleared trees in Woodford Bay Reserve (“Sydney gardener fined over destruction of 287 foreshore trees”, August 9), and anyone else who illegally clears trees, they should be made, under council supervision, to replace the felled trees with mature or semi-mature trees and bear all the costs from purchase, to transporting and planting. This penalty should also be strictly enforced when developers clear land, and if it prevents their development plans, well so be it. The environment and native animals are more important than any profit a developer might make. Victor Marshall, Meander (Tas) Warm-hearted Four letters in Monday’s Herald were critical of Australia’s fossil fuel exporters for contributing towards global warming (Letters, August 10). But there was no mention of the buyers of these exports, the countries that burn the fuels and create the emissions. I think we should bear in mind that the main importers of Australia’s coal and gas – Japan, China, South Korea and India – are all committed to and actively working towards carbon neutrality. Even in Australia, with our access to abundant sun and wind, we have seen how slow that transition can be, so we have to accept that there will continue to be a reasonable short- to medium-term global demand for coal and gas, which has to be produced somewhere. Of course, Australia should not be promoting the consumption of fossil fuels, and we should be demanding a proper financial benefit from their sale, but it is surely not unreasonable for Australian miners to continue to help meet the global demand? Col Nicholson, Hawks Nest Dams and statistics Your recent articles and letters in today’s paper are correct that we must prepare and adapt rapidly to the changing climate (Letters, August 10). The severe fires in Europe and North America are sure signs of a warming planet. In this context, it’s patently obvious that water is an increasingly valuable resource. However, no dam has been built in NSW in about 40 years. Our population has doubled, we face climate change, destructive fires, and yet no additional water reserves have been secured. How is this good and responsible government? More wind farms and solar farms are not going to provide the water we’ll need in the future. We must build more dams. Dennis Bluth, Cammeray



Airport safety I think the quote from the chief executive of airline peak body A4ANZ Stephen Beckett on the recent run of Sydney airport near-misses highlights a disregard for the air safety workforce (“Two planes involved in second recent near-miss at Sydney Airport”, August 9). He is quoted as saying that “workers calling in sick or for carer duties were causing the network to grind to a halt”. How dare those workers request time off for these issues? May I suggest that the real problem is a lack of adequate workforce planning and development to cover these contingencies. What a poor message to send to your workforce. Geoff Delaney, Chipping Norton A Jetstar and a Qatar Airways plane came within metres of colliding on the tarmac at Sydney Airport. Nine News Memory lanes Thank you, Julia Baird, for your article (“My daughter’s European backpacker odyssey is nothing like mine. That’s her loss”, August 8). I tore it out of the Herald (yes, I still read the paper edition) and gave it to my eldest son with a dusty box of about 160 handwritten aerograms, postcards and letters. Most of the correspondence passed between my girlfriend (now my wife of 46 years) and myself when I took off backpacking alone around the planet for 12 months in 1979. Will today’s travellers have their emails, posts and Instagrams in 50 years to pass on to their loved ones? Peter Baker, Blacktown Letters play Thank you, Michael Deeth, for the exclusive invitation to join the duo epistolary group (Letters, August 10). I must confess, though, that I have long been a serial correspondent, but to preserve your ego, I have written under a persona. Let the duel of duos begin. Kim Deeth, Como

World.title: ‘I haven’t done enough’: Jake Weatherald admits he could be dropped without hometown runs
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket ‘I haven’t done enough’: Jake Weatherald admits he could be dropped without hometown runs Daniel Brettig August 10, 2026 — 6:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Darwin: As Travis Head committed to opening the batting throughout Australia’s strenuous next 12 months of Test series, his opening partner Jake Weatherald has admitted he won’t last long at the other end without hometown runs against Bangladesh. Former opener Matt Renshaw was part of the extended 19-man training squad ahead of this week’s first Test, and the plain-speaking Weatherald was frank about his prospects should he not make a couple of notable scores in the top end. Jake Weatherald leaves the field during an Ashes Test last summer. AP Allrounders Beau Webster and Cameron Green are likely to play together this week after both played key roles at Australia’s main training session, which was brought forward to give the fast bowlers more recovery time from Darwin’s heat. Josh Inglis would then miss out. Josh Hazlewood appears to be shading Scott Boland for the third pace bowling spot.



Mark Waugh has been one seasoned judge to state that Weatherald must make the top order spot his own after a patchy debut series in last summer’s Ashes, and while a recent stint in county cricket helped the left-hander iron out some technical issues exposed by England, the proof will be in the run-scoring in Darwin and Mackay. “With someone like Mark Waugh saying that, he’s probably just stating the obvious isn’t he, to be fair,” Weatherald said on Monday. “You are required to make runs all the time when you’re out there, and I’ve got a good opportunity to play two games hopefully and make some runs. If I don’t do that, then yeah I put my fate in someone else’s hands and I haven’t done enough. Editor's pick Australian cricket Bowled out for 54 in their warm-up game, can Bangladesh avoid Test match humiliation? “It’s a challenge when people you respect say things about your batting, or your game. You’re naturally always looking for affirmation, and people to respect what you’re doing, but at the same time it’s a part of cricket. “I understand now it’s just a part of the game I’m playing, but it’s a great challenge as well. That’s what makes Test cricket so hard, you’re in the spotlight, you need to do a lot of things, not just make runs. If you can do it all, it makes for a good career.”



As a former Territorian who moved to South Australia and then Tasmania to earn his chance in Tests, Weatherald is everywhere this week, from promotional posters and media rounds to a growing group of fans wandering around Darwin in skull caps to mimic his shaved head. “I won’t hide away from the fact it’s always nerve-wracking to play for your country, but I’m just excited to get out there and try to put on a bit of a show,” he said. “It’s such a big thing for the Territory to have a Territorian play ... it’s not just for me, it’s for everyone else too.” Jake Weatherald has proven to be a prime lbw candidate. 7 Network Full deliveries at the stumps got Weatherald into trouble against England, but a fruitful county stint (483 runs at 60.37 with a century in six games for Leicestershire) gave him a chance to tighten up. “There’s been a few tinkerings, hopefully someone sees it,” he said. “It feels completely different, but everyone says I’m pretty similar, which is sort of what I wanted.



Editor's pick Exclusive

Australian cricket ‘They hid it away’: The DNA test that revealed an Australian cricketer’s family secret “I tried to understand what I was really good at and do well in first-class cricket, and what I can improve on what I did in the Ashes to make a better game plan overall. I think I’ve done that, so I’m pretty pumped to go out there and show that. “The conditions were very conducive to improving my technique, getting the ball straighter and hitting the stumps a lot more. So it was a great learning curve for me.” Head, meanwhile, has advised Weatherald not to think too much about high expectations this week. As a state and national teammate, Head is hopeful of the partnership enduring beyond this series, into what are likely to be bruising encounters with South Africa, New Zealand, India and England. “Sometimes playing the better countries, you sit there with expectations going into a Test and say ‘I just hope I get through it’ sometimes,” Head said. “Then you may come up against a team like Bangladesh with the week they’ve had and the expectation of ‘I really expect myself to get runs’.



Related Article Australian cricket Cricket hoped the AB Medal would rival Brownlow glitz and glamour. This year’s award was not even broadcast on TV “That’s sometimes the hardest place to be, when you go out there expecting to, because the game is brutal. So it’s just about tempering expectations around the next little period.” Australia’s head coach Andrew McDonald has confirmed a reduced role for assistant coach Dan Vettori, following the New Zealander’s increased role for the Sunrisers Hyderabad network of franchise teams. “I think there’s choice in the marketplace,” he said. “There’s a market for players and there’ clearly. market for coaches. Dan’s explored that market and we’ve been able to balance that out with him doing some great work with us, so long may that continue.” Sports news, results and expert commentary.

World.title: Eleven teens and adults charged with torturing boy
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland Police Eleven teens and adults charged with torturing boy Julius Dennis Updated August 10, 2026 — 6:19pm ,first published 5:44pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Eleven people, including several teenagers, have been charged for allegedly torturing a teenage boy before binding him with zip ties, wrapping him in plastic in a large park near Townsville. The 17-year-old boy was discovered by joggers in the vast public park north of the city called Town Commons about 6.30am on Saturday, July 18. A police spokesperson said the teenager was left off Cape Pallarenda Road, near Pallarenda, which runs along the beach from near Townsville airport to the waterfront community of Pallarenda. Police have arrested 11 people linked to the alleged torture. Tourism and Events Queensland On Friday, Detective Senior Sergeant David Miles said the boy had been at an address in the Townsville suburb of Heatley, where police will allege he was assaulted before he was taken to the park and left for between five and six hours.



He was taken to Townsville University Hospital in a stable condition, but required surgery for some of his injuries, Miles said. He alleged the attack was not random, and orchestrated by a group who knew the young man. Child protection police opened an investigation, which led to the arrest of a 13-year-old boy from the Townsville suburb of Deeragun on July 24. He was charged with allegedly depravation of liberty, assault occasioning bodily harm, grievous bodily harm and torture. Four days later a 35-year-old woman and a 14-year-old girl from nearby Kirwan were charged with the same offences, with a charge of driving without a licence added for the woman.



Eight more people have been charged since Friday. A 36-year-old woman from Cranbrook, a 32-year-old from Kirwan, and a 40-year-old woman and 30-year-old man and a 24-year-old man all from Heatley were given the same charges. They all faced the Townsville Magistrates Court on Friday and were remanded in custody. Three 15-year-old boys – two from Kirwan charged on Friday, and one from Mount Low charged on Monday – are facing the same charges. Miles said the investigations led his team to a car crash on the same morning the boy was found, on The Strand in Townsville.



“The examination of a motor vehicle there led to significant items relative to this investigation, and that then generated further inquires,” he said. A police spokesperson said the investigation was ongoing. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Albanese, Taylor hammer out deals on gambling and tech, but ignore Howard’s last-ditch plea
World.content:
PoliticsFederalOnline gambling Albanese, Taylor hammer out deals on gambling and tech, but ignore Howard’s last-ditch plea Paul Sakkal Updated August 10, 2026 — 6:13pm ,first published 10:20am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Opposition Leader Angus Taylor are hammering out deals on charging tech giants for news, cutting the NDIS, and curbing betting promotions, prompting the Coalition to mull a broader bargain on tax and migration. A last-minute plea from former prime minister John Howard to go further on sports betting s appears unlikely to sway the leaders, who excluded the Greens to do a rare Labor-Coalition deal on a set of thorny issues as One Nation eats into their vote. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, former prime minister John Howard and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. Alex Ellinghausen, Dylan Coker Resisting pressure from Labor and Liberal backbenchers and Howard to go further on gambling, Albanese insisted he had got the balance right between acknowledging those who “have a punt on a Saturday” and protecting kids and addicts, pitching his day of deal-making as delivering “outcomes over outrage”. “We choose a different road: we choose progress over protest,” he told Labor MPs in Canberra, after this masthead reported worry in cabinet over One Nation portraying a full ban on betting ads as a nanny-state solution.



“We choose unity over division … We’re here to make a difference.” Albanese is expected to yield from his positions by restricting betting inducements and reversing a change to the News Bargaining Incentive that large media outlets said would crimp their revenue. Both were aimed at winning Taylor’s support and satisfying corporate demands, clearing the path for a clutch of legislative wins in the first parliamentary session after the winter break. Powerful media and sporting stakeholders were worried about the Greens’ more strident positions on policies where Albanese was keen to bank quick wins. Taylor and Albanese face off in parliament earlier this year. Alex Ellinghausen Coalition sources involved in the talks with Labor said the party would now think about how it could leverage its in-principle agreement to move quickly on the NDIS. The opposition may demand speedy resolution of a quirk in Labor’s negative gearing laws that hurts widows or seek a commitment to give the Coalition some wins on its upcoming migration overhaul, which One Nation has sought to exploit. As politicians returned to Canberra on Monday after the winter break, one of Albanese’s first items of businesses was scheduling a meeting with Taylor to salvage his big tech agenda from the brink of defeat and to win support for plans to force US platforms to pay for news and block gambling advertising.



Sources on both sides said that Albanese and Taylor had a detailed discussion on betting ads. The long-running policy debate has pitted gambling harm advocates against big media firms, including this masthead’s owner Nine, and sports. Albanese and Taylor agreed to work on amendments that would strengthen restrictions on inducements, a week after bombshell allegations that betting firms were holding drug-fuelled events with big gamblers. Labor has initially resisted going further on inducements. Country Racing Victoria chief executive Scott Whiteman said cash-strapped regional racing would be “up the creek” financially if it could not reward punters with free bets and other “generosities”. Loading Howard made a last-ditch plea for Albanese and Taylor to take on powerful media and sports outfits by cracking down hard on sports betting ads. The former leader rubbished Labor’s proposed opt-out system which relies on people telling a social media platform or broadcaster they do not want to see ads, telling this masthead it was “against human nature to expect people to sit down and opt out”. Instead, Howard declared it would be “far better” to create a new opt-in system whereby people would be shielded from promotions unless they volunteered to see them. The opt-in model is supported by the Greens and some major party MPs, but the major party cabinets view the idea as too extreme.



“I think it should be the attitude of all the major political parties, both Labor and Coalition, to legislate in the public interest. And if that means disappointing major companies, then disappoint them,” Howard said in an interview. Related Article Media & marketing News Corp says plan to make tech giants pay for news has been ‘gutted’ “It’s a very poor thing that young people grow up thinking that gambling on sport is a normal part of life.” Taylor told reporters in Canberra: “We’ve seen three years of delay from Labor on dealing with this but … we will work with the government to make sure it is right.” Albanese and Taylor also held looser discussions on the NDIS, which the Coalition delayed but was always likely to eventually support, and the News Bargaining Incentive. The NDIS changes, which could pass the Senate next week, would shift 160,000 people away from the bulging system and save up to $38 billion over four years. Every month in which the laws were not tightened would cost the budget about $1.5 billion.



A week after the largest news firms pleaded with the prime minister to reverse last-minute changes to the News Bargaining Incentive, Albanese also expressed optimism about settling on a model to push Meta, Google and TikTok to pay for news articles. The tech giants argue there is no justification for the policy because news outlets benefit from distributing their work on social media. Albanese has pledged to stand up for the scheme in the face of threats from the Trump administration, which has described the tech taxes as extortion. The news scheme was at risk of collapse after Nine and News Corp savaged amendments that may have lowered payments to big media outlets and pushed money to smaller ones. The news bargaining incentive is a world-first framework to draw revenue from tech giants to fund journalism. The key change that infuriated the news organisations would hypothetically reduce any one firm’s portion of the fund from $25 million to less than $17 million.



The change was made by Labor without consultation. It was designed to benefit smaller publishers, but large outlets argued it undervalued the bigger players who hire the most journalists. World.title: Saint. Martyr. Heroine. Next year the story of Joan of Arc will be told anew
World.content:
CultureMusicArts Saint. Martyr. Heroine. Next year the story of Joan of Arc will be told anew Kerrie O'Brien August 10, 2026 — 6:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The trial material of 15th-century saint Joan of Arc will serve as the inspiration for a new work of music and the centrepiece of the 2027 Melbourne Symphony Orchestra program. Composer Mary Finsterer, together with librettist Tom Wright, has created a new work, Joan of Arc, which will make its world premiere with the Melbourne Symphony Orchestra in October next year, conducted by Benjamin Northey. Composer Mary Finsterer’s new work will lead the MSO’s 2027 program. Dean Golja It’s one of 13 world premieres in the orchestra’s 2027 season, which includes 12 works from Australians, including two by Indigenous composers. More than 40 Australian soloists will appear with the state orchestra across the year. Joan of Arc, a 16-year-old peasant, helped fight for France’s freedom against the English, believing she was acting under divine guidance. Now regarded as a heroine, she was tried by an ecclesiastical court that eventually condemned her as a heretic. At age 19 she was burnt to death at the stake.



Finsterer says Joan of Arc is at once medieval and completely contemporary. “Joan is an outsider who refuses to allow powerful institutions to define her,” the former MSO composer-in-residence says, adding that she is a figure of resistance. “Resistance in a broad sense – she resists political power, she resists institutional authority, and ultimately the attempt to make her deny her own conscience. “We’re living at a time when questions of power and authority and individual conscience feel particularly acute,” she adds. MSO chief conductor Jaime Martín will open the season with a tribute to Beethoven. Lucas Allen MSO’s program announcement comes after a tumultuous few years for the orchestra, involving the high-profile suit brought by pianist Jayson Gillham. The London-based, Queensland-born pianist had sued the MSO for unfair dismissal for expressing political beliefs, after he spoke about journalists killed in Gaza before playing a piece at the MSO’s Iwaki Auditorium in August 2024. He had not sought permission from management to make the remarks. Gillham lost the three-week case in June this year, when it was heard in the Federal Court.

“We constantly ask ourselves what a living Australian orchestra must aspire to be,” says MSO CEO Richard Wigley. He says a big part of that is commitment to new music and Australian artistry.



The free concerts at the Sidney Myer Music Bowl will return in summer, the opening of which will be curated by Noongar man and local artist Aaron Wyatt and feature a new work written by William Barton. First Look Seats, which allow people to see shows for $20 a ticket will be back for 2027, as will a program that brings performances to neighbourhoods around Victoria. Aaron Wyatt conducts the 2026 MSO First Nations Showcase. Laura Manariti Next year’s program also celebrates the traditional, showcasing Beethoven, in commemoration of the 200th anniversary of the German composer’s death. In February, chief conductor Jaime Martín opens the season with a program of three works including Beethoven’s Ninth Symphony, featuring the MSO choir with Ode to Joy. He will also lead the MSO in performances of Schubert and Mahler, Mozart and Brahms, Rachmaninov and Dvořák, Mozart and the Mendelssohns and Sibelius and Shostakovich. Martín described next year’s program – his sixth as chief conductor – as “a celebration of the spirit of discovery”, adding that the MSO is a “wonderful group of supremely talented musicians whose every turn of a musical phrase is pure poetry”. Making their Australian debuts with the orchestra are conductors Yutaka Sado (Japan) and Eva Ollikainen (Finland), soprano Claire Booth (UK), violinist Inmo Yang (South Korea) and mezzo-soprano Fleur Barron (UK/Singapore).



International artists on the slate next year include conductors Chloé van Soeterstède (France) and Rodolfo Barráez (Venezuela), acclaimed British pianist Paul Lewis, and MSO’s 2027 featured artist, Romanian pianist Alexandra Dariescu, who will perform across four events. Melbourne-born conductor Nicholas Carter will return as chief guest conductor with the MSO in 2027 Matthias Baus Valley of the Dry Bones, composed by Yitzhak Yedid and narrated by Stan Grant, makes its world premiere, unveiled in June. Featuring the MSO chorus, it is described as a biblical, universal story about conflict. Brett Dean’s The World’s Wife makes its Australian premiere in November, after its first airing at the 2026 BBC Proms. Dean sets Carol Ann Duffy’s poetry to music and reimagines the famous stories of men through a feminine perspective, including figures like Mrs Darwin, Frau Freud, Queen Herod and Anne Hathaway. Melbourne-born conductor Nicholas Carter, who has made his name in Europe, will return as chief guest conductor with the MSO next year. General music director of the Staatsoper and Staatsorchester Stuttgart, he will lead the orchestra in two concerts, Strauss & Schumann in August, and Bruckner’s Eighth Symphony later that month.



Related Article Arts From the Wiggles to the MSO, this creative collective puts the heart in art Carter is looking forward to conducting the monumental Bruckner work. “In our fragmented, anxious and increasingly digital world, this music offers us a rare opportunity to reconnect with the magnificence of the human mind and spirit,” he said. “At times meditative, at others terrifying and intensely dramatic, the symphony gives us the time and space simply to be with ourselves, and to focus on what is beautiful, profound and enriching in our lives.” The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. World.title: Sex worker charged alongside banker committed to stand trial
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCourts Sex worker charged alongside banker committed to stand trial Cloe Read August 10, 2026 — 5:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Brisbane sex worker who was charged alongside a former Sydney-based banker has been committed to stand trial over allegations she tried to procure underage girls for sex. Shauntelle Elizabeth Went will face a District Court trial on charges of using the internet to procure a person under the age of 16 to engage in a sexual act. Former Commonwealth Bank executive Christopher James McCann, 50, allegedly engaged Went, 18, to supply the services of two girls aged 14 or 15, the court earlier heard. Shauntelle Elizabeth Went leaving court on Monday. Brisbane Times / Cloe Read McCann, based in Sydney, frequently travelled interstate, and asked Went whether she had younger friends that she worked with, according to previous court hearings.



The court earlier heard McCann was accused of making an arrangement and agreeing on a price to use Went’s services, alongside two underage girls. Later that evening, Went and the girls attended a five-star hotel in Brisbane’s CBD, the court heard. The girls were not alleged to have entered the room, after McCann contacted the front desk to ask them to leave. McCann was found dead in Springbrook, in the Gold Coast hinterland, two days after he was released on bail in July last year. His death was not suspicious. Carolyn Juratowitch, representing Went for her committal hearing, told the court her client did not wish to enter a plea. Juratowitch also submitted for her client’s bail conditions to be varied, to remove her reporting to police.



“She’s now been on bail in excess of a year. It’s my submission that bail condition is just unnecessary,” she said, adding Went was not a flight risk. “She is, I think because of her mental health, in fairly regular contact with police for welfare checks in any event and I’m asking that be removed simply because it is not necessary.” Christopher James McCann leaving the Brisbane Watch House last year. AAP The court heard Went had been charged twice for breaching her bail. Prosecutor William Orrah told the court that Went had failed to report to police twice, and on the second time, police took her phone for inspection.



Encrypted messaging apps were found on her phone, which were against her bail conditions. “The facts of the offence have to do with using an internet service to be able to procure a child for these sexual acts,” he said. He said the encrypted apps were only found because Went had been reporting to police. The court heard Went had also been charged with wilful damage and threatening violence this year. Magistrate Belinda Merrin ultimately upheld the existing police reporting conditions, saying it was appropriate to ameliorate the risks.



When asked if she had anything to say in relation to the charge, Went answered: “No, your Honour.” She was committed to stand trial in the District Court at a later date. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service (1800RESPECT) on 1800 737 732. If you, or someone you know, needs support you can call Lifeline on 13 11 14 or Beyond Blue on 1300 224 636. World.title: ‘Bizarre display of gutter politics’: WA One Nation leader returns serve to premier’s broadside
World.content:
PoliticsWAOne Nation ‘Bizarre display of gutter politics’: WA One Nation leader returns serve to premier’s broadside Michael Philipps August 10, 2026 — 6:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

West Australian Premier Roger Cook has launched a scathing attack on One Nation for promoting “people who are convicted rapists, people who have charges pending, people who have been accused of sexual assault” as the battle for a looming byelection in Perth’s south heats up. However, One Nation’s WA leader Rod Caddies returned serve, accusing Cook of “desperate and bizarre tactics” ahead of the vote in Secret Harbour, sparked by the resignation of former minister Paul Papalia in July. WA Premier Roger Cook. AFR Speaking at a press conference on Monday, Cook was asked to comment on a 2021 podcast featuring Labor’s candidate for Secret Harbour, Georgia Tree, who was working for federal Brand MP Madeleine King at the time. On the episode of the In the House & In the Senate podcast, Tree spoke of Labor having potential “skeletons in the closet” in the aftermath of Brittany Higgins’ allegations that she was raped in Parliament House in Canberra.



On Monday, Cook defended Tree’s appearance, and said her comments showed she stood up for her community. “She doesn’t take bullcrap,” Cook said. “She calls it out when she sees it, and she was making a comment about the people who don’t have a voice, the people who are voiceless. “She was providing a voice to those people, so I’m proud of the comments that she made.” Cook added that Tree’s stance stood in contrast to One Nation.



“[One Nation] are the people who promote people who have been charged or convicted of outstanding arrest warrants for sexual assault,” Cook said. Related Article One Nation Pauline Hanson opens up on domestic violence, prison and racism claims “They promote as their campaign leader someone who is a convicted rapist. “So when it comes to standing up for women, I back Georgia Tree any day.” In April, One Nation leader Pauline Hanson said she had fired Sean Black, who was rehired by the party as its national campaign after he was jailed in 2018 for raping and violently assaulting a woman.



In March, South Australian One Nation candidate Aoi Baxter was dumped on the eve of the election after it was revealed he was wanted in the UK for allegedly failing to appear in court over sexual touching charges. Cook said a lot had changed in parliament since he was first elected in 2008. “A lot has changed in relation to the culture, not only of all parts of Parliament, but certainly on my side of politics,” he said. “We are promoting women today, and as a result of that, our party is much stronger. “It stands in contrast to the sort of people that One Nation are putting up, people who are convicted rapists, people who have charges pending, people who have been accused of sexual assault.



“They are the sort of people that they are promoting, and that is the sort of person that [WA Liberal leader] Basil Zempilas is trying to get up in Western Australia by directing Liberal Party preferences to One Nation.” WA One Nation leader Rod Caddies. Trevor Collens However, Caddies said he wouldn’t be “pulled down into the gutter” by the premier. “All sides of politics are noticing Labor and the premier’s desperate and bizarre tactics,” Caddies said. “Their attempt to use weasel words to imply nefarious things about my candidate or me shows the premier’s lack of moral standards and character, and I won’t be pulled down into the gutter with him.



“It is interesting to see the premier endorse his candidate’s podcast comments; he seems to agree there are skeletons in his party’s closet, and perhaps he and his candidate should open up about what they are.” Caddies said it was disappointing to see the government behave this way. “We are on opposite sides of politics, but even I was still expecting certain basic standards of behaviour,” he said. “We expected a robust campaign that pulls no punches, not this bizarre display of gutter politics.” Tree said she stood by her comments on the podcast, adding that she had always been outspoken, and would always fight for what is right – particularly when it comes to women’s experiences in the workplace.



“I led a sit-in in Federal Parliament in 2021 to stand up against ‘don’t ask, don’t tell’ culture and sexual harassment in the workplace,” she said. Related Article Updated

Public transport WA Labor and Liberals battle it out over Karnup train station promise “I was backed and fully supported by my boss at the time, Minister Madeleine King. Just as I have been ever since I spoke out on this issue.” Tree added that since 2021, there had been great shifts within the Labor Party. “Both the federal and WA Caucus is now made up of more than 50 per cent women,” she said.



“This is one of the reasons why I am running, we need to see more young women entering politics to fight for change and not be afraid to stand up, speak out and take their seat at the table.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: KPMG chair-elect admits to sending ‘naive, embarrassing and wrong’ email
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesWhistleblowers KPMG chair-elect admits to sending ‘naive, embarrassing and wrong’ email Colin Kruger Updated August 10, 2026 — 6:30pm ,first published 3:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

KPMG’s chairman-elect Michael Ebeid has issued a grovelling apology for dismissing allegations from a whistleblower that have rocked the consultancy as he fights to win his job on a permanent basis. And in a bigger issue for the consultancy, documents released by parliament on Monday showed that two major law firms that reviewed the whistleblower’s claims early in the saga failed to take basic steps, such as interviewing people involved or checking staff emails. KPMG’s incoming chairman Michael Ebeid issued a grovelling apology to Senator Deborah O’Neill. Getty Images But in March, Ebeid had emailed his colleagues on the KPMG board accusing Labor’s Senator Deborah O’Neill of airing “completely false” allegations when she read out the whistleblower’s claims that top staff at the firm had misused confidential client information. Those allegations have since been substantiated. Ebeid, who has essentially been functioning as the chairman of the firm that is trying to recover from its top executives’ misuse of clients’ confidential audit documents, needs to get the backing of KPMG partners in a vote that concludes on Wednesday.



Related Article Big four accountants KPMG directors flee as whistleblower scandal worsens On Monday, documents released by O’Neill’s parliamentary committee, which is investigating the scandal, revealed Ebeid’s personal apology to O’Neill for the March email. “What I wrote was wrong,” Ebeid told O’Neill on Saturday, according to one document. “I described statements about the whistleblower’s allegations made by you to the Senate as false. I described the firm’s process as thorough. Events since have shown that neither was true, and that the concerns you raised on the whistleblower’s behalf have helped uncover serious wrongdoing and I can only thank you for that.” He said he thought he was being helpful, based on his knowledge at the time. “However, with what I know now, my email was naive, embarrassing and wrong on every level,” Ebeid wrote. And in a fresh issue for the embattled firm, the committee also released documents that KPMG had battled to keep hidden under claims of legal professional privilege. The committee said it was in the public interest to release these documents ahead of another public grilling this Friday.



The legal documents were the reports from two law firms, Allens and Ashurst, and relate to their work on the whistleblower complaints. KPMG had initially used the reports from the law firms to claim that the whistleblower’s complaints were unsubstantiated while refusing to make the actual documents public. A fresh investigation by Allens has led to a purge of KPMG’s most senior people as some of the most serious allegations have now been substantiated. “The Ashurst and Allens processes were central to the claim that KPMG had undertaken comprehensive internal and external investigations prior to the speech given by Senator Deborah O’Neill on 24 March 2026,” the committee – chaired by O’Neill – said in a statement. It said the committee had found there was a “compelling public interest” in examining the results of the law firms’ investigations at its next hearing, allowing it to publish the previously legally privileged documents. KPMG’s new chief executive John Sams told partners that the parliamentary committee informed the firm of its intentions to publish the documents on Friday.



“We acknowledged the Committee’s role and the importance of scrutiny and transparency, while noting that the reports reflect a point in time and do not correctly represent the current status of the investigations,” he said. One of the documents was a report submitted to KPMG in December last year by Allens that said all the whistleblower’s allegations were unsubstantiated. This includes the claim that KPMG’s Lendlease audit team stole confidential board papers and shared them internally to help win multimillion-dollar external audit tenders for Westpac and Dexus. Given the credibility of the KPMG executives involved, Allens said it was “disproportionate and unnecessary” to search staff emails to check what they had said was correct. A subsequent investigation by Allens confirmed that senior partners had illicitly accessed sensitive Lendlease board documents and kept them in a work locker, and led to the immediate expulsion of former chief operating officer Eileen Hoggett.



Another document released was an Ashurst report from February last year. At the committee’s public hearing last month the law firm described its work for KPMG as legal advice. This report also cleared KPMG personnel of any wrongdoing “based on the material reviewed”, but the report contained a significant caveat. “In coming to these conclusions we have not had the benefit of speaking directly to any of the individuals concerned and assessing their credibility,” Ashurst’s lawyers wrote. Ashurst and Allens, two of Australia’s largest law firms, declined to comment. Since May, the firm has lost its chief executive Andrew Yates, chairman Martin Sheppard, and Hoggett after she lied the board documents. KPMG audit partner Kim Lawry also resigned from her senior roles last month after Westpac requested that she be removed from its audit “to ensure there is no distraction”.



KPMG independent board member Patty Akopiantz quietly left the firm’s regional board last month, following former NSW premier Mike Baird’s exit in September, and fellow independent director Jane Hemstritch is expected to resign once replacements have been found. World.title: ‘I haven’t done enough’: Jake Weatherald admits he could be dropped without hometown runs
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket ‘I haven’t done enough’: Jake Weatherald admits he could be dropped without hometown runs Daniel Brettig August 10, 2026 — 6:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Darwin: As Travis Head committed to opening the batting throughout Australia’s strenuous next 12 months of Test series, his opening partner Jake Weatherald has admitted he won’t last long at the other end without hometown runs against Bangladesh. Former opener Matt Renshaw was part of the extended 19-man training squad ahead of this week’s first Test, and the plain-speaking Weatherald was frank about his prospects should he not make a couple of notable scores in the top end. Jake Weatherald leaves the field during an Ashes Test last summer. AP Allrounders Beau Webster and Cameron Green are likely to play together this week after both played key roles at Australia’s main training session, which was brought forward to give the fast bowlers more recovery time from Darwin’s heat. Josh Inglis would then miss out. Josh Hazlewood appears to be shading Scott Boland for the third pace bowling spot.



Mark Waugh has been one seasoned judge to state that Weatherald must make the top order spot his own after a patchy debut series in last summer’s Ashes, and while a recent stint in county cricket helped the left-hander iron out some technical issues exposed by England, the proof will be in the run-scoring in Darwin and Mackay. “With someone like Mark Waugh saying that, he’s probably just stating the obvious isn’t he, to be fair,” Weatherald said on Monday. “You are required to make runs all the time when you’re out there, and I’ve got a good opportunity to play two games hopefully and make some runs. If I don’t do that, then yeah I put my fate in someone else’s hands and I haven’t done enough. Editor's pick Australian cricket Bowled out for 54 in their warm-up game, can Bangladesh avoid Test match humiliation? “It’s a challenge when people you respect say things about your batting, or your game. You’re naturally always looking for affirmation, and people to respect what you’re doing, but at the same time it’s a part of cricket. “I understand now it’s just a part of the game I’m playing, but it’s a great challenge as well. That’s what makes Test cricket so hard, you’re in the spotlight, you need to do a lot of things, not just make runs. If you can do it all, it makes for a good career.”



As a former Territorian who moved to South Australia and then Tasmania to earn his chance in Tests, Weatherald is everywhere this week, from promotional posters and media rounds to a growing group of fans wandering around Darwin in skull caps to mimic his shaved head. “I won’t hide away from the fact it’s always nerve-wracking to play for your country, but I’m just excited to get out there and try to put on a bit of a show,” he said. “It’s such a big thing for the Territory to have a Territorian play ... it’s not just for me, it’s for everyone else too.” Jake Weatherald has proven to be a prime lbw candidate. 7 Network Full deliveries at the stumps got Weatherald into trouble against England, but a fruitful county stint (483 runs at 60.37 with a century in six games for Leicestershire) gave him a chance to tighten up. “There’s been a few tinkerings, hopefully someone sees it,” he said. “It feels completely different, but everyone says I’m pretty similar, which is sort of what I wanted.



Editor's pick Exclusive

Australian cricket ‘They hid it away’: The DNA test that revealed an Australian cricketer’s family secret “I tried to understand what I was really good at and do well in first-class cricket, and what I can improve on what I did in the Ashes to make a better game plan overall. I think I’ve done that, so I’m pretty pumped to go out there and show that. “The conditions were very conducive to improving my technique, getting the ball straighter and hitting the stumps a lot more. So it was a great learning curve for me.” Head, meanwhile, has advised Weatherald not to think too much about high expectations this week. As a state and national teammate, Head is hopeful of the partnership enduring beyond this series, into what are likely to be bruising encounters with South Africa, New Zealand, India and England. “Sometimes playing the better countries, you sit there with expectations going into a Test and say ‘I just hope I get through it’ sometimes,” Head said. “Then you may come up against a team like Bangladesh with the week they’ve had and the expectation of ‘I really expect myself to get runs’.



Related Article Australian cricket Cricket hoped the AB Medal would rival Brownlow glitz and glamour. This year’s award was not even broadcast on TV “That’s sometimes the hardest place to be, when you go out there expecting to, because the game is brutal. So it’s just about tempering expectations around the next little period.” Australia’s head coach Andrew McDonald has confirmed a reduced role for assistant coach Dan Vettori, following the New Zealander’s increased role for the Sunrisers Hyderabad network of franchise teams. “I think there’s choice in the marketplace,” he said. “There’s a market for players and there’ clearly. market for coaches. Dan’s explored that market and we’ve been able to balance that out with him doing some great work with us, so long may that continue.” Sports news, results and expert commentary.

World.title: Eleven teens and adults charged with torturing boy
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland Police Eleven teens and adults charged with torturing boy Julius Dennis Updated August 10, 2026 — 6:19pm ,first published 5:44pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Eleven people, including several teenagers, have been charged for allegedly torturing a teenage boy before binding him with zip ties, wrapping him in plastic in a large park near Townsville. The 17-year-old boy was discovered by joggers in the vast public park north of the city called Town Commons about 6.30am on Saturday, July 18. A police spokesperson said the teenager was left off Cape Pallarenda Road, near Pallarenda, which runs along the beach from near Townsville airport to the waterfront community of Pallarenda. Police have arrested 11 people linked to the alleged torture. Tourism and Events Queensland On Friday, Detective Senior Sergeant David Miles said the boy had been at an address in the Townsville suburb of Heatley, where police will allege he was assaulted before he was taken to the park and left for between five and six hours.



He was taken to Townsville University Hospital in a stable condition, but required surgery for some of his injuries, Miles said. He alleged the attack was not random, and orchestrated by a group who knew the young man. Child protection police opened an investigation, which led to the arrest of a 13-year-old boy from the Townsville suburb of Deeragun on July 24. He was charged with allegedly depravation of liberty, assault occasioning bodily harm, grievous bodily harm and torture. Four days later a 35-year-old woman and a 14-year-old girl from nearby Kirwan were charged with the same offences, with a charge of driving without a licence added for the woman.



Eight more people have been charged since Friday. A 36-year-old woman from Cranbrook, a 32-year-old from Kirwan, and a 40-year-old woman and 30-year-old man and a 24-year-old man all from Heatley were given the same charges. They all faced the Townsville Magistrates Court on Friday and were remanded in custody. Three 15-year-old boys – two from Kirwan charged on Friday, and one from Mount Low charged on Monday – are facing the same charges. Miles said the investigations led his team to a car crash on the same morning the boy was found, on The Strand in Townsville.



“The examination of a motor vehicle there led to significant items relative to this investigation, and that then generated further inquires,” he said. A police spokesperson said the investigation was ongoing. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Albanese, Taylor hammer out deals on gambling and tech, but ignore Howard’s last-ditch plea
World.content:
PoliticsFederalOnline gambling Albanese, Taylor hammer out deals on gambling and tech, but ignore Howard’s last-ditch plea Paul Sakkal Updated August 10, 2026 — 6:13pm ,first published 10:20am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Opposition Leader Angus Taylor are hammering out deals on charging tech giants for news, cutting the NDIS, and curbing betting promotions, prompting the Coalition to mull a broader bargain on tax and migration. A last-minute plea from former prime minister John Howard to go further on sports betting s appears unlikely to sway the leaders, who excluded the Greens to do a rare Labor-Coalition deal on a set of thorny issues as One Nation eats into their vote. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, former prime minister John Howard and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. Alex Ellinghausen, Dylan Coker Resisting pressure from Labor and Liberal backbenchers and Howard to go further on gambling, Albanese insisted he had got the balance right between acknowledging those who “have a punt on a Saturday” and protecting kids and addicts, pitching his day of deal-making as delivering “outcomes over outrage”. “We choose a different road: we choose progress over protest,” he told Labor MPs in Canberra, after this masthead reported worry in cabinet over One Nation portraying a full ban on betting ads as a nanny-state solution.



“We choose unity over division … We’re here to make a difference.” Albanese is expected to yield from his positions by restricting betting inducements and reversing a change to the News Bargaining Incentive that large media outlets said would crimp their revenue. Both were aimed at winning Taylor’s support and satisfying corporate demands, clearing the path for a clutch of legislative wins in the first parliamentary session after the winter break. Powerful media and sporting stakeholders were worried about the Greens’ more strident positions on policies where Albanese was keen to bank quick wins. Taylor and Albanese face off in parliament earlier this year. Alex Ellinghausen Coalition sources involved in the talks with Labor said the party would now think about how it could leverage its in-principle agreement to move quickly on the NDIS. The opposition may demand speedy resolution of a quirk in Labor’s negative gearing laws that hurts widows or seek a commitment to give the Coalition some wins on its upcoming migration overhaul, which One Nation has sought to exploit. As politicians returned to Canberra on Monday after the winter break, one of Albanese’s first items of businesses was scheduling a meeting with Taylor to salvage his big tech agenda from the brink of defeat and to win support for plans to force US platforms to pay for news and block gambling advertising.



Sources on both sides said that Albanese and Taylor had a detailed discussion on betting ads. The long-running policy debate has pitted gambling harm advocates against big media firms, including this masthead’s owner Nine, and sports. Albanese and Taylor agreed to work on amendments that would strengthen restrictions on inducements, a week after bombshell allegations that betting firms were holding drug-fuelled events with big gamblers. Labor has initially resisted going further on inducements. Country Racing Victoria chief executive Scott Whiteman said cash-strapped regional racing would be “up the creek” financially if it could not reward punters with free bets and other “generosities”. Loading Howard made a last-ditch plea for Albanese and Taylor to take on powerful media and sports outfits by cracking down hard on sports betting ads. The former leader rubbished Labor’s proposed opt-out system which relies on people telling a social media platform or broadcaster they do not want to see ads, telling this masthead it was “against human nature to expect people to sit down and opt out”. Instead, Howard declared it would be “far better” to create a new opt-in system whereby people would be shielded from promotions unless they volunteered to see them. The opt-in model is supported by the Greens and some major party MPs, but the major party cabinets view the idea as too extreme.



“I think it should be the attitude of all the major political parties, both Labor and Coalition, to legislate in the public interest. And if that means disappointing major companies, then disappoint them,” Howard said in an interview. Related Article Media & marketing News Corp says plan to make tech giants pay for news has been ‘gutted’ “It’s a very poor thing that young people grow up thinking that gambling on sport is a normal part of life.” Taylor told reporters in Canberra: “We’ve seen three years of delay from Labor on dealing with this but … we will work with the government to make sure it is right.” Albanese and Taylor also held looser discussions on the NDIS, which the Coalition delayed but was always likely to eventually support, and the News Bargaining Incentive. The NDIS changes, which could pass the Senate next week, would shift 160,000 people away from the bulging system and save up to $38 billion over four years. Every month in which the laws were not tightened would cost the budget about $1.5 billion.



A week after the largest news firms pleaded with the prime minister to reverse last-minute changes to the News Bargaining Incentive, Albanese also expressed optimism about settling on a model to push Meta, Google and TikTok to pay for news articles. The tech giants argue there is no justification for the policy because news outlets benefit from distributing their work on social media. Albanese has pledged to stand up for the scheme in the face of threats from the Trump administration, which has described the tech taxes as extortion. The news scheme was at risk of collapse after Nine and News Corp savaged amendments that may have lowered payments to big media outlets and pushed money to smaller ones. The news bargaining incentive is a world-first framework to draw revenue from tech giants to fund journalism. The key change that infuriated the news organisations would hypothetically reduce any one firm’s portion of the fund from $25 million to less than $17 million.



The change was made by Labor without consultation. It was designed to benefit smaller publishers, but large outlets argued it undervalued the bigger players who hire the most journalists. World.title: Saint. Martyr. Heroine. Next year the story of Joan of Arc will be told anew
World.content:
CultureMusicArts Saint. Martyr. Heroine. Next year the story of Joan of Arc will be told anew Kerrie O'Brien August 10, 2026 — 6:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The trial material of 15th-century saint Joan of Arc will serve as the inspiration for a new work of music and the centrepiece of the 2027 Melbourne Symphony Orchestra program. Composer Mary Finsterer, together with librettist Tom Wright, has created a new work, Joan of Arc, which will make its world premiere with the Melbourne Symphony Orchestra in October next year, conducted by Benjamin Northey. Composer Mary Finsterer’s new work will lead the MSO’s 2027 program. Dean Golja It’s one of 13 world premieres in the orchestra’s 2027 season, which includes 12 works from Australians, including two by Indigenous composers. More than 40 Australian soloists will appear with the state orchestra across the year. Joan of Arc, a 16-year-old peasant, helped fight for France’s freedom against the English, believing she was acting under divine guidance. Now regarded as a heroine, she was tried by an ecclesiastical court that eventually condemned her as a heretic. At age 19 she was burnt to death at the stake.



Finsterer says Joan of Arc is at once medieval and completely contemporary. “Joan is an outsider who refuses to allow powerful institutions to define her,” the former MSO composer-in-residence says, adding that she is a figure of resistance. “Resistance in a broad sense – she resists political power, she resists institutional authority, and ultimately the attempt to make her deny her own conscience. “We’re living at a time when questions of power and authority and individual conscience feel particularly acute,” she adds. MSO chief conductor Jaime Martín will open the season with a tribute to Beethoven. Lucas Allen MSO’s program announcement comes after a tumultuous few years for the orchestra, involving the high-profile suit brought by pianist Jayson Gillham. The London-based, Queensland-born pianist had sued the MSO for unfair dismissal for expressing political beliefs, after he spoke about journalists killed in Gaza before playing a piece at the MSO’s Iwaki Auditorium in August 2024. He had not sought permission from management to make the remarks. Gillham lost the three-week case in June this year, when it was heard in the Federal Court.

“We constantly ask ourselves what a living Australian orchestra must aspire to be,” says MSO CEO Richard Wigley. He says a big part of that is commitment to new music and Australian artistry.



The free concerts at the Sidney Myer Music Bowl will return in summer, the opening of which will be curated by Noongar man and local artist Aaron Wyatt and feature a new work written by William Barton. First Look Seats, which allow people to see shows for $20 a ticket will be back for 2027, as will a program that brings performances to neighbourhoods around Victoria. Aaron Wyatt conducts the 2026 MSO First Nations Showcase. Laura Manariti Next year’s program also celebrates the traditional, showcasing Beethoven, in commemoration of the 200th anniversary of the German composer’s death. In February, chief conductor Jaime Martín opens the season with a program of three works including Beethoven’s Ninth Symphony, featuring the MSO choir with Ode to Joy. He will also lead the MSO in performances of Schubert and Mahler, Mozart and Brahms, Rachmaninov and Dvořák, Mozart and the Mendelssohns and Sibelius and Shostakovich. Martín described next year’s program – his sixth as chief conductor – as “a celebration of the spirit of discovery”, adding that the MSO is a “wonderful group of supremely talented musicians whose every turn of a musical phrase is pure poetry”. Making their Australian debuts with the orchestra are conductors Yutaka Sado (Japan) and Eva Ollikainen (Finland), soprano Claire Booth (UK), violinist Inmo Yang (South Korea) and mezzo-soprano Fleur Barron (UK/Singapore).



International artists on the slate next year include conductors Chloé van Soeterstède (France) and Rodolfo Barráez (Venezuela), acclaimed British pianist Paul Lewis, and MSO’s 2027 featured artist, Romanian pianist Alexandra Dariescu, who will perform across four events. Melbourne-born conductor Nicholas Carter will return as chief guest conductor with the MSO in 2027 Matthias Baus Valley of the Dry Bones, composed by Yitzhak Yedid and narrated by Stan Grant, makes its world premiere, unveiled in June. Featuring the MSO chorus, it is described as a biblical, universal story about conflict. Brett Dean’s The World’s Wife makes its Australian premiere in November, after its first airing at the 2026 BBC Proms. Dean sets Carol Ann Duffy’s poetry to music and reimagines the famous stories of men through a feminine perspective, including figures like Mrs Darwin, Frau Freud, Queen Herod and Anne Hathaway. Melbourne-born conductor Nicholas Carter, who has made his name in Europe, will return as chief guest conductor with the MSO next year. General music director of the Staatsoper and Staatsorchester Stuttgart, he will lead the orchestra in two concerts, Strauss & Schumann in August, and Bruckner’s Eighth Symphony later that month.



Related Article Arts From the Wiggles to the MSO, this creative collective puts the heart in art Carter is looking forward to conducting the monumental Bruckner work. “In our fragmented, anxious and increasingly digital world, this music offers us a rare opportunity to reconnect with the magnificence of the human mind and spirit,” he said. “At times meditative, at others terrifying and intensely dramatic, the symphony gives us the time and space simply to be with ourselves, and to focus on what is beautiful, profound and enriching in our lives.” The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. World.title: Sex worker charged alongside banker committed to stand trial
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCourts Sex worker charged alongside banker committed to stand trial Cloe Read August 10, 2026 — 5:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Brisbane sex worker who was charged alongside a former Sydney-based banker has been committed to stand trial over allegations she tried to procure underage girls for sex. Shauntelle Elizabeth Went will face a District Court trial on charges of using the internet to procure a person under the age of 16 to engage in a sexual act. Former Commonwealth Bank executive Christopher James McCann, 50, allegedly engaged Went, 18, to supply the services of two girls aged 14 or 15, the court earlier heard. Shauntelle Elizabeth Went leaving court on Monday. Brisbane Times / Cloe Read McCann, based in Sydney, frequently travelled interstate, and asked Went whether she had younger friends that she worked with, according to previous court hearings.



The court earlier heard McCann was accused of making an arrangement and agreeing on a price to use Went’s services, alongside two underage girls. Later that evening, Went and the girls attended a five-star hotel in Brisbane’s CBD, the court heard. The girls were not alleged to have entered the room, after McCann contacted the front desk to ask them to leave. McCann was found dead in Springbrook, in the Gold Coast hinterland, two days after he was released on bail in July last year. His death was not suspicious. Carolyn Juratowitch, representing Went for her committal hearing, told the court her client did not wish to enter a plea. Juratowitch also submitted for her client’s bail conditions to be varied, to remove her reporting to police.



“She’s now been on bail in excess of a year. It’s my submission that bail condition is just unnecessary,” she said, adding Went was not a flight risk. “She is, I think because of her mental health, in fairly regular contact with police for welfare checks in any event and I’m asking that be removed simply because it is not necessary.” Christopher James McCann leaving the Brisbane Watch House last year. AAP The court heard Went had been charged twice for breaching her bail. Prosecutor William Orrah told the court that Went had failed to report to police twice, and on the second time, police took her phone for inspection.



Encrypted messaging apps were found on her phone, which were against her bail conditions. “The facts of the offence have to do with using an internet service to be able to procure a child for these sexual acts,” he said. He said the encrypted apps were only found because Went had been reporting to police. The court heard Went had also been charged with wilful damage and threatening violence this year. Magistrate Belinda Merrin ultimately upheld the existing police reporting conditions, saying it was appropriate to ameliorate the risks.



When asked if she had anything to say in relation to the charge, Went answered: “No, your Honour.” She was committed to stand trial in the District Court at a later date. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service (1800RESPECT) on 1800 737 732. If you, or someone you know, needs support you can call Lifeline on 13 11 14 or Beyond Blue on 1300 224 636. World.title: Isaah Yeo’s scans delivered good news. This is when the Panthers hope he can return
World.content:
Updated SportNRLNRL 2026 Isaah Yeo’s scans delivered good news. This is when the Panthers hope he can return Christian Nicolussi Updated August 10, 2026 — 5:57pm ,first published August 10, 2026 — 9:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Penrith are hoping their inspirational co-captain Isaah Yeo can make a swift recovery from a pectoral injury in time for the NRL finals – and possibly as early as round 27 against Wests Tigers – after putting surgery on hold. The Panthers confirmed on Monday Yeo would not require immediate surgery, and said the lock forward had already commenced “rehabilitation in a bid to return to the field during the 2026 NRL season”. Isaah Yeo will avoid surgery and remains an outside chance of returning for the Panthers. Getty Images There were fears Yeo’s season was over after he reeled out of a tackle clutching his pec in the first half of the Panthers’ 28-12 loss to the New Zealand Warriors on Friday night He was spotted with a Game Ready ice compression machine strapped to his right pec at the Panthers Academy on Monday.



A club spokesperson not authorised to speak publicly confirmed Yeo would be given every chance to prove his fitness in time for week one of the finals. An even better scenario, according to the same club source, would be for Yeo to return in the final round of the regular season against Wests Tigers and get a run under his belt before the more rigorous tests in September. Panthers captain Isaah Yeo charges into the Warriors’ defence before injuring his pec on Friday night. Getty Images Yeo has made it known to Panthers officials he hopes to be fit enough to captain Australia at the World Cup in October and early November before going under the knife. The suggestion in the Panthers statement that Yeo would require surgery at some point indicates he suffered a high-grade partial tear or even a rupture, according to several medical sources.



No player in the NRL has returned to play from a ruptured pectoral without surgery. The only player to have overcome a serious tear without the need for surgery was Michael Gordon, who was back in six weeks while playing for the Sydney Roosters in 2017. Related Article Opinion

NRL 2026 Penrith can still win the title without Yeo. Could your team survive loss of its best player? Malcolm Knox Journalist, author and columnist The main problem for Yeo, 31, will not be the pain but his range of movement and effectiveness in the middle of the park. Manly star Tom Trbojevic ruptured his pectoral muscles in 2019 and 2023 and said he flirted with the idea of delaying surgery on the first occasion due to the Sea Eagles being in finals contention and Australia playing Tests against New Zealand and Tonga at the end of that year, but soon realised he was no chance and had the operation. Yeo’s enforced absence from the field will give player and club the chance to hold negotiations over a contract extension. Yeo, the club’s most capped player, remains without a deal beyond 2027, but has made it known he would like to keep playing.



The Panthers host the Sydney Roosters on Thursday night, then travel to Melbourne to face the Storm, who will have Cameron Munster on deck after the match review committee backflipped on a one-match ban and instead handed him a fine for a dangerous tackle. Lindsay Smith is one option to replace Yeo at No.13, along with Isaiah Papali’i and Billy Phillips, while Luron Patea, 21, and 29-year-old Kalani Leuluai-Going are decent middle-forward bench options. Fullback Dylan Edwards is likely to return from a shoulder injury against the Roosters, while Mitch Kenny (foot/ankle) and Casey McLean (hand) are also due back before September starts.
